parole.significato: Synonym of -opia (“seeing”).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὄψις (ópsis, “aspect, appearance”).

parole.significato: examination
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek -οψίᾱ (-opsíā, “sight, view”).

parole.significato: Used to form, from one noun, a second meaning "wide view of" the first, or (with ironic reference to the preceding sens…
parole.testo: Back-formation from panorama and cyclorama (which are modern coinages, not Greek words), and thus from Ancient Greek ὅρᾱμᾰ (hórāmă, “sight”, “spectacle”), in turn evolved from the Proto-Indo-European *wer-, meaning to perceive or look out for.

parole.significato: Related to appetite and eating disorders.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὄρεξις (órexis, “appetite”). Modeled on anorexia.

parole.significato: Smell; odour.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell, scent, odour”).

parole.significato: Having or equipped with a certain feature or structure.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -ωτά (-ōtá), neuter plural of -ωτός (-ōtós), verbal adjective from the stem of -όω (-óō, denominal verb suffix). Related to translingual -ota.

parole.significato: conjoined twins
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πάγος (págos, “fixed, set”), from πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “fasten, fix, set”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns indicating someone with a particular disorder
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

parole.significato: deficiency
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πενῐ́ᾱ (penĭ́ā, “poverty, lack”).

parole.significato: Fixing (in place), fastening.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πῆξις (pêxis).

parole.significato: eating, biting or swallowing
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -φαγία (-phagía) (compare -φάγος (-phágos, “eater”)), suffix corresponding to φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”), infinitive of ἔφαγον (éphagon, “I eat”), which serves as aorist for the defective verb ἐσθίω (esthíō, “I eat”).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from prefixes, to denote diet types
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -φαγία (-phagía), combining form of φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”), infinitive aorist of ἐσθίω (esthíō, “I eat”).

parole.significato: Feeding on; consumption of.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -φαγία (-phagía), combining form of φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”), infinitive aorist of ἐσθίω (esthíō, “I eat”).

parole.significato: Appearing; visible; seeming.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek -φανής (-phanḗs, “having a certain appearance”).

parole.significato: Forms adjectives describing a material's appearance or the conditions under which this appearance changes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -φανής (-phanḗs, “appearing”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “I shine, appear”), compare diaphanous and apophanous.

parole.significato: Concerning a manifestation or (first) appearance.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “I shine, appear”), modelled after terms such as ἐπιφάνεια (epipháneia, “divine manifestation, epiphany”).

parole.significato: Used to form the names of disorders and phenomena relating to words and speech.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “utterance”), from φημί (phēmí, “I say”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns meaning liking, love (for something).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “(fraternal) love”).

parole.significato: Synonym of -philous.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “love”) + -ic. By surface analysis, -phile + -ic.

parole.significato: having an affinity, attraction, preference or love of something
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “love”) + -ous.

parole.significato: liking for
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “(fraternal) love”).

parole.significato: A type of sound.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound, voice, speech, language”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoh₂neh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”); related to fame and fable. Some terms ending in phone, such as textphone, are actually compounds made with phone.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives relating to sound.
parole.testo: Partly from -phone + -ic, and partly from -phony + -ic, ultimately from Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). Attested from the 19th century.

parole.significato: transmission or movement of particles
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek φόρησῐς (phórēsĭs, “an act of bearing, wearing”), from φορέω (phoréō, “to bear repeatedly or habitually; to be carried along”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, action noun suffix).

parole.significato: Forms names of speech disorders.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “speech”).

parole.significato: leaf
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: Having a specified number or kind of leaves.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”) and Latin Latin -ōsus.

parole.significato: Tribehood.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φυλή (phulḗ).

parole.significato: Growth or growing.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis, “growth, I bring forth”).

parole.significato: A member of a taxonomic group of plants or algae, chiefly one whose taxonomic name ends (or ended) in -phyta.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φυτόν (phutón, “plant”).

parole.significato: The contents of a cell.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something molded”); a doublet of plasma and plasm used mostly in biology.

parole.significato: A small body, structure, particle, or granule, especially of living matter.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πλᾰστός (plăstós, “molded, formed”).

parole.significato: Repair or restoration of a part or function.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πλᾰστός (plăstós, “molded, formed”).

parole.significato: paralysis
parole.testo: From paraplegia, from Ancient Greek παραπληγία (paraplēgía), ultimately from πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”). By surface analysis, para- + -plegia.

parole.significato: Indicating the number of homologous sets of chromosomes in a cell.
parole.testo: Back-formation from haploid and diploid. Equivalent to Ancient Greek -πλ(όος) (-pl(óos), “-fold”) + -oid.

parole.significato: breathing, respiration
parole.testo: Representing -πνοια (-pnoia), the common terminal element of the Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia, “apnea”), δύσπνοια (dúspnoia, “dyspnea”), εὔπνοια (eúpnoia, “eupnea”), ὀρθόπνοια (orthópnoia, “orthopnea”), etc, from πνέω (pnéō, “I blow”) and πνοή (pnoḗ, “breath, breathing”).

parole.significato: Related to or resembling a foot or similar limb.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποδός (podós), genitive singular of πούς (poús, “foot, leg”).

parole.significato: footed; having a certain number or type of feet or legs
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

parole.significato: A unit or line consisting of a specified number of metrical feet
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -ποδία (-podía) from πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: production, creation or formation
parole.testo: Suffixed form of poiesis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the number of sellers in a market.
parole.testo: Derived from the root of Ancient Greek πωλέω (pōléō, “I sell”), by analogy with monopoly. Unrelated to poly-.

parole.significato: Forms names of impairments of motor control.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action”), whence also praxis.

parole.significato: wing
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”).

parole.significato: type of leaf
parole.testo: Representing the Ancient Greek πτῐ́λον (ptĭ́lon, “feather”, “down”; “leaf”); in the botanical sense denoting leaves, probably after the French -ptile. Compare ptilo-.

parole.significato: Alteration of -orama, used in suffixing a word ending with an r or vowel sound.
parole.testo: A libfix, a modification of -orama, influenced by diorama and panorama, and thus indirectly derived from Ancient Greek ὅρᾱμᾰ (hórāmă, “sight, spectacle”).

parole.significato: suture
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -ρραφία (-rrhaphía), from ῥάπτω (rháptō, “I sew”).

parole.significato: flowing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥοία (rhoía, “flow, flux”).

parole.significato: Used to make terms denoting an instrument used for viewing or examination.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σκοπέω (skopéō, “examine, inspect, look to or into, consider”).

parole.significato: observation, viewing
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σκοπέω (skopéō, “to see”).

parole.significato: forming nouns of action or process
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek -σις (-sis, “forms noun of action”), often via Latin or French. Identical in meaning with Latin -entia, English -ing.

parole.significato: Body.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”). For the "chromosome" sense, by analogy with chromosome.

parole.significato: wisdom, knowledge, learning
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σοφία (sophía, “knowledge, wisdom”).

parole.significato: Having or relating to a medical condition in -spermia
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -σπερμος (-spermos) [itself from σπέρμα (spérma) + -ος (-os)] (as used, for example, in ἄσπερμος (áspermos)) + -ic.

parole.significato: Having a specified number or type of seeds.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -σπερμος (-spermos) [itself from σπέρμα (spérma) + -ος (-os)] (as used, for example, in ἄσπερμος (áspermos)) + -ous.

parole.significato: Used to refer to things (eg, water layers in the ocean) characterized by their constant physical quantities.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek στάδην (stádēn), meaning "in an upright position"

parole.significato: Forms terms relating to binding behaviors towards enzymes and receptors. See Allostery.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid, three-dimensional”) + -ic. The principal derivations are allosteric and orthosteric.

parole.significato: mouth or mouth-like opening
parole.testo: See Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns indicating a turn or twist of the indicated kind
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “a turn, bend, twist”).

parole.significato: column(s); forming adjectives
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar, column”), or -στῦλος (-stûlos, “columned”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to styles.
parole.testo: From -style + -y (“noun suffix”), from Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”).

parole.significato: grave; burial
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τάφος (táphos, “grave”) as a final member of compounds. Doublet of tapho-.

parole.significato: Ribbon-like structure; Used to form words relating the structure of chromosomes in meiosis
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía, “ribbon, band, fillet”).

parole.significato: used to name types of animal having a specified form of body temperature mechanism
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “warm”).

parole.significato: Relating to heat or temperatures.
parole.testo: Mid 19th century, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “heat”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Placed, positioned, or located in a manner or place (indicated by the first element).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ‑θετικός (‑thetikós) (in, e.g., νομοθετικός (nomothetikós)), from θετικός (thetikós, “that can be placed”).

parole.significato: Forms nouns referring to states of mind.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θυμός (thumós, “spiritedness”)

parole.significato: Forms adjectives from nouns ending with -sis, -o, or -a
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -τικός (-tikós).

parole.significato: An instrument for cutting.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -τομον (-tomon, “that cuts”), from τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”).

parole.significato: A section or segment.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τομή (tomḗ), τόμος (tómos, “a cutting”), from τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”).

parole.significato: Cutting, incision, section
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”).

parole.significato: place, area or region
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”).

parole.significato: Place; position; location; geographic region.
parole.testo: Back-formation from utopia and other words ultimately deriving from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns referring to a surgical procedure involving the crushing, breaking, rubbing, or pulverization of a s…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τρῖψῐς (trîpsĭs, “rubbing, friction”) + -y, from τρίβειν (tríbein, “to rub, thresh, pound, wear out”).

parole.significato: Used to name various electronic and neutronic devices.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek -τρον (-tron), a suffix denoting an instrument, as in Ancient Greek ἄροτρον (árotron, “plow”). The word cyclotron in particular has served as a motivation for use in high-technology terms. Compare also electron (and electronic), which is unrelated to the -τρον suffix.

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting members of classes of organisms distinguished by trophic modes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives corresponding to nouns ending in -trophy
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τροφικός (trophikós, “pertaining to food or nourishment”), from τροφή (trophḗ, “food”).

parole.significato: nutrition
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τροφή (trophḗ, “food, nourishment”), from τρέφω (tréphō, “I congeal, thicken”).

parole.significato: turning, movement; identical in origin to -tropy but more commonly associated with medicine, especially eye conditions.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -τροπίᾱ (-tropíā), from τρόπος (trópos, “a turn”).

parole.significato: Turning or changing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic; tropical; etc.”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”). Compare trope and tropic.

parole.significato: impressed form; stamp; print
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, type”), see type.

parole.significato: A tail.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek οὐρᾱ́ (ourā́, “tail”)..

parole.significato: A technique for working with something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: guest, stranger, host
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξενία (xenía), from ξένος (xénos, “foreign, strange; foreigner, stranger, guest”).

parole.significato: Relating to some specified form of animal existence
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζωϊκός (zōïkós), from ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: Not, without, opposite of.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-), preconsonantal form of ἀν- (an-). Distant doublet of un-.

parole.significato: A trepan having a conical shape so that injurious penetration of the brain is impossible.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀβάπτιστος (abáptistos, “not dipped”).

parole.significato: A loss of the ability to realise or estimate the weight of an object.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βάρος (báros, “weight”) + γνῶσις (gnôsis, “knowledge”).

parole.significato: An enclosure in the temple of Asclepios where patients slept.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄβατον (ábaton), nominalized neuter form of ἄβατος (ábatos, “inaccessible”).

parole.significato: An ancient counting board containing grooves in which counters were placed; a forerunner of the abacus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “board covered with sand”). Doublet of abacus and abaque.

parole.significato: The origination of living organisms from lifeless matter; such genesis as does not involve the action of living parents.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not-”, the alpha privative) + βῐ́ος (bĭ́os, “life”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”)) + γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source; manner of birth; creation”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis (“birth; production”)); equivalent to abio- + gen

parole.significato: The absence of life.
parole.testo: From abio- + -osis; from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not, without, opposite of”), βίος (bíos, “life”), and -ωσις (-ōsis, “action, process, condition”).

parole.significato: Nonliving, inanimate, characterised by the absence of life; of inorganic matter.
parole.testo: First attested in 1874. From a- + biotic, the first element from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-) and the second from Ancient Greek βιωτικός (biōtikós, “of life”), from βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós).

parole.significato: An immunoglobulin G antibody efficient against some protozoans, specifically Trypanosoma lewisi, by preventing reproduc…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄβλαστος (áblastos, “not germinating”) + English -in (“enzyme”).

parole.significato: Lacking a germ or bud.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄβλαστος (áblastos, “not germinating”).

parole.significato: ablepharia
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βλέφαρον (blépharon, “eyelid”).

parole.significato: Lack of sight; blindness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀβλεψία (ablepsía, “blindness”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βλέπω (blépō, “see”).

parole.significato: The congenital absence of both arms
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βραχίων (brakhíōn, “arms”).

parole.significato: acephalobrachia; abrachiocephaly; a congenital absence of arms and head.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βραχίων (brakhíōn, “arm”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + -ia.

parole.significato: A liar or sycophant who boasts of his falsehood.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἀβυδοκόμης (Abudokómēs), after the town Ἄβυδος (Ábudos, “Abydos”), the inhabitants of which were known for inventing slanders and boasting of them.

parole.significato: Rigidity of a joint.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκαμψία (akampsía, “inflexibility”) (from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κάμπτω (kámptō, “bend”)).

parole.significato: A prickle.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A mineral form of silver sulfide, Ag₂S, that is a major ore of silver, that forms slender prisms.
parole.testo: Named in 1855, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”) + -ite, because of the crystal shapes.

parole.significato: Having the fruit covered with spines.
parole.testo: From acantho- (“having thorns”) + -carpous (“relating to fruit”), from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos) and κᾰρπός (kărpós) respectively.

parole.significato: Any of parasitic intestinal worms comprising the phylum Acanthocephala.
parole.testo: From acantho- + Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + -an.

parole.significato: Having spiny branches.
parole.testo: From acantho- + Ancient Greek κλάδος (kládos), + -ous.

parole.significato: A pathological, irregularly spiked red blood cell without central pallor.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”) + κύτος (kútos, “cell”)

parole.significato: A thickening of the horny portion of the skin on the hand palms and soles of the feet.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “bear's foot (plant)”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”)

parole.significato: A cystic tumor that is hereditary and occurs on the chest and face among other regions.
parole.testo: From acanth- + -oma (“tumor consisting of a specified cell”) + from Ancient Greek ἀδενοειδής (adenoeidḗs, “glandular”), from ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”) + Latin cystis (“cyst”).

parole.significato: Spine-bearing .
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “spine”) + -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”).

parole.significato: A skin sign often associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes exhibiting velvety, thickened, and darkened sk…
parole.testo: Via Latin ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorny flower”) + -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”) + Latin nigricans (“blackish”).

parole.significato: Lacking a heart.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκάρδιος (akárdios, “without a heart”) + -ac, after cardiac; by surface analysis, a- + cardi- + -ac.

parole.significato: Synonym of acarid.
parole.testo: From taxonomic name Acaridae + -an, from Ancient Greek ἀκαρί (akarí, “mite”). By surface analysis, acarid + -an.

parole.significato: The study of ticks and mites.
parole.testo: From acaro- + -logy, based on Ancient Greek ἄκαρι (ákari, “cheese mite, tick”) + -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: Not producing fruit; unfruitful; sterile.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἄκαρπος (ákarpos, “fruitless”), from privative ἀ- (a-) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit”).

parole.significato: Incomprehensibility of things; the doctrine held by the ancient skeptic philosophers, that human knowledge never amount…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-) + καταλαμβάνειν (katalambánein, “to seize”).

parole.significato: A Greek liturgical hymn in honour of Mary.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκάθιστος (akáthistos, “not sitting, standing”).

parole.significato: A field of bloodshed, a place of slaughter.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἀκελδαμάχ (Akeldamákh), from Aramaic חקל (“field”) + דמא (“blood”).

parole.significato: Not centered; without a centre.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”, privative prefix) + κέντρο (kéntro, “a point, a center”). By surface analysis, a- + centric.

parole.significato: One of the Acephala.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”). Compare French acéphale, Late Latin acephalus. Doublet of acephalus.

parole.significato: A larval entozoön in the form of a subglobular or oval vesicle, or hydatid, filled with fluid, sometimes found in the t…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”) + κύστις (kústis, “bladder”).

parole.significato: Destitute of tentacles.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: A neuromuscular condition where a ring of muscles is unable to relax fully, causing obstruction of a lumen, as:
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χάλασις (khálasis, “relaxation”), from χαλάω (khaláō, “I loosen”).

parole.significato: lipless
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek χεῖλος (kheîlos, “lip”) with privative a- + -ous.

parole.significato: Without a lip.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χεῖλος (kheîlos, “lip”).

parole.significato: Not possessing a mantle.
parole.testo: From a- (“not”) + Ancient Greek χλᾰμῠ́ς (khlămŭ́s, Latinized form: khlamýd) + -ate, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χλαμύς (khlamús, “cloak, mantle”).

parole.significato: The fear of darkness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀχλύς (akhlús, “darkness”) and -phobia.

parole.significato: Of or relating to achluophobia (a morbid fear of darkness or nightfall).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀχλύς (akhlús, “mist”) and -phobic.

parole.significato: A diminished capacity of any of the hollow viscera (such as the bladder or stomach).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek *ἀχώρησις (*akhṓrēsis), from χωρέω (khōréō, “have room for”). Compare Greek χωρητικότητα (choritikótita, “capacity”).

parole.significato: A colourless form of tourmaline
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄχροος (ákhroos), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χρώς (khrṓs, “color”), + -ite.

parole.significato: Free from color; transmitting light without color-related distortion.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀχρωμάτιστος (akhrōmátistos, “uncolored”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”), equivalent to a- + chromatic; compare French achromatique.

parole.significato: To deprive of colour; to make achromatic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”).

parole.significato: Colorless; achromatic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄχροος (ákhroos) (from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χρώς (khrṓs, “color”)) + -ous.

parole.significato: Dextrin not colorable by iodine.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek privative ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χρώς (khrṓs, “color”) + dextrin.

parole.significato: Operative surgery.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκίς (akís, “point”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: Having the anus located dorsally.
parole.testo: a- + Ancient Greek κλείς (kleís, “collarbone”) + πρωκτός (prōktós, “anus”) (see procto-).

parole.significato: Without inclination or dipping.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκλινής (aklinḗs, “unswerving”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κλίνω (klínō, “bend”).

parole.significato: Any of the order Acoela of xenacoelomorphs that resemble flatworms and were originally classified as such.
parole.testo: From group name Acoela, from Ancient Greek ἄκοιλος (ákoilos, “not hollow”).

parole.significato: An order of fifth-century monks who, by turns, kept up a divine service day and night.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκοιμητής (akoimētḗs, “one who doesn't sleep”), from κοιμάω (koimáō).

parole.significato: licentiousness
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκολασία (akolasía, “licentiousness”), from κολάζω (kolázō, “to check, chastise”).

parole.significato: Materia medica; the science of medical remedies, or of therapeutics.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκος (ákos, “remedy”) + -logy. The first element could be from Proto-Indo-European *Hieh₂ḱ-. Or, less likely, related to Old Irish ícc (“healing, cure”). Or, of Semitic/Egyptian origin.

parole.significato: A fully reciprocal synonym.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, analog”).

parole.significato: Relieving weariness; restorative.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κόπος (kópos, “weariness”).

parole.significato: Not self-intersecting.
parole.testo: Introduced by the mathematician Branko Grünbaum to clarify terminology in the geometry of polygons and polyhedra. From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring the acuteness of the sense of hearing.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκούω (akoúō, “I hear”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The measuring of the power or extent of hearing.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκούω (akoúō, “I hear”) + -metry.

parole.significato: The vascular areas of the body most removed from the heart.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ̆κρᾰ (ăkră), probably back-formed from German Akren as this is more easily encountered and even the English is most likely found in books written by Germans.

parole.significato: The scientific study of grasshoppers and locusts (of the infraorder Acrididea).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκρίς (akrís) + -logy.

parole.significato: One who eats grasshoppers and locusts.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκρίς (akrís) + -phagy.

parole.significato: Any small, non-acid-soluble (i.e. non-carbonate, non-siliceous) organic fossil that cannot be classified.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκριτος (ákritos, “doubtful, indistinguishable”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning, origin”).

parole.significato: Color blindness, achromatopsia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκριτος (ákritos, “indistinguishable”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”) + -acy.

parole.significato: acroamatic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκροατικός (akroatikós, “of or proper to hearing”), from ἀκροᾶσθαι (akroâsthai, “to hear”).

parole.significato: The condition of suffering from a pointed skull.
parole.testo: From acro- + -cephaly, from Ancient Greek ἄκρος (ákros, “highest, on the extremity”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: That run parallel to the edges of the leaf and meet at the tip
parole.testo: acro- + Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “course”)

parole.significato: Producing archegonia from the apical cell of a reproductive branch.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκρος (ákros, “tip”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “female”).

parole.significato: An ancient Greek wooden statue furnished with a rupestral head and limbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀκρόλιθος (akrólithos). By surface analysis, acro- + -lith.

parole.significato: A form of dwarfism characterised by both acromelia and mesomelia
parole.testo: acro- + meso- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ia

parole.significato: The outermost point of the shoulder blade.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκρώμιον (akrṓmion), variant of ἀκρωμία (akrōmía, “acromion”), from ἄκρος (ákros, “summit”) + ὦμ- (ôm-, “shoulder”) + -ιον (-ion, “noun suffix”). Compare -ion, especially in acropodion.

parole.significato: An abnormal protrusion of the navel that sometimes leads to umbilical hernia
parole.testo: acro- + Ancient Greek ὀμφᾰλός (omphălós, “navel”)

parole.significato: The slender section of a flagellum
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “end”) and Ancient Greek νῆμα (nêma, “thread”).

parole.significato: That develops, matures or opens from the base towards the apex in sequence.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “the top”) + Latin petō, petere (“fall, rush out”) + -al.

parole.significato: The naming of letters in an alphabetic writing system using words whose initial sounds are represented by the respectiv…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκρος (ákros, “uppermost, beginning”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). From acro- + -phony.

parole.significato: A promontory (usually fortified with a citadel) forming the hub of many Grecian cities, and around which many were buil…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀκρόπολις (akrópolis), from ἄκρος (ákros, “topmost”, “tip”, “summit”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”); By surface analysis, acro- + -polis.

parole.significato: The end of a verse or psalm, or something added to it, to be sung by the people by way of a response.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκροτελεύτιον (akroteleútion, “extreme end”).

parole.significato: Relating to the extremities of the limbs or to the tip of the nose
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκρωτήριον (akrōtḗrion, “extremity”).

parole.significato: A paraphilia involving sexual attraction toward amputees.
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek ἀκρότομος (akrótomos, “having the top cut off”) + φιλία (philía).

parole.significato: A globular structural protein that polymerizes in a helical fashion to form an actin filament (or microfilament).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκτίς (aktís, “ray”), based on the shape of the filament formed, + -in.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the side or surface around the mouth in an animal that has radial symmetry such as a starfish.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκτίς, ἀκτῖν- (aktís, aktîn-, “ray”) + -al. The usage was coined by Louis Agassiz (See quotations below.).

parole.significato: Related to radiation; used most often in reference to light, especially in the ultraviolet range.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκτίς, ἀκτῖν- (aktís, aktîn-, “ray”) + -ic.

parole.significato: ray, ray-shaped
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκτίς (aktís, “ray”).

parole.significato: Having straight projecting spines
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A bone at the base of a paired fin (of a fish)
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀκτίς (aktís, “ray”) + ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).

parole.significato: A kind of larva of certain hydroids (Tubularia).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκτίς (aktís, “ray”) (genitive ἀκτῖνος (aktînos)) + -ula.

parole.significato: a Julianist sect which stood in opposition to the Ctistolatræ an believed that Jesus shouldn't be spoken of as a create…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄκτιστος (áktistos, “uncreated”)

parole.significato: The measurement of tinnitus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”) + φαίνομαι (phaínomai, “to appear”) + -metry. Compare French acouphène, Italian acufene, Spanish acúfeno, and so on. The expected English spelling would be acouphenometry (cf. acoustic), but this term is mainly used by non-native speakers.

parole.significato: The use of words incompatible with or contrary to the speaker's meaning.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκυρον (ákuron, “incorrect phraseology”).

parole.significato: The quality of being adamant
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas) + -ance.

parole.significato: The property of being adamant.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas) + -ancy.

parole.significato: A crystal characterized by being bound by 48 equal triangles; a hexoctahedron.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “invincible”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “form”). Equivalent to adamant + -oid.

parole.significato: Applied to hydroids' sexual zooids that have a saclike form and do not become free.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄδηλος (ádēlos, “invisible”) + κώδων (kṓdōn, “bell”).

parole.significato: An obscure Christian sect, possibly from the 4th century, which held prohibitions about eating in front of others, eith…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄδηλος (ádēlos, “invisible”) + -φάγος (-phágos, “eater”).

parole.significato: Describing a form of polyandry in which a woman is married to two or more brothers
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀδελφικός (adelphikós, “brotherly”), from ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother”). By surface analysis, adelpho- + -ic.

parole.significato: Related to siblings.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother”)

parole.significato: The brothers and sisters of Jesus Christ, named in the New Testament as James, Joses, Simon, and Jude; unnamed sisters…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἀδελφοί (adelphoí)

parole.significato: The consumption of one embryo by another in utero, particularly among certain amphibians, sharks and fishes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother”) and the suffix -φαγία (-phagía), combining form of φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”). By surface analysis, adelpho- + -phagy.

parole.significato: Fraternisation between men.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀδελφοποίησις (adelphopoíēsis), from ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother”) + ποίησις (poíēsis, “creation”). By surface analysis, adelpho- + -poiesis.

parole.significato: A sister taxon.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother”) + taxon.

parole.significato: Having coalescent or clustered filaments.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Shaped like a gland
parole.testo: From adeno- (from Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”)) + -form.

parole.significato: gland
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”).

parole.significato: Relating to adenocystomas
parole.testo: From adeno- + cystic, from Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”) and Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “bladder”).

parole.significato: greedy, gluttonous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀδηφάγος (adēphágos).

parole.significato: The absence of epidermal ridges (fingerprints and toeprints).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, the alpha privativum, a prefix forming words having a sense opposite to the word or stem to which it is attached; a-) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”) + γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”) + -ία (-ía, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns); analysable as a- + dermato- + glyph + -a.

parole.significato: The division or defective coherence of an organ that is usually whole.
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek δεσμός (desmós, “bonds”) + -y.

parole.significato: Without gain or loss of heat (and thus with no change in entropy, in the quasistatic approximation).
parole.testo: 19th-century coinage (introduced by W. J. M. Rankine in the 1860s) based on Ancient Greek ἀδιάβατος (adiábatos, “impassable”), used of terrain (rivers, forests) by Xenophon, from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + διά (diá, “through”) + βατός (batós, “passable”), from βαίνω (baínō, “to go”).

parole.significato: An expression intended to be understood one way by part of the audience and in an opposing way by another part.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀδιανόητος (adianóētos, “unintelligible, not understanding”).

parole.significato: An indifferent matter.
parole.testo: Neuter of Ancient Greek ἀδιάφορος (adiáphoros, “indifferent”).

parole.significato: indifference
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: Absence of thirst.
parole.testo: From a- + -dipsia, or from Ancient Greek ἄδιψος (ádipsos).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Adonis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἄδωνις (Ádōnis).

parole.significato: A beautiful man.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἄδωνις (Ádōnis).

parole.significato: Lack or loss of strength, usually due to a disease.
parole.testo: From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + -dynamia, from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis) strength, force

parole.significato: Synonym of adytum.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄδυτον (áduton); compare adytum.

parole.significato: A descendant of King Aeacus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Αἰακίδης (Aiakídēs).

parole.significato: Relating to genitalia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek αἰδοῖα (aidoîa, “privy parts, pudenda”).

parole.significato: The wild goat Capra aegagrus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αίγαγρος (aígagros, “wild goat”).

parole.significato: In continuous change.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰόλος (aiólos, “changeful, lively”).

parole.significato: The Gnostic study of aeons.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰωνιολογία (aiōniología, “the study of aeons”), from αἰώνιος (aiṓnios, “eternal, everlasting, endless”) from αἰῶν (aiôn, “lifetime, lifespan, aeon, epoch”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”). By surface analysis, aeon + -logy.

parole.significato: Living or taking place in the air.
parole.testo: From Latin āeri(us) + -al, from Ancient Greek ἀέριος (aérios), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + -ιος (-ios). By surface analysis, aer- (“air”) + -ial.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to aviation.
parole.testo: Back-formation from aero- (prefix), from Ancient Greek ἀέρος (aéros).

parole.significato: air or aircraft
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀέρος (aéros), the genitive singular of ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”).

parole.significato: An air-filled cavity
parole.testo: aero- + Ancient Greek κήλη (kḗlē, “tumour”)

parole.significato: Vaginal gas; air or gas trapped in the vagina.
parole.testo: aero- + Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “bosom, fold, womb”).

parole.significato: An airfield.
parole.testo: * (aircraft): In the obsolete sense of “flying machine” coined by American aviation pioneer Samuel Langley in 1897, from Ancient Greek ἀεροδρόμος (aerodrómos, “traversing the air”). * (airfield): In the sense of “airfield”, from aero- + -drome, a suffix formed in analogy with hippodrome (“horse race

parole.significato: Composed of or containing air and water.
parole.testo: From aero- + Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The observation or examination of the air via specialized organs.
parole.testo: From aero- (“air”) + scepsis (“examination”), from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) and Ancient Greek σκέψις (sképsis, “examination, contemplation”).

parole.significato: The ability to perceive the state of the atmosphere.
parole.testo: From aero- + Ancient Greek σκέψις (sképsis, “a viewing, perception”), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “consider”).

parole.significato: The branch of meteorology that involves the scientific examination of the various properties and composition of the atm…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἁεροσκοπία (haeroskopía, “divination by observing the heavens”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “I examine”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to sensation or perception
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰσθητής (aisthētḗs, “one who perceives”).

parole.significato: sensory
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἴσθησις (aísthēsis, “sensation”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”) + -ic; compare French esthésodique.

parole.significato: Someone who cultivates an unusually high sensitivity to beauty, as in art or nature, often in a manner perceived to pri…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰσθητής (aisthētḗs, “one who perceives”).

parole.significato: A cryptogam; a plant of the obsolete taxonomic class Cryptogamia, having neither stamina nor pistils, and therefore no…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀήθης (aḗthēs, “unusual”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”).

parole.significato: A device for measuring temperature variations due to different atmospheric conditions, such as cloud or clear skies.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “air; ether”) in combination with σκοπέω (skopéō, “examine, inspect”).

parole.significato: The origin and development of a pathological condition (other than an illness)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰτία (aitía, “cause”) + γένεσις (génesis, “creation”).

parole.significato: An afrotherian.
parole.testo: From Afrotheria, from Afro- + Ancient Greek θηρίον (thēríon, “beast”).

parole.significato: Belonging or pertaining to the superorder Afrotheria, which includes the elephants, aardvarks, golden moles, tenrecs, e…
parole.testo: From Afrotheria, from Afro- + Ancient Greek θηρίον (thēríon, “beast”), + -n.

parole.significato: To think about after the fact, reflect on.
parole.testo: Compound of after- + think, probably a calque of Ancient Greek μετάνοια (metánoia).

parole.significato: The soft, aromatic, resinous wood of Aquilaria malaccensis (formerly Aquilaria agallocha).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγάλοχον (agálokhon).

parole.significato: A cult image or votive offering.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγαλμα (ágalma).

parole.significato: A soft, compact stone, of a grayish, greenish, or yellowish color, which was used in China for carvings in pagodas. It…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγαλμα (ágalma, “statue”, stem amalgat-) + -o- + -lite.

parole.significato: The study and practice of the production and allocation of non-scarce goods.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἄγαλμα (ágalma, “votive offering”) + -ics.

parole.significato: Asexual reproduction.
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek γάμος (gámos, “marriage”) + -genesis.

parole.significato: Absence or nonrecognition of marriage, or absence of a pair bond.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄγαμος (ágamos, “unmarried, single (of men)”). From a- (“not”) + -gamy (“marriage”).

parole.significato: An exclamation made out of a sense of deep indignation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγᾰνάκτησῐς (agănáktēsĭs, “physical pain and irritation”).

parole.significato: The love of God for mankind, or the benevolent love of Christians for others.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγάπη (agápē).

parole.significato: Any community characterised by mutual love or free love.
parole.testo: Irregular formation from Hellenistic Ancient Greek ἀγάπη (agápē, “love”) and μονή (monḗ, “abode”).

parole.significato: A plant of genus Agastache, a giant hyssop.
parole.testo: Coined by John Clayton from Ancient Greek ἄγαν (ágan, “very much”) + Ancient Greek στάχυς (stákhus, “ear of grain”)

parole.significato: The doctrine that the ultimate end of all things is good, although the intermediate means may be evil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγαθός (agathós, “good”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A person who believes in agathism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγαθός (agathós, “good”) + -ist.

parole.significato: A benevolent spirit, as opposed to a cacodemon (an evil daemon).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγαθοδαίμων (agathodaímōn).

parole.significato: Composed of both good and evil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγαθός (agathós, “good”) + κακός (kakós, “bad”) + -logical.

parole.significato: Any plant in the large, variable genus Agave of succulent plants, commonly armed with formidable prickles, flowering at…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀγαυή (Agauḗ, “Agave”), from ἀγαυός (agauós, “noble, illustrious”).

parole.significato: Eternal, everlasting.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek αἰώνιος (aiṓnios, “eternal, everlasting, endless”), which is composed of αἰών (aiṓn, “age, eon”) + -ιος (-ios, adjective suffix). First used in Young's Literal Translation.

parole.significato: One who never laughs (especially at jokes); a mirthless person.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγέλαστος (agélastos, “not laughing”), from γελάω (geláō, “to laugh”). Attributed to a French coinage by François Rabelais (ca.1483–1494—1553).

parole.significato: Impotence; sterility.
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek γέννησις (génnēsis, “engendering”).

parole.significato: An outward appearance more youthful than one's true age.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγηρασία (agērasía, “eternal youth”). Compare gero-, athanasy.

parole.significato: Absence of the sense of taste.
parole.testo: From a- (negative prefix) + Ancient Greek γεῦσις (geûsis, “taste”) + -ia. See also γεύω (geúō, “to taste”).

parole.significato: The velar nasal consonant found in such words as song or wink.
parole.testo: From Late Ancient Greek ἆγμα (âgma, “fragment, fracture”), from ἄγνῡμῐ (ágnūmĭ) + -μᾰ (-mă).

parole.significato: The fragmentation of one or more chromosomes (particularly all chromosomes), leading to an increased chromosome number…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγματ- (ágmat-), stem of ἄγμα (ágma, “fragment”) + -o- + -ploidy. Coined by Malheiros-Gardé and Gardé (1950).

parole.significato: An agnathan.
parole.testo: From Agnatha, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without”) + γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”).

parole.significato: An agnathan.
parole.testo: From Agnatha, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without”) + γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”).

parole.significato: Belonging or pertaining to the superclass Agnatha, the jawless vertebrates.
parole.testo: From Agnatha, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without”) + γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”).

parole.significato: A birth defect in which the mandible is missing.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without”) + γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Jawless.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without”) + γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”) + -ic.

parole.significato: The study of things of which cannot be known.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγνοια (ágnoia, “the state of not knowing or perceiving: ignorance, unawareness”) + -ology, from -o- + -logy, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “knowledge”). Coined by Scottish philosopher James Frederick Ferrier.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the absence of set purpose or intention.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + γνώμη (gnṓmē, “thought, purpose”) + -ical.

parole.significato: The inability to recognise objects by use of the senses.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ἀγνωσῐ́ᾱ (agnōsĭ́ā, “ignorance”).

parole.significato: Epistemologically necessary lack of, indifference to, denial or shunning of knowledge; defective knowledge.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without, lacking”) + γνῶσις (gnôsis, “knowledge”), literally, “lacking knowledge”.

parole.significato: Synonym of blindsight.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγνωστος (ágnōstos, “ignorant, not knowing”) (see a- (“not”), gnosis) + -opsia. Literally, "not knowing what one sees". Coined by S. Zeki and D. H. ffytche in 1998.

parole.significato: Doubtful or uncertain about the existence or demonstrability of God or other deity.
parole.testo: Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley in 1870. Either from Ancient Greek ἄγνωστος (ágnōstos, “ignorant, not knowing”), or from a- + Gnostic, deriving (either way) from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “I know”).

parole.significato: A tree, Vitex agnus-castus, formerly believed to preserve chastity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγνος (ágnos), confused with ἁγνός (hagnós, “chaste”) + by reinforcement Latin castus (“chaste”).

parole.significato: In ancient Greek music, tempo or pace; rhythmical movement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγωγή (agōgḗ).

parole.significato: toothless
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγόμφιος (agómphios, “without molars”) (from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + γομφίος (gomphíos, “molar”), from γόμφος (gómphos, “peg”)) + -ious.

parole.significato: A person engaged in a struggle.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a contestant in the public games”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest, struggle”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to contests that were originally participated in by the Ancient Greeks; athletic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγωνιστικός (agōnistikós).

parole.significato: A type of paraphilia or sexual interest characterized by arousal from acts of struggling, fighting, or pretending to re…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ᾰ̓γών (ăgṓn, “struggle”) + -philia.

parole.significato: An officer who presided over the great public games in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγωνοθέτης (agōnothétēs).

parole.significato: A place for gathering.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá).

parole.significato: An elected overseer of the marketplace in the cities of Ancient Greece and the Byzantine Empire.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγορανόμος (agoranómos).

parole.significato: The love of public life, crowds, and activity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “assembly”) + φιλία (philía, “love”).

parole.significato: A revolutionary political philosophy that advocates the creation of a voluntaryist society by means of counter-economic…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “agora (open place for assembly and market)”) + -ism. Coined by Samuel Edward Konkin III in his 1980 New Libertarian Manifesto.

parole.significato: Of, supporting, relating to, or advocating agorism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “agora (open place for assembly and market)”) + -ist. Coined by Samuel Edward Konkin III in his 1980 New Libertarian Manifesto.

parole.significato: Describing a structure in which a hydrogen atom is bonded to both a carbon (or silicon) atom and a metal atom in a thre…
parole.testo: From the supposed Ancient Greek ἀγοστέω (agostéō, “to clasp, hold”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of the sayings of Jesus found in various ancient texts but not in the four Gospels.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́γρᾰφον (ắgrăphon), ᾰ̓́γρᾰφᾰ (ắgrăphă), inflection of ᾰ̓́γρᾰφος (ắgrăphos, “unwritten, not registered”).

parole.significato: Any of several damselflies of the genus Calopteryx (syn. Agrion).
parole.testo: From the neuter, ἄγρῐον (ágrĭon), of Ancient Greek ἄγριος (ágrios, “wild, fierce; living in open fields”).

parole.significato: Any proper name by which a field or other unit of agricultural land is known.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ᾰ̓γρός (ăgrós, “field, tilled land, farm”) + English -onym (“name”)

parole.significato: The scientific description of grasses.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγρώστη (agrṓstē, “grass”) + + -graphy.

parole.significato: The scientific study of grasses.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγρωστις (ágrōstis, “grass”), from ἄγρωστης (ágrōstēs, “farmer”), from ἀγρός (agrós, “field”) + λόγος (lógos, “study, speech, reason”).

parole.significato: Persistent loss of sleep; insomnia; sleeplessness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγρυπνία (agrupnía, “sleeplessness, vigilance”).

parole.significato: The smooth appearance of the brain in cases of lissencephaly.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not, without”) + γῦρος (gûros, “ring, circle”).

parole.significato: The fear of needles and other pointed or sharp objects.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αιχμή (aikhmḗ, “spearhead”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Erotomania.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰδοῖον (aidoîon, “pudendum”) + -mania.

parole.significato: shame, modesty, or humility, regarded as a virtue in Ancient Greece
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek αἰδώς (aidṓs).

parole.significato: Any member of the family †Aigialosauridae of extinct semi-aquatic varanoid lizards.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰγιαλός (aigialós, “seashore”) and -saur.

parole.significato: Cat.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἴλουρος (aílouros, “cat”). By surface analysis, ailur- + -o-.

parole.significato: A person with ailurophilia; a cat-lover.
parole.testo: From ailuro- (“cat”) + -phile (“lover”), from Ancient Greek αἴλουρος (aílouros, “cat”) + φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: A fondness or love for cats or other felines.
parole.testo: From ailuro- (“cat”) + -philia (“love”), from Ancient Greek αἴλουρος (aílouros, “cat”) + φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: Appropriate or pleasing to ailurophiles.
parole.testo: From ailuro- (“cat”, from Ancient Greek αἴλουρος (aílouros)) + -philiac.

parole.significato: Of or relating to ailurophilia or ailurophiles.
parole.testo: From ailuro- (“cat”) + -philic, both from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: An irrational fear or hatred of cats or other felines.
parole.testo: First recorded in 1905. From ailuro- (“cat”) + -phobia (“fear, hatred”), both from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Having or relating to a fear or hatred of cats.
parole.testo: From ailuro- (“cat”) + -phobic, both from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: lauds; a prayer service following matins
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek αἶνοι (aînoi), plural of αἶνος (aînos).

parole.significato: The worship of filth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰσχρός (aiskhrós, “disgraceful”) + λατρεία (latreía, “worship”).

parole.significato: reddish-brown, ruddy
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰθός (aithós, “reddish brown”) + χρώς (khrṓs, “color”).

parole.significato: An origin story or myth in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἴτιον (aítion, “cause”).

parole.significato: A sensation of restlessness characterized by an inability to sit still/down or remain motionless/seated, arising from a…
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek κάθισις (káthisis, “sitting”) + -ia. See also κᾰθῐ́ζω (kăthĭ́zō, “to sit down”).

parole.significato: A hymn dedicated to a saint, holy event, or person of the Holy Trinity, in Eastern Christian traditions.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκάθιστος (akáthistos, “unseated, standing”). Attested in the 1850s (as Akathist and Akathistos), after slightly earlier (1830s) German usage.

parole.significato: The Achaeans.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἀχαιοί (Akhaioí).

parole.significato: Synonym of lithsexual
parole.testo: From akoisexual, itself a common shortening of akoinesexual, which was coined by Tumblr user cisphobeofficial from a- (“lacking, without”) + Ancient Greek κοινή (koinḗ, “common, shared”) + -sexual on 18 May 2014. By metathesis of oi into io, likely due to rebracketing of interconsonantal -o- + -sexu

parole.significato: A rule or precept, especially one of the list of rules laid down by Pythagoras.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄκουσμα (ákousma, “oral instruction”).

parole.significato: Lack of physical or (especially) mental strength; poor willpower; also, the tendency to act contrary to one's better ju…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓κρᾰσῐ́ᾱ (ăkrăsĭ́ā), a variant of ᾰ̓κρᾰ́τειᾰ (ăkrắteiă, “lack of power, debility, impotence; lack of self-control, incontinence; self-indulgence”), from ἀκρατής (akratḗs, “having no authority, powerless; unable to exercise self-control, incontinent”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́

parole.significato: A monoclinic-prismatic reddish brown mineral containing arsenic, hydrogen, magnesium, manganese, and oxygen.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκροχορδών (akrokhordṓn, “wart”) + -ite. By surface analysis, akro- + Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ) + -ite.

parole.significato: The tip of the foreskin which extends beyond the glans.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀκροπόσθιον (akropósthion), from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “tip”) + Ancient Greek πόσθη (pósthē, “penis; foreskin”). By surface analysis, akro- + Ancient Greek πόσθιον (pósthion).

parole.significato: A mineral form of manganese sulfide, MnS, sometimes found in meteorites
parole.testo: From ancient city of Alabanda in modern Turkey, from Ancient Greek Ἀλάβανδα (Alábanda).

parole.significato: A kind of ancient pottery vase used for holding oils, and originally made from alabaster.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρον (alábastron).

parole.significato: A war cry of Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλαλαγμός (alalagmós), from ἀλαλάζω (alalázō), compare Greek αλαλάζω (alalázo).

parole.significato: An avenging spirit or deity, variously associated with the Erinyes, Nemesis, and more.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλάστωρ (alástōr).

parole.significato: A mythical beast resembling a griffin with no wings, often classified as a male griffin.
parole.testo: Possibly from Ancient Greek ἀλκή (alkḗ, “courage, prowess; guard, defense”).

parole.significato: cockfighting
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλεκτορομαχία (alektoromakhía), from ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr) + μάχη (mákhē) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: Cockfighting
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλεκτρυών (alektruṓn), ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “a rooster”) + -machy (a fight).

parole.significato: A practitioner of alectryomancy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλεκτρυών (alektruṓn), ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “a rooster”) + -mancer, equivalent to alectryomancy + -er.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to alectryomancy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλεκτρυών (alektruṓn), ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “a rooster”) + -mantic.

parole.significato: The fear of chickens.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “rooster”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the various modalities of truth, such as the possibility or impossibility of something being true.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλήθεια (alḗtheia, “truth”) + -ic.

parole.significato: The branch of logic dealing with truth and error.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλήθεια (alḗtheia, “truth”) + -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: true, truth
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλήθεια (alḗtheia, “truth”).

parole.significato: The true name of a person.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀληθής (alēthḗs, “true”) and ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”), equivalent to aletho- + -onym.

parole.significato: An instrument, invented in the 1860s, for viewing magnified pictures by means of a single lens inside a box. By varying…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλήθεια (alḗtheia, “truth”) + -scope, equivalent to aletho- + -scope.

parole.significato: Any plant that grows by the wayside or where the natural vegetation has been disrupted.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλήτης (alḗtēs, “wanderer, vagrant”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: of or relating to wheat flour
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλευρον (áleuron, “flour”).

parole.significato: The protein content of the embryo, endosperm, or perisperm of cereals, in the form of minute particles.
parole.testo: 1865/70; from Ancient Greek ἄλευρον (áleuron, “flour, meal”).

parole.significato: An ornamental shrub of species Danae racemosa, in the asparagus family, with glossy leaf-like stems.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δάφνη Ἀλεξανδρεία (dáphnē Alexandreía), from δάφνη (dáphnē, “laurel”) + Ἀλεξανδρεία (Alexandreía, “of Alexander, Alexandrian”).

parole.significato: The inability, due to a cerebral disorder, to comprehend or understand writing.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + λέξις (léxis, “speech”) + -ia.

parole.significato: A deficiency in understanding, processing, or describing emotions.
parole.testo: From a- + lexi + -thymia. Created by psychiatrists John Case Nemiah and Peter Sifneos from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + λέξις (léxis, “speaking”) + θυμός (thumós, “heart”), meaning “without words for emotions”.

parole.significato: A person who has difficulty feeling, processing or understanding emotions
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “speech”) + θυμός (thumós, “soul”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to both pleasure and pain.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + ἡδονή (hēdonḗ) ‘pleasure’. Coined by Henry Rutgers Marshall in 1894.

parole.significato: The scientific study of pleasure and pain responses.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”) + -ics. Coined by Henry Rutgers Marshall in the late 19th century.

parole.significato: Producing or having relation to pain.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek, as if *ἄλγητικός (*álgētikós), from ἀλγεῖν (algeîn, “have pain”).

parole.significato: Painful urination; dysuria.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) and uresis.

parole.significato: pain
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos). By surface analysis, alg- + -o-.

parole.significato: Fear of pain.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Of a class of organic compounds in which the carbon atoms are arranged in an open chain.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Ancient Greek ἄλειφαρ (áleiphar, “oil, ointment”) + -ic.

parole.significato: sausage-shaped
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form; more at allantoid § Etymology and allantois § Etymology.

parole.significato: A sac, having a number of functions, that develops in the alimentary canal of the embryos of mammals, birds and reptile…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἀλλαντοειδής (allantoeidḗs, “sausage-shaped”). Compare Greek αλλαντικό (allantikó).

parole.significato: One another, each other, mutually, reciprocally.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ᾰ̓λλήλων (ăllḗlōn, “one another, each other, mutually, reciprocally”) + -o-.

parole.significato: Synonym of allele.
parole.testo: From allelo- (“other”) + -morph (“shape”), from Ancient Greek ἀλλήλων (allḗlōn, “one another, each other, mutually, reciprocally”) from ἄλλος (állos, “other”). Coined by English biologists William Bateson and Edith Rebecca Saunders in 1902, in a paper titled "The facts of heredity in the light of Me

parole.significato: The relationship between the pleasure associated with a stimulus and the internal state of an organism
parole.testo: Coined by Michel Cabanac and Stylianos Nicolaïdis in 1971. From Ancient Greek ἀλλοῖος (alloîos, “changed, different”) + -esthesia (“sensation”).

parole.significato: thiamine allyl disulfide, a lipid-soluble form of vitamin B1 that occurs naturally in garlic
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγλῑθος (áglīthos) + -amine

parole.significato: Nonself; nonself but of the same species.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”), from Proto-Hellenic *ál͏̌l͏̌os, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos (English else).

parole.significato: Changed in color, as plumage after moulting
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλλόχροος (allókhroos, “changed in color”) (from ἄλλος (állos) + χρώς (khrṓs, “color”)) + -ous.

parole.significato: Originating in a place other than where it is found.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + χθών (khthṓn, “earth, ground”).

parole.significato: A brittle monoclinic sulfosalt mineral of the arsenopyrite group.
parole.testo: allo- (“different”) + Ancient Greek κλάω (kláō, “break”) + -ite, due to its cleavage pattern distinct from that of marcasite.

parole.significato: Relating to or denoting foreign hormones being taken up and eliciting a response in an organism (for example, hormones…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos) + κρίνω (krínō, “separate”). First attested in the late 20th century.

parole.significato: deposited as a sediment from a turbid current
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλλοδαπός (allodapós, “foreign”) + -ic, perhaps on the basis that the sediment originates elsewhere.

parole.significato: Fear of other people's opinions.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”) + -φοβία (-phobía).

parole.significato: The condition of being allopatric.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “different”) + πᾰτρῐ́ς (pătrĭ́s, “fatherland”).

parole.significato: Relating to a race or a language neither Aryan nor Semitic.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + φυλή (phulḗ, “tribe, lineage”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A large, carnivorous dinosaur, of genus Allosaurus, that lived in the Jurassic period.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other, different”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).

parole.significato: the flexible part of the dorsal body wall behind the rigid scutum in a hard tick, particularly a female — the alloscutu…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) and from Latin scūtum (“shield”).

parole.significato: The process of achieving stability, or homeostasis, in the body, through physiological or behavioral change.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos) + στάσις (stásis).

parole.significato: Any form of an element that has a distinctly different molecular structure to another form of the same element, with di…
parole.testo: Back-formation from allotropy, as allo- + -trope, from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”), and τρόπος (trópos, “way, manner”).

parole.significato: A property, exhibited by some elements, of existing in multiple forms with different atomic structures.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek άλλοτροπἱα (állotrophia), from allo- + -tropy, coined by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius.

parole.significato: Capable of causing allœosis; alterative.
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek ἀλλοιωτικός (alloiōtikós, “fit for changing”).

parole.significato: A general lack of additional, unprompted content in normal speech, a common symptom of schizophrenia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλογία (alogía, “absurdity; confusion; irrationality; speechlessness”). By surface analysis, a- + -logia.

parole.significato: Similar to or resembling a fox.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx, “fox”) + -oid.

parole.significato: A Thracian cap made from a fox scalp.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκίς (alōpekís).

parole.significato: The first and last; the beginning and end.
parole.testo: From alpha and omega, first and final letters of the Greek Alphabet, from Revelation 1:8, see quotations. Translation of Ancient Greek τὸ ἄλφα καὶ τὸ ὦ (tò álpha kaì tò ô).

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek method of divination using barley meal, used for instance to reveal guilty parties; it entailed feedin…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀλφῐτόμαντις (alphĭtómantis, “diviner who used barley meal”), from ἄλφῐτον (álphĭton, “barley meal”) and μαντεία (manteía, “prophecy”).

parole.significato: The line of zero luminance in a color space.
parole.testo: Coined by Erwin Schrödinger from Ancient Greek, Literally, “no light”.

parole.significato: catenary
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἅλυσις (hálusis, “chain”).

parole.significato: An official responsible for maintaining order at the ancient Olympic Games.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλυτάρχης (alutárkhēs).

parole.significato: Without long processes.
parole.testo: From a- (“not”) + Ancient Greek μᾰκρός (măkrós, “long”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Outgoing; gregarious.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἅμα (háma, “together”) + ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brotherly”).

parole.significato: Any of very many agaric mushrooms, of the genus Amanita, most of which are very poisonous.
parole.testo: From the genus name, from Ancient Greek ἀμανίτης (amanítēs), mushrooms.

parole.significato: A dark reddish-purple colour.
parole.testo: Coined by Milton, originally meaning "unfading", as amaranth + -ine, from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos, “unfading”). Later used for color. First attested in the 1660s.

parole.significato: Any member of the family Amaryllidaceae; an amaryllidaceous plant.
parole.testo: From the genus name Amaryllis, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀμαρύσσω (amarússō, “dazzle”).

parole.significato: A sexual attraction to darkness or being in the dark, or a partner being blind either through disability or physical re…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμαυρός (amaurós, “dark, blind”) + -philia which is again Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “love, affection”).

parole.significato: Fear of being in or riding in a vehicle.
parole.testo: Formed in English from Ancient Greek ἅμαξα (hámaxa, “waggon”) + -phobia, the latter element itself deriving from the Ancient Greek -φοβία (-phobía). The etymologically consistent spelling is *hamaxophobia, but that spelling is not attested outside word-lists and dictionaries.

parole.significato: A tall, strong, athletic woman.
parole.testo: From Amazon, from Ancient Greek Ἀμαζών (Amazṓn).

parole.significato: An old mechanical contrivance, ascribed to Hippocrates, for reducing dislocations of the shoulder.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄμβη (ámbē, “raised edge”), Ionic form of ἄμβων (ámbōn, “crest, edge”).

parole.significato: Having equal or comparable ability in both hands; in particular, able to write well with both hands.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ambidexter + -ous, the former from ambi- (“both”) + dexter (“right”), thus literally “both hands being like a right hand”. By surface analysis, ambi- (“both”) + dextrous (“skillful; agile”). The Latin word is first attested in the Vetus Latina, calquing Ancient Greek ἀμφοτεροδέξι

parole.significato: Synonym of alembic.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup, cap of a still”). Doublet of alembic and lambic.

parole.significato: Blunt, dull, not sharp, dim.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μβλῠ́ς (ămblŭ́s, “blunt, dull, not sharp, dim”).

parole.significato: Having relatively short and blunt jaws.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμβλύς (amblús, “blunt”) + -gnathous. By surface analysis, ambly- + -gnathous.

parole.significato: An obtuse-angled shape, especially an obtuse triangle.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμβλύς (amblús) + -gon. By surface analysis, ambly- + -gon.

parole.significato: A mineral, a mixed fluoride and aluminophosphate of sodium and lithium that is an important ore of lithium.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμβλύς (amblús, “blunt, dull”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle, corner”) + -ite. By surface analysis, ambly- + -gon + -ite.

parole.significato: A person afflicted with amblyopia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμβλυωπός (ambluōpós). By surface analysis, ambly- + -ope.

parole.significato: One who wishes to excessively modernize churches, particularly by removing traditional screens.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn, “pulpit”) + -o- + -clast. In reference to the rood screen that separated the choir (where priests were) from the nave (where the congregation was) in a medieval church, and from which was sometimes also read.

parole.significato: An early type of photograph in which a glass negative appears positive when displayed on a black background.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄμβροτος (ámbrotos, “immortal”) and τύπος (túpos, “impression”).

parole.significato: The congenital absence of one or more limbs.
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Born without limbs.
parole.testo: From a- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ic; formed in English as an adjectival counterpart to amelia.

parole.significato: A type of asbestos with long, soft, thin fibers.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμίαντος (amíantos, “undefiled”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μιαίνω (miaínō, “I defile”).

parole.significato: amnion; amniotic
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ἀμνῐ́ον (amnĭ́on, “caul, membrane around the fetus”).

parole.significato: A member of the genus Amoeba of unicellular protozoa that moves by means of temporary projections called pseudopodia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμοιβή (amoibḗ, “change”), referring to constantly changing shape of these organisms.

parole.significato: Any species of the genus Amorpha of leguminous shrubs.
parole.testo: From the genus name, Amorpha, from Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (ámorphos, “shapeless, deformed”), because the flowers have only one petal rather than the three of other genera in the subfamily Faboideae.

parole.significato: Lacking a definite form or clear shape.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (ámorphos, “without form, shapeless, deformed”) (itself from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”) + -ous. By surface analysis, a- + -morphous.

parole.significato: vine or grape
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄμπελος (ámpelos, “vine”).

parole.significato: Located on the opposite side of, or referring to two distinct sides or ends of a region or object.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμφίς (amphís), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi (“round about, around”), possibly from *h₂énts, from *h₂ent- (“face, forehead; front”) + *-s. Doublet of ambi-.

parole.significato: Capable of functioning on land or in water.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios), from ἀμφί (amphí) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: The retina.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφιβληστροειδής (amphiblēstroeidḗs, “net-like”), from ἀμφίβληστρον (amphíblēstron, “casting-net”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like”). See retina for more.

parole.significato: A grammatical construction that can be interpreted in two or more different ways; an ambiguous or equivocal statement a…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”), from ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “ambiguous, doubtful”) [citation:5][citation:8]. The form amphibologia appears in Late Latin.

parole.significato: Ambiguity in writing; amphiboly.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”), from ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “ambiguous, doubtful”).

parole.significato: Having both ends concave; biconcave.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφίκοιλος (amphíkoilos, “hollowed on both sides”). By surface analysis, amphi- + -coelous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the amphictyons or their League or Council.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀμφικτυονικός (Amphiktuonikós). By surface analysis, amphictyon + -ic.

parole.significato: A religious foundation or co-operative shared between Greek city states during the classical period, typically to suppo…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφικτυονία (amphiktuonía), from ἀμφί (amphí, “around, near”) + κτίζω (ktízō, “I found, people”).

parole.significato: One of a pair of chemosensory sense organs positioned laterally on the head of a nematode.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφιδέα (amphidéa, “anything that binds or is bound around”), from ἀμφιδέω (amphidéō, “to bind around”) + -ᾱ (-ā, action noun suffix).

parole.significato: That extends in front of, and behind, the beak
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí, “around”) + δέω (déō, “tie”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A figure in which the speaker corrects or qualifies both what has been said and the hearer's potential reaction; a doub…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφιδιόρθωσις (amphidiórthōsis), from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + διά (diá, “through”) + ὀρθόω (orthóō, “to set straight”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greece, a ceremonial feast celebrated on the fifth or seventh day after the birth of a child.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφιδρόμια (amphidrómia).

parole.significato: An ancient Greek postnatal festive ceremony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀμφιδρόμια (amphidrómia).

parole.significato: bisexual (attracted to both males and females).
parole.testo: From amphi- + Ancient Greek γένος (génos, “gender”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The lancelet, particularly of the genus Branchiostoma.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí, “both”) + Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, keen”).

parole.significato: Describing a molecule, such as a detergent, which has both hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups.
parole.testo: From amphi- + Ancient Greek παθικός (pathikós, “remaining passive in a sexual intercourse”), from Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”).

parole.significato: That lives in the tropics (and thus casts shadows northward and southward at different times of the year).
parole.testo: From amphi- (from Ancient Greek ἀμφίς (amphís, “both ways”)) + Ancient Greek σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + -an.

parole.significato: A host or entertainer.
parole.testo: From Amphitryon, from Ancient Greek Ἀμφιτρύων (Amphitrúōn). So named from the portrayal of Amphitryon in Molière's comedy (itself based on Plautus's) as giving a great dinner.

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek unit of liquid measure reckoned as equivalent to about 9 gallons.

parole.significato: A two-handled jar anciently used to hold perfume, etc.

parole.significato: Having the characteristics of both an acid and a base, and capable of reacting as either.

parole.significato: A woman's headband (sometimes of metal), for binding the front hair in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄμπυξ (ámpux).

parole.significato: Shaped like an almond

parole.significato: Of each; an equal quantity.

parole.significato: In a direction analogous to up, but along the additional axis added by the fourth dimension.

parole.significato: up, above, upward
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-), from ἀνά (aná, “on, up, above, throughout”). Doublet of on-.

parole.significato: A military march up-country, especially that of Cyrus the Younger into Asia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνάβασις (anábasis, “a going up, an ascent”), from ἀναβαίνω (anabaínō), from ᾰ̓νᾰ- (ănă-, “up”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go”). parole.significato: rising (up a slope)

parole.significato: The ascending lunar node, where the Moon moves into the northern ecliptic hemisphere.

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which the speaker returns to the original subject after a digression.

parole.significato: That produces vomiting.

parole.significato: A brief restatement or repetition of the principal heads or main points of an argument or discourse; a recapitulation,…

parole.significato: The transportation of foreign bodies via blood or lymph and subsequent collection at a site of inflammation.

parole.significato: Something that is incongruous with the spirit of the country.

parole.significato: an exchange of place between a short syllable and a preceding long one that is frequent in Ionic metres.

parole.significato: Produced by the refraction of light, as seen through water.

parole.significato: A rhetorical device by which a speaker appeals to their hearers or opponents for their opinion on the point or matter i…

parole.significato: A non-reciprocal synonym; a word of meaning similar to a word but that cannot substitute for that word in all uses.

parole.significato: A cyclical theory of political evolution.

parole.significato: That lives in the sea and breeds in fresh water.

parole.significato: The deuterocanonical books, those books present in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew Bible.

parole.significato: An instrument for making accurate engravings of any embossed object, such as a medal.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνάγλυπτος (anágluptos, “wrought in low relief”) (ultimately from γλύφω (glúphō)) + -graph.

parole.significato: The art of copying works in relief, or of engraving as to give the subject an embossed or raised appearance; used in re…

parole.significato: Mystical interpretations or studies, especially of the Scriptures.

parole.significato: To produce an anagram of; to transpose the letters of.

parole.significato: An inventory; a record.

parole.significato: A palace that only hierophants were permitted to enter as part of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνακτόρῐος (anaktórĭos, “belonging to a lord”), from ἀνάκτωρ (anáktōr, “lord”), from ἄναξ (ánax, “lord”).

parole.significato: A sodium aluminosilicate with a chemical formula NaAlSi₂O₆·H₂O, having a zeolite structure, found in alkaline basalts.
parole.testo: Named in 1801 after the property of attaining weak electricity when heated or subjected to friction; from the Ancient Greek ἀνάλκιμος (análkimos, “weak”).

parole.significato: A collection of excerpts or quotes.
