parole.significato: Being or involving a special kind of convex lens for a telescope that reduces the stadia constant to zero.

parole.significato: Part of the habit of a senior monk in the Eastern Orthodox Church, similar to a scapular.

parole.significato: The ability to recall past events; recollection.

parole.significato: A distorted image of an object that may be viewed correctly from a specific angle or with a specific mirror.

parole.significato: Necessity beyond all supplications or sway. Conceived as the ultimate dictator of all fate and circumstances, to which…

parole.significato: Destitute of flowers; flowerless, nonflowering

parole.significato: Tactile anesthesia; the total or partial absence of the sense of touch.

parole.significato: The repetition of a phrase at the beginning of phrases, sentences, or verses, used for emphasis.

parole.significato: Denoting to anarchy and anarchism.

parole.significato: Unusual word order, often involving an inversion of the usual pattern of the sentence.

parole.significato: compound interest
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνατοκισμός (anatokismós), from ἀνα- (ana-) + τοκισμός (tokismós, “usury”).

parole.significato: A thing that is out of its proper place; the geographic counterpart to anachronism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “against”) and τόπος (tópos, “place”), apparently by analogy with anachronism.

parole.significato: Rebutting; overthrowing; defeating; applied to Plato's refutative dialogues.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνατρέπω (anatrépō, “overturn, upset, refute”).

parole.significato: The use of friction or rubbing as therapy, a form of massage
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek ἀνατρῖψις (anatrîpsis, “rubbing up”), ultimately from τρίβω (tríbō, “rub”).

parole.significato: Of the root of a tooth, spongy; porous.
parole.testo: Perhaps ana- + Ancient Greek αὖλαξ (aûlax, “ridge; groove”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root; radix”).

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek tribal chief or leader.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄναξ (ánax). Doublet of wanax.

parole.significato: Almost, nearly, near, nigh, like, resembling.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγχι (ánkhi)

parole.significato: Being or relating to a landlocked body of water with a subterranean connection to the ocean.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγχίαλος (ankhíalos, “near the sea”), from ἄγχι (ánkhi) and ἅλς (háls), + -ine.

parole.significato: Having a composition that crystallizes as a single phase.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγχι (ánkhi) + Ancient Greek εὔτηκτος (eútēktos, “easily melted”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + τήκω (tḗkō, “to melt”). By surface analysis, anchi- + eutectic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to independent or semi-independent bodies of water near to the sea, especially in coastal hollows.
parole.testo: Apparently coined from Ancient Greek ἄγχι (ánkhi, “near”) + ἅλινος (hálinos, “saline”).

parole.significato: Hook-shaped.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγκιστρον (ánkistron) + -oid.

parole.significato: A basic carbonate mineral of strontium and rare earth elements.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγκύλος (ankúlos, “curved”). Analyzable as ancyl- + -ite.

parole.significato: human
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνδρός (andrós), genitive of ἀνήρ (anḗr).

parole.significato: Having masculine reproductive organs.
parole.testo: From andro- + -ecious, from Ancient Greek ἀνήρ (anḗr, “male”) in combination with οἰκία (oikía, “residency”).

parole.significato: A medical condition in which the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen to the tissues is reduced, either because of…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀναιμία (anaimía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, an- + -emia.

parole.significato: wind
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́νεμος (ắnemos, “wind”).

parole.significato: Nostalgia for a time or a place one has never known.
parole.testo: Coined by American author and neologist John Koenig in 2012, whose project, The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, aims to come up with new words for emotions that currently lack words. From Ancient Greek ἄνεμος (ánemos, “wind”) + -oia, extracted from loanwords like paranoia where -νοια (-noia) refers t

parole.significato: Without a brain.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνεγκέφαλος (anenképhalos, “brainless”), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “brain”).

parole.significato: A work with no (known) title; an anepigraphous work.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νεπῐ́γρᾰφος (ănepĭ́grăphos, “without title or inscription”, adjective).

parole.significato: The "uncountable laughter" of ocean waves sparkling in sunlight.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνήριθμον γέλασμα (anḗrithmon gélasma), from Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound (90).

parole.significato: Remission of disease symptoms.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄνεσις (ánesis, “loosening, abatement, remission”).

parole.significato: An abnormal blood-filled swelling of an artery or vein, resulting from a localized weakness in the wall of the vessel.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνεύρυσμα (aneúrusma, “a widening, a dilation”), from ἀνευρύνω (aneurúnō, “to dilate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + εὐρύς (eurús, “wide”).

parole.significato: vessel; relating to blood vessels, lymph vessels, or both.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel, urn, pot”), itself from ἄγγος (ángos, “vessel”).

parole.significato: describing an angiocarpous plant
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “container”) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit, grain”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the clade Angiosperms, characterized by having ovules enclosed in an ovary; a flowering plant.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “receptacle”) + σπέρμα (spérma, “seed”), equivalent to angio- + sperm.

parole.significato: dissection of the blood vessels and lymphatics of the body
parole.testo: From angio- + -tomy (from Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel, urn, pot”) + τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”)).

parole.significato: A Turkish Angora cat.
parole.testo: From the name of the city of Ankara in Turkey, from Ancient Greek ἄγκυρα (ánkura, “anchor”).

parole.significato: Without definite structure.
parole.testo: From an- + Ancient Greek ἱστός (histós, “web, tissue”) -ous.

parole.significato: Having little or no water.
parole.testo: From an- + Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The quality of Jesus Christ's humanity, such that it has its existence entirely from the hypostatic union, rather than…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνῠποστασία (anŭpostasía), from ἀνῠπόστᾰσῐς (anŭpóstăsĭs, “unsubstantiality”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, suffix forming nouns). ἀνῠπόστᾰσῐς is derived from ἀν- (an-) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *n̥- (“un-”)) + ὑπόστᾰσῐς (hupóstăsĭs, “existence; essence; substance”) (from ῠ̔πο-

parole.significato: Pertaining to nonimaging transfer of light, particularly in the domain of indoor natural lighting.
parole.testo: Coined around 1990 (see first quotation), from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “non-”) + Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “figure, representation”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A negatively charged ion.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνιόν (anión, “(thing) going up”), neuter present participle of ἄνειμι (áneimi, “go up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + εἶμι (eîmi, “go”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, an-

parole.significato: unequal; not the same; not the selfsame: forming compounds words; often formed to contrast with similar words in iso-).
parole.testo: Representing a combining form of Ancient Greek ἄνισος (ánisos, “unequal”), equivalent to an- + iso-.

parole.significato: A congenital oral anomaly in which the lingual frenulum is unusually short and thick, decreasing mobility of the tongue…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγκύλος (ankúlos) + γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). By surface analysis, ankylo- + -glossia.

parole.significato: The growing together of bones to form a single unit.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγκύλωσις (ankúlōsis, “a stiffening of the joints”), from ἀγκυλόω (ankulóō, “to crook, bend”), from ἀγκύλος (ankúlos, “bent, crooked”). By surface analysis, ankyl- + -osis.

parole.significato: Hook-shaped; uncinate.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγκυρα (ánkura, “anchor, hook”) + -oid. Cognate with French ancyroïde.

parole.significato: upwards
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄνω (ánō, “upwards, above”).

parole.significato: An electrode, of a cell or other electrically polarized device, through which a positive current of electricity flows i…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) and ὁδός (hodós, “path”), forming the New Greek compound ἄνοδος (ánodos). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, an- (“up, forward, away”) + -ode (“way”).

parole.significato: Extreme mental deficiency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄνοια (ánoia).

parole.significato: Want of proper arrangement; a figure in which words are confused and set without order.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνοικονόμητον (anoikonómēton, “not set in order, without arrangement”), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + οἰκονομέω (oikonoméō, “to arrange, manage”).

parole.significato: A rodent of any species of the family Anomaluridae, having membranes between their front and hind legs like those of a…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “anomalous”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: A raw food diet based on the sensory pleasure instinct.
parole.testo: From an- (“not, without”) + Ancient Greek ὄψον (ópson, “delicacies”) + -ology, from Ancient Greek ἄνοψος (ánopsos, “without relish”).

parole.significato: An intersex condition of XY individuals where both testes are absent at birth.
parole.testo: From an- + Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “testicle”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Characterised by a lack of appetite, especially as suffering from anorexia nervosa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνόρεκτος (anórektos, “without appetite”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὀρέγω (orégō, “to desire”). By surface analysis, an- + orectic.

parole.significato: An eating disorder characterized by self-starvation due to an irrational fear of gaining weight.
parole.testo: From the scientific term anorexia nervosa (1957), from the symptom anorexia (“loss of appetite”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ν- (ăn-, “without”) + ὄρεξις (órexis, “appetite, desire”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

parole.significato: A variety of plagioclase feldspar, the calcium endmember of that series.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αν- (an-, “not”) + ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) "not perpendicular; less than straight", in reference to its odd.

parole.significato: The inability of a person to recognize their own illness or handicap.
parole.testo: From a- (“not”) + noso- (“disease”) + -gnosia (“knowledge”), from Ancient Greek ἁ- (ha-) + νόσος (nósos) + γνῶσις (gnôsis).

parole.significato: A strong natural dislike or hatred; antipathy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “antagonize”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”) (English agon).

parole.significato: To work against; to oppose (especially to incite a reaction).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai), from ἀντι- (anti-) + ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai). By surface analysis, ant- + agon + -ize.

parole.significato: antagonism (opposition, contest)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντᾰγωνίᾱ (antăgōníā).

parole.significato: alleviating pain
parole.testo: From anti- + Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + -ic. Compare French antalgique.

parole.significato: The repeated use of the same word or phrase, but with a different meaning each time; a kind of paronomasia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντανάκλασις (antanáklasis, “reflection, bending back”), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἀνά (aná, “up”) + κλάσις (klásis, “breaking”).

parole.significato: Answering the charge of an adversary by a countercharge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνταναγωγή (antanagōgḗ, “a leading or bringing up”).

parole.significato: Alternating, reciprocal, or continuing subtraction used in the Euclidean algorithm.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνταναίρεσις (antanaíresis), from ἀντί (antí, “opposite”) + ἀναίρεσις (anaíresis, “subtraction”). Used by Aristotle; identified by Alexander of Aphrodisias as Aristotle's term for ἀνθυφαίρεσις (anthuphaíresis, “anthyphairesis”), from ἀνθυφαιρέω (anthuphairéō, “to subtract in turn,

parole.significato: The counterlove or affectionate response a philerast gives to the love of an erastes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντέρως (antérōs), reputedly coined by Plato. That in turn comes from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἔρως (érōs, “love”), hence the translation as counterlove.

parole.significato: A faint, white halo rarely seen in the sky opposite the sun on the parhelic circle
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθήλιον (anthḗlion); see anti-, helio-.

parole.significato: An ornamental design consisting of palmettes or lotus flowers.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθέμιον (anthémion), from ἄνθος (ánthos).

parole.significato: One of the mobile male reproductive bodies in the antheridia of cryptogams.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery”) + ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + -oid.

parole.significato: The event of a flower opening.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἄνθησις (ánthēsis, “flowering”), from ἀνθέω (anthéō), from ἄνθος (ánthos).

parole.significato: A traditional cavalry display in Ancient Athens; in particular, a series of contests occurring later in the democratic…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθιππασία (anthippasía), from ἀντί (antí) + ἱππεύς (hippeús) + -ιον (-ion), literally “knightly-contest”.

parole.significato: Forms words relating to flowers
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A polyp that develops asexually on the skeletons of some coral species.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”) + καυλός (kaulós, “stem”).

parole.significato: A collection of literary works, such as poems or short stories, especially a collection from various authors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”), from ἀνθολογέω (anthologéō, “I gather flowers”), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”) + λέγω (légō, “I gather, pick up, collect”), coined by Meleager of Gadara circa 60 BCE, originally as Στέφανος (στέφανος (stéphanos, “garland”)) to d

parole.significato: A description or definition contrary to that which is given by the opposing party.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθορισμός (anthorismós) from ἀνθορίζω (anthorízō, “make a counterdefinition”) from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

parole.significato: Derivatives of anthracene.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of anthracene, from Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “coal”) + -ene.

parole.significato: Divination by studying burning coals
parole.testo: From anthraco- + -mancy, from Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “coal”) and μαντεία (manteía, “prophecy”).

parole.significato: Any of several artiodactyl ungulates, of the extinct family †Anthracotheriidae, related to the hippopotamus.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Anthracotherium (genus name; see Anthracotherium § Etymology). By surface analysis, anthraco- + -there from Ancient Greek θηρίον (thēríon, “beast”).

parole.significato: An acute infectious disease of herbivores, especially sheep and cattle, caused by Bacillus anthracis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “abscess, boil”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to mankind or humans, or the period of humanity's existence.
parole.testo: Originated 1795–1805, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπικός (ánthrōpikós, “pertaining to human”).

parole.significato: Forming words related to men or people.
parole.testo: Combining form of Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, human”).

parole.significato: An attempt, or an argument attempting, to justify that human beings are fundamentally good despite the commission of ev…
parole.testo: Blend of anthropo- (prefix meaning ‘human beings, people’) + theodicy (“justification of a deity or of particular attributes of a deity; specifically, a justification of the existence of evil and suffering in the world”). Anthropo- is derived from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human being, per

parole.significato: Having characteristics of a human, usually in terms of shape or appearance.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποειδής (anthrōpoeidḗs). By surface analysis, anthrop- + -oid.

parole.significato: divination by the interpretation of human sacrificial entrails.
parole.testo: From anthropo- + -mancy, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, mankind, human, humanity”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: The ascribing of human characteristics and behaviors to nonhuman entities.
parole.testo: Coined in the mid-1700s. From Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, human”) and μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). By surface analysis, anthropo- + -morphism.

parole.significato: Any disease that is spread from humans to animals.
parole.testo: From anthropo- + Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) (compare also nosology); the surface analysis is almost, although not quite, anthropo- + -osis; compare also zoonosis.

parole.significato: The study of personal names.
parole.testo: English anthrop- (“person, human”) + Ancient Greek ὠνυμία (ōnumía) (from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”)); By surface analysis, anthrop- + -onymy = anthropo- + -nymy.

parole.significato: Scientific enquiry aimed at the deduction of the laws that regulate the interactions of the anatomical, biological, and…
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποποιΐα (anthrōpopoiḯa), from ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, human being”) + -ποιία (-poiía, “making”).

parole.significato: A profound fear of human beings, or of human society.
parole.testo: From anthropo- + -phobia. Both elements are borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, human”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”) respectively.

parole.significato: The anatomy or dissection of the human body; androtomy.
parole.testo: From anthropo- + -tomy, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A device in which the author poses an opposing argument, then immediately refutes it.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀνθυποφορά (anthupophorá); see anti- and hypophora.

parole.significato: Against, opposed to.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντι- (anti-, “against”). Cognate with Old English and- (“against, in return, back, un-”), German ent- (“off, away, un-”). Doublet of ante- and un-.

parole.significato: Having the power to eliminate offensive smells.
parole.testo: From anti- + Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A hypothetical Earth on the opposite side of the Sun.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίχθων (antíkhthōn), from ἀντί (antí, “against, opposite”) + χθών (khthṓn, “Earth”).

parole.significato: Those peoples who inhabit the antipodes, regions on opposite sides of the Earth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίχθονες (antíkhthones), plural of ἀντίχθων (antíkhthōn), from χθών (khthṓn, “earth”).

parole.significato: curved in opposite ways in two directions; saddle-shaped
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντί (antí, “opposite”) + κλαστός (klastós, “broken in pieces”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Waterproof leggings.
parole.testo: From anti- + Ancient Greek ὑγρός (hugrós, “wet”) πηλός (pēlós, “mud”).

parole.significato: Certain books of the New Testament which were for a time not universally received, but which are now considered canonic…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντιλεγόμενα (antilegómena), from ἀντι- (anti-, “against”) + λέγω (légō, “to speak”).

parole.significato: Of the contrary name or character; opposite.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίλογος (antílogos).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to the magnetic pole that becomes negative as its temperature increases and positive as its temperatur…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀντίλογος (antílogos, “contradictory, reverse”), from ἀντιλέγω (antilégō, “speak against, gainsay, contradict”). Equivalent to anti- + -logue.

parole.significato: The technique of repeating a phrase while reversing the order of certain elements or its grammatical structure, as a fo…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντιμεταβολή (antimetabolḗ). By surface analysis, anti- (“opposite”) + Ancient Greek μετᾰβολή (metăbolḗ, “transformation”).

parole.significato: A rectangular piece of linen or silk, usually decorated with religious emblems and inscriptions, and containing a small…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἀντιμήνσιον (Antimḗnsion).

parole.significato: Of birds: having a zygodactylous foot with one tendon to flex the third toe and another, trifurcate tendon to flex the…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίος (antíos, “opposed”) + πέλμα (pélma, “sole of the foot”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Synonym of antipathic.
parole.testo: Irregularly from either antipathy or Ancient Greek ἀντιπαθής (antipathḗs) + -ous.

parole.significato: Substitution of one grammatical case for another.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίπτωσις (antíptōsis).

parole.significato: A discrediting or rejection of an authority.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίρρησις (antírrhēsis, “altercation”)

parole.significato: The mirror image, or shadow, of a planet, based upon a line of reference which is the axis of 0 Cancer/0 Capricorn (the…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίσκιον (antískion), from ἀντι- (anti-, “opposite”) + σκιά (skiá, “shadow”).

parole.significato: An unattested Claudian letter, possibly resembling Ↄ or ↃC.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ντῐ́σῑγμᾰ (ăntĭ́sīgmă).

parole.significato: The repetition of a word in an opposing sense.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίστασις (antístasis).

parole.significato: A counterargument as a retort
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίστροφος (antístrophos, “turned towards each other”), from στρέφω (stréphō).

parole.significato: Something that is symbolized or represented by a type, such as Christ by the Paschal Lamb; the fulfillment of a type.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀντίτυπος (antítupos).

parole.significato: resistant to blows; hard
parole.testo: From anti- + Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “a blow”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The fear of floods or inundation.
parole.testo: Presumably from Ancient Greek ἄντλος (ántlos, “hold of a ship; bilgewater”), also defined in LSJ as "a flood of water" + -phobia.

parole.significato: A particular ode sung in response to another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀντῳδή (antōidḗ), from ᾠδή (ōidḗ).

parole.significato: An idea which is discovered to be true in itself, or which supports itself; that which is absolutely or necessarily tru…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ανυπόθετον (anupótheton), negation of Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”, literally “a placing under”), itself from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I put, place”).

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek bard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀοιδός (aoidós).

parole.significato: A verb paradigm found in certain languages, usually an unmarked form or one that expresses the perfective or aorist asp…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀόριστος (aóristos, “unbounded”).

parole.significato: The great artery which carries the blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs; the main trunk of th…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ, “the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω (aortéō), lengthened form of ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”).

parole.significato: An indirect argument which proves a thing by showing the impossibility or absurdity of the contrary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀπαγωγή (apagōgḗ).

parole.significato: Any of several species of birds in the genus Apalis.
parole.testo: From the genus name Apalis, from Ancient Greek ἁπαλός (hapalós, “delicate, tender”).

parole.significato: The broadening of the ambit of one’s preoccupations and concerns away from a narrow focus on those things most palpably…
parole.testo: Coined by C. Grant B. Allen in 1880 in volume 5 of the quarterly-review journal Mind : Ap- (from Ancient Greek ἀπ- (ap-, “off, away”)) + anthropinism (“human-focused consideration”) + -isation, noun suffix denoting the action of the suffixed verb. See also apanthropy.

parole.significato: A word formed by removing the end of a longer word.

parole.significato: A copy or transcript of a manuscript (called the antigraph).

parole.significato: In an orbit around the planet Mercury, the point that is most distant from Mercury.

parole.significato: Identifying a molecular position in an organic chemical compound.

parole.significato: Ipe (kind of wood).

parole.significato: book

parole.significato: The use of books.

parole.significato: A person who steals books.

parole.significato: The study of the history of books and the art of printing.

parole.significato: A person who loves to read books; a bookworm.

parole.significato: The making of books.

parole.significato: Budding or growth of new mineral crystals in solid rock.

parole.significato: bud; budding; germination
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek βλαστός (blastós, “a germ, bud, sprout, shoot”), from βλαστάνω (blastánō, “to bud, sprout, grow, properly of plants, but also of animals”).

parole.significato: Being in the centre; central.

parole.significato: Relating to the centre of gravity or the process of finding it.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: A pain in the head; headache.

parole.significato: Headache.

parole.significato: Relating to the head; sometimes, particularly, the brain.

parole.significato: Any of a group of saints depicted in art carrying heads in their hands.

parole.significato: A surgical instrument for performing cephalotripsy.

parole.significato: Having a head; applied chiefly to the former division of mollusks Cephalata, or Cephalophora (mollusks with a head).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the tail.

parole.significato: Any of several marine worms of the phylum Chaetognatha.

parole.significato: A fungal spore produced asexually in a conidiophore.

parole.significato: A magnesian variety of dolomite.

parole.significato: Relating to excrement or dung.

parole.significato: A fear of feces.

parole.significato: An offering to God, especially in fulfilment of a vow.

parole.significato: A lascivious dance featuring in Ancient Greek comedy.

parole.significato: A corm.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk of a tree with the boughs cut off”), from κείρω (keírō, “shear”).

parole.significato: A kind of frenzy in which the patient is tormented by fantastic visions and lack of sleep.

parole.significato: Of or from or pertaining to the cosmos or universe.

parole.significato: A ruler of the entire world or cosmos.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek κοσμοκράτωρ (kosmokrátōr, “cosmocrator”), from κόσμος (kósmos, “universe”) + κράτωρ (krátōr, “ruler”).

parole.significato: The creation of maps of the universe.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to croconic acid or its derivatives.

parole.significato: dark blue-green in colour

parole.significato: A person with fair hair and brown eyes.

parole.significato: A delusion in which a person believes he or she is transformed into a dog.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the belief that human actions are motivated only or primarily by base desires or selfishness.

parole.significato: Any of several small carnivorous synapsids in the clade Cynodontia, ancestral to mammals and extinct close relatives.

parole.significato: A long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), native to Asia, that feeds on shellfish.

Apparently from a word coined by Aristophanes of Byzantium for a race of humans with long hair and beards who hunted with dogs and, according to Aristophanes, milked them. (See Crab-eating macaque on Wikipedia.Wikipedia ).

parole.significato: The larva of an ectoproct or bryozoan.

parole.significato: The protoplasm, out of which life was thought to arise.

parole.significato: The chief magistrate of a deme.

parole.significato: A township or other subdivision of ancient Attica.

parole.significato: Member of a demogerontia.

parole.significato: The area of knowledge relating to the care and culture of the people; sociology in its broadest sense.

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek mixing-bowl or cauldron, without handles or feet.

parole.significato: An electronic device that allows current to flow in one direction only; used chiefly as a rectifier.
parole.testo: From di- (“two”) + -ode. Learned formation, coined by William Henry Eccles in 1919, after Ancient Greek δίοδος (díodos, “passage through”), which however is formed not with δι- (di-, “two”) but with δια- (dia-, “through”).

parole.significato: The condition of being dioecious, namely having separate sexes, especially of plants.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δι- (di-, “twice”) + οἰκία (oikía, “house, family, tribe”).

parole.significato: The irrational fear of being chased, regardless of the pursuer or the potential danger.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διώκω (diṓkō, “to pursue, chase”) + -phobia. Coined online in 2018.

parole.significato: Any of the ancient festivals held in honour of the Olympian god Dionysus, and corresponding to the Roman Bacchanalia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Διονῡ́σια n pl (Dionū́sia), from Διόνῡσος (Diónūsos, “Dionysus”).

parole.significato: logical distinction; definition
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διορισμός (diorismós), from διορίζω (diorízō, “to delimit, distinguish”).

parole.significato: corrective.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διορθωτικός (diorthōtikós, “corrective”), from ὀρθόω (orthóō, “set straight”).

parole.significato: double, twofold
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διφυ- (diphu-), from διφυής (diphuḗs, “double”).

parole.significato: Describing a symmetric tailfin in which the vertebral column extends to the tip.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διφυής (diphuḗs, “of double nature”) (compare δι- (di-) and φύω (phúō)) + κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).

parole.significato: Having two modes of embryonic development.
parole.testo: Of diphy- + -genic, from Ancient Greek διφυής (diphuḗs, “double”) and -γενής (-genḗs, “offspring”)

parole.significato: Having two leaves.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίφυλλος (díphullos) [from φύλλον (phúllon)] + -ous; compare French diphylle. By surface analysis, di- + -phyllous.

parole.significato: Having two successive sets of teeth (deciduous and permanent), one succeeding the other.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διφυής (diphuḗs, “double”) + ὀδόντος (odóntos) (genitive of ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”)).

parole.significato: The condition, in some animals, of having only one set of replacement teeth following a first erupted set.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek διφυής (diphuḗs, “double”) + ὀδόντος (odóntos) (genitive of ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”)).

parole.significato: One of the free-swimming sexual zooids of Siphonophorae.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διφυής (diphuḗs, “double”) + English zooid.

parole.significato: A mark > once used in margins to draw attention to an important passage in a text.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διπλῆ (diplê), from διπλοῦς (diploûs).

parole.significato: Any of several herbivorous sauropod dinosaurs, of the genus Diplodocus, known as fossils from the late Jurassic in Nort…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διπλόος (diplóos, “double”) + δοκός (dokós, “beam”).

parole.significato: The thin layer of soft, spongy, or cancellate tissue between the bone plates which constitute the skull.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διπλόη (diplóē, “literally, a fold”), noun use of feminine of διπλόος (diplóos, “double”).

parole.significato: A part of the peplos whipped over the shoulders.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διπλοΐδιον (diploḯdion), ultimately from διπλόος (diplóos).

parole.significato: The thin layer of soft, spongy or cancellate tissue between the bone plates which constitute the skull.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διπλόη (diplóē, “literally, a fold”), noun use of feminine of διπλόος (diplóos, “double”).

parole.significato: A unit of two metrical feet.
parole.testo: From di- + -pody, from Ancient Greek δι- (di-, “two”) and πούς, ποδός (poús, podós, “foot”).

parole.significato: A condition in which part of the face is duplicated on the head.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face”). By surface analysis, di- (“two”) + prosop- + Latin -us.

parole.significato: Abnormal or excessive thirst; hyperdipsia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίψησις (dípsēsis), from διψάω (dipsáō).

parole.significato: Tending to produce thirst.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: thirst; drinking
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίψα (dípsa, “thirst”).

parole.significato: The study of the thirst for alcoholic beverages.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίψα (dípsa, “thirst”) + -logy.

parole.significato: A building with double peristyle or colonnade.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίπτερος (dípteros).

parole.significato: A type of scapolite (mineral).
parole.testo: From di- + Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”); so called from the double effect of fire upon it, in fusing it and rendering it phosphorescent.

parole.significato: Involving or possessing two nostrils.
parole.testo: From di- + Ancient Greek ῥίς (rhís, “nose”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A word that occurs only twice in a given corpus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δὶς λεγόμενον (dìs legómenon, “(something) said only twice”), from δίς (dís, “twice, doubly, again”) and λεγόμενον (legómenon), passive participle of λέγω (légō).

parole.significato: Having a flat, rounded shape.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disc”) + -form

parole.significato: A discus thrower.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δισκοβόλος (diskobólos, “discus thrower”), from δίσκος (dískos, “discus”) + βάλλω (bállō, “throw”).

parole.significato: To harrow.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “a circular plate suited for hurling”), from δικέω (dikéō, “to hurl, to launch”). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, discus, dish, and diskos.

parole.significato: A small plate used to hold eucharistic bread which is to be consecrated; a paten.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos) (nominative plural δίσκοι (dískoi)). Doublet of dais, desk, disc, discus, dish, and disk.

parole.significato: In phytogeography, a plant of which the subterranean parts are adapted to mesophytic or even hydrophytic conditions, an…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek δισσός (dissós, “double”) + -phyte (“plant”)

parole.significato: Having two ears or spikes.
parole.testo: From di- + Ancient Greek στάχυς (stákhus, “ear of wheat”).

parole.significato: Kyanite.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek twice + force: compare French disthène. So called in allusion to its unequal hardness in two different directions, or from its positive and negative electric properties.

parole.significato: The splitting of the distal ends of the hair.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δίς (dís, “apart”) + θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

parole.significato: Having two kinds of young, such as offspring from asexual reproduction versus those from sexual reproduction.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek δίς (dís, “twice”) + τόκος (tókos, “a bringing forth, offspring”).

parole.significato: Synonym of dittography (“erroneous repetition in a text”).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διττός (dittós, “double”) + -gram.

parole.significato: The accidental error of repeating a word, phrase or combination of letters by a scribe or copyist.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek διττός (dittós, “double”) + -graphy. Not related to English ditto.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or containing, the dochmius.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δοχμιακός (dokhmiakós, “dochmiac”), from δόχμιος (dókhmios) (see dochmius).

parole.significato: of, or relating to an experiment, test or assay
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δοκιμαστικός (dokimastikós), from δοκιμάζω (dokimázō) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: The art by which the nature and proportions of an ore are determined; assaying.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δοκιμασία (dokimasía, “examination”).

parole.significato: Prevocalic form of docosa- (“twenty-two”).
parole.testo: From do- + -cos-, from Ancient Greek δώδεκα (dṓdeka) and Latinized form of Ancient Greek εἴκοσι (eíkosi, “twenty”).

parole.significato: twenty-two
parole.testo: From IUPAC do- (ultimately from Ancient Greek δώδεκα (dṓdeka, “twelve”)) + -cosa- (ultimately from Ancient Greek εἴκοσι (eíkosi, “twenty”)).

parole.significato: twelve
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δώδεκα (dṓdeka, “twelve”).

parole.significato: The duodenum.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δωδεκαδάκτυλον (dōdekadáktulon), from δώδεκα (dṓdeka, “twelve”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”) ≅ “twelve-fingers[-long thing]”; compare English duodenum and German Zwölffingerdarm; cognate with Greek δωδεκαδάκτυλο (dodekadáktylo) and Italian dodecadattilo.

parole.significato: A polyhedron with twelve faces; the regular dodecahedron has regular pentagons as faces and is one of the Platonic soli…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δωδεκάεδρον (dōdekáedron). Equivalent to dodeca- + -hedron.

parole.significato: A practitioner or proponent of dodecaphony, i.e. use of the dodecaphonic musical scale, which has twelve tones per octa…
parole.testo: International word formed circa 1950 from Ancient Greek δώδεκα (dṓdeka, “twelve”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”) + -ist, recorded in English since 1953, presumably modeled on German Dodekaphonist.

parole.significato: A member of a group of twelve rulers
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δωδεκάρχης (dōdekárkhēs). By surface analysis, dodec- + -arch.

parole.significato: A twelfth, specifically each of the twelve divisions of the Zodiac.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δωδεκατημόριον (dōdekatēmórion), from δωδέκατος (dōdékatos, “twelfth”) + μόριον (mórion, “piece”).

parole.significato: A gymnastics competition comprising twelve subcompetitions.
parole.testo: Seemingly from Ancient Greek δωδέκαθλος (dōdékathlos, “twelve labors”), referring to the twelve labors of Hercules.

parole.significato: long
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δολιχός (dolikhós).

parole.significato: A long-distance race in the ancient Olympic Games.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δόλιχος (dólikhos).

parole.significato: The art of putting one's foot in one's mouth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”) and pes (“foot”), + -logy. Purportedly coined in 1960 by Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh.

parole.significato: The fear of touching the fur or skin of an animal.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δορά (dorá, “skin, hide”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: A member of a Dorcas association.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Δορκάς (Dorkás, “gazelle”), translation of Tabitha in the Bible.

parole.significato: Relating to one of the Greek orders of architecture, distinguished by its simplicity and solidity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Δωρικός (Dōrikós, “related to Dorians”). The senses referring to dialects of Scottish are thought to have come from the Scots’ rusticness associated with the Athenians’ view of Dorians as uncivilised.

parole.significato: One's girlfriend, wife or significant other.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Δωρίς (Dōrís). Etymology 1 sense 7 is owing to similarity to Boris.

parole.significato: An unusual urge or preoccupation with giving gifts.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek δῶρον (dôron, “gift”) + -mania.

parole.significato: A wooden pike or spear about three metres (ten feet) in length with a flat, leaf-shaped iron spearhead and a bronze but…
parole.testo: PIE word  *dóru Borrowed from Ancient Greek δόρυ (dóru).

parole.significato: Popular opinion or belief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δόξα (dóxa).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or depending on opinion or belief.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δοξασία (doxasía, “belief, opinion, conviction”).

parole.significato: Induced by one's own ideas or beliefs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δόξα (dóxa, “opinion, belief”) + -o- + -genic.

parole.significato: Common bistort, a perennial herb of Europe and Asia, of species Bistorta officinalis (syns. Persicaria bistorta, Polygo…
parole.testo: From dragon + wort. Compare Middle English dragaunce, dragunce, dragance, dragans (“dragonwort”), from Old French dragonce, dragance, from Medieval Latin draguncia, dragancia (“dragonwort”), disfigured from the plural of dracontium (“dragonwort”), from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion, “dragonwo

parole.significato: The practice of viewing all symptoms as valid communications, including words, posture, tone of voice, and movements of…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “an act, a theatrical act, a play”), and -ology, -λογία (-logía, “study of”).

parole.significato: The desire of slaves to run away, viewed as a mental illness.
parole.testo: Coined in 1851 by Samuel A. Cartwright as a name for a supposed mental illness that caused black slaves to flee captivity. Ancient Greek δραπέτης (drapétēs, “runaway slave”) + μανία (manía, “madness”).

parole.significato: Having a strong or far-reaching effect; extreme, severe.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δραστικός (drastikós, “active, efficient”), from δρᾶσις (drâsis, “strength, efficacy”), itself from δράω (dráō, “to do”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sickle-cell disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δρεπάνη (drepánē) and English cytosis, the latter also borrowed from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: An exact, nonlinear solution of any of a large class of two-dimensional partial differential equations
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “race-track”) + -on (“particle”), confer soliton.

parole.significato: Speed, race, or racecourse.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “a course, race course, road”).

parole.significato: A Byzantine bireme, similar to the chelandion, but used primarily for naval combat.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρόμων (drómōn).

parole.significato: An avenue, especially in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “running; racetrack”).

parole.significato: Affecting the conductivity of cardiac muscle, used of the influence of cardiac nerves.
parole.testo: From dromo- (“course, speed”) + -tropic (“affecting, changing”), from Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “course, race”) + τρόπος (trópos, “turn, direction, way”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A device for measuring the amount of dew on a surface.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρόσος (drósos, “dew”) + -meter.

parole.significato: A South Slavic group who settled in the Balkans in the 7th century.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Δρουγουβῖται (Drougoubîtai).

parole.significato: A kind of military commander in the late Roman and Byzantine Empires, usually commanding roughly a battalion on land or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δρουγγάριος (droungários), from Late Latin drungārius, from drungus (“a troop”).

parole.significato: A government where servants and slaves have so much license and privilege that they domineer; predominance of slaves.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δουλοκρατία (doulokratía), from δοῦλος (doûlos, “servant, slave, thrall”) + κρατέω (kratéō, “rule”).

parole.significato: The process by which parasitic ants steal pupae from the nests of other ants and raise them in their own nest, so that…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δούλωσις (doúlōsis, “enslavement”).

parole.significato: A set of two elements treated as one; a pair.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυάς (duás), δυάδ- (duád-) from δύο (dúo, “two”), from Proto-Indo-European *duwó, *duwéh₃ (*dwóh₁). The mathematics sense was coined by American scientist Josiah Willard Gibbs in 1884 in the second half of his book Elements of Vector Analysis.

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring the intensity of photogenic rays and computing the power of object glasses.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “force”) + actino- + -meter.

parole.significato: Potentiality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis).

parole.significato: Great energy, drive, force, or power; vigour of body, mind, or personality; oomph or pizzazz.
parole.testo: From English dynam(ic) (or directly from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”)) + ism.

parole.significato: A class of explosives made from nitroglycerine in an absorbent medium such as kieselguhr, used in mining and blasting.
parole.testo: Coined by Alfred Nobel in 1867. Ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”) + -ite, most likely under the influence of dynamo or dynamic.

parole.significato: Characterized by movement or change; dynamic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, “powerful”), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “I am able”).

parole.significato: An electricity generator; a dynamo-electric machine.
parole.testo: A shortening of dynamo-electric machine. The element dynamo- is ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”).

parole.significato: power, usually physical.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, “powerful”), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “I am able”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a dynasty.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυναστικός (dunastikós). By surface analysis, dynasty + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of a group of enzymes that hydrolyze ATP and thus provide motive power for motile structures such as microtubules.
parole.testo: From dyne + -in, from the Ancient Greek δῠ́νᾰμῐς (dŭ́nămĭs, “force”).

parole.significato: Any of a series of electrodes within a photomultiplier tube.
parole.testo: From 1939 from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power, might, strength”) + -ode. By surface analysis, dyne + -ode.

parole.significato: Someone who believes in the doctrine that there are ‘two natures’, human and divine, in Christ.
parole.testo: From ecclesiastical Ancient Greek δυοφυσῖται (duophusîtai), from δύο (dúo, “two”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature”).

parole.significato: Unhealthy condition of blood.
parole.testo: From dys- + -æmia, from Ancient Greek: δυσ- (dus-, “bad, unfortunate”) in combination with αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: A medical condition caused by microbial imbalances within the body.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) and βίωσις (bíōsis, “way of living”); the intended meaning of the compound word is contrasted with symbiosis - a relationship of mutual benefit. By surface analysis, dys- + -biosis.

parole.significato: A learning disability characterized by significantly below average mathematical ability.
parole.testo: From dys- (from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”)) + calculate (from Latin calculare).

parole.significato: Imbalance of the four bodily humors (blood, black and yellow bile, phlegm) that was thought to cause disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δυσκρασία (duskrasía, “bad mixture”).

parole.significato: A neurological sign where a person has difficulty performing rapid, alternating movements, usually indicating cerebella…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-) + διάδοχος (diádokhos) + κίνησις (kínēsis) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: A variety of the zinc spinel or gahnite.
parole.testo: From dys- + Ancient Greek λύω (lúō) + -ite.

parole.significato: Any congenital disorder of the limbs, such as amelia or syndactyly.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek δῠσ- (dŭs-, “bad”) + μέλος (mélos, “limb”).

parole.significato: An inability to control or to limit muscular movement.
parole.testo: 1910-1915. Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δυσμετρία (dusmetría), from δυσ- (dus-) + μέτρον (métron) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: dysmorphism
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυσμορφίᾱ (dusmorphíā, “misshapenness, ugliness”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad, mal-”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “shape, form”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). Note that sense 2 is a semantic extension from "physical deformity" to a disorder of the perception of one’s bodily form. By surface analysis, dys- + -morp

parole.significato: A soft, finely laminated, greenish or yellowish-grey impure earthy or coaly bitumen, which emits a highly foetid odour…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δῠσώδης (dŭsṓdēs, “ill-smelling”), from δῠσ- (dŭs-) + ὄζω (ózō, “smell”), + -ile.

parole.significato: A disorder of the development of bone.
parole.testo: From dys- + Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”) + -osis.

parole.significato: Painful or difficult sexual intercourse, especially in women.
parole.testo: From dys- + Ancient Greek πάρευνος (páreunos, “lying beside, lying with”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Any mild disorder of digestion characterised by stomach pain, discomfort, heartburn, and nausea, often following a meal.
parole.testo: From dys- + Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or having dyspepsia or indigestion.
parole.testo: First attested in 1694. From Ancient Greek δύσπεπτος (dúspeptos, “difficult to digest”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + πέπτω (péptō, “to digest”).

parole.significato: A difficulty in producing vocal sounds.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “ill, hard”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound, voice”), equivalent to dys- + -phonia.

parole.significato: An agent which can create a state of feeling unwell or unhappy; a stimulus of feeling(s) of emotional and mental discom…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυσφορία (dusphoría, “excessive pain”), from δύσφορος (dúsphoros, “grievous”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + φέρω (phérō, “I bear, carry”).

parole.significato: A tendency to be depressed, without hope.
parole.testo: From dys- + -thymia. From Ancient Greek δυσθυμία (dusthumía, “despondency, despair; ill-temper”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + θυμός (thumós, “soul, spirit”).

parole.significato: A slow or difficult labour or delivery.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυστοκία (dustokía, “difficult childbirth”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + τόκος (tókos, “childbirth”), from τίκτω (tíktō, “I give birth”).

parole.significato: Having imperfect fracture or cleavage.
parole.testo: From dys- (“defective”) + -tome (“cutting, section”) + -ic (“adjectival suffix”), ultimately from Ancient Greek τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”).

parole.significato: A miserable, dysfunctional state or society that has a very poor standard of living or severe censorship, oppression, e…
parole.testo: From dys- + -topia, as if from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”) + -ία (-ía), based on utopia being reinterpreted as eu-topia.

parole.significato: The fear of accidents.
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Ancient Greek δυστυχία (dustukhía, “misfortune, ill luck”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Causing the earth to vibrate; very loud.
parole.testo: From earth + shaking as a calque of Ancient Greek ἐννοσίγαιος (ennosígaios), ἐνοσίχθων (enosíkhthōn).

parole.significato: A member of an early Jewish Christian sect that lived in and around Judea and Palestine from the 1st to the 4th century.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἐβιωναῖοι (Ebiōnaîoi), from Hebrew אביונים (Ebyonim, “the Poor Ones”), plural of Hebrew אֶבְיוֹן (ʾeḇyōn, “needy, poor”), itself likely a borrowing from Coptic ⲉⲃⲓⲏⲛ (ebiēn, “poor”).

parole.significato: The production of buds within flowers.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκβλάστησις (ekblástēsis, “budding”).

parole.significato: A digression, (especially) one in which a person is introduced speaking his or her own words.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκβολή (ekbolḗ, “a digression”), from ἐκβάλλω (ekbállō, “to throw out”).

parole.significato: An alkaloid constituting the active principle of ergot, probably equivalent to ergotoxine
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκβόλιον (ekbólion, “abortive”) + -ine. ekbólion is from ἐκβάλλω (ekbállō) and refers to the compounds ability to induce abortions.

parole.significato: A 19th-cetury contrivance for hatching eggs by means of artificial heat.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκκαλέω (ekkaléō, “call forth”) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: A mild laxative.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκκοπρωτικός (ekkoprōtikós, “excrementitious”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a sweat gland.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκ (ek, “out of”) and κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate”).

parole.significato: Any remedy that promotes discharges.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκκριτικός (ekkritikós, “secretive”), ultimately from κρίνω (krínō, “to separate; to distinguish”).

parole.significato: A wheeled device, used in ancient Greek plays, that could be rolled out to allow a tableau to be viewed.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐκκύκλημα (ekkúklēma).

parole.significato: The stripping off of an outer layer of skin by snakes and certain other animals; typically in accommodation to growth o…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔκδυσις (ékdusis, “stripping”), from ἐκδύω (ekdúō, “I take off”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + δύω (dúō, “I get in”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of hormones responsible for moulting in insects and other functions in other invertebrates and plants.
parole.testo: From ecdysis (“shedding, moulting”) (from Ancient Greek ἔκδυσις (ékdusis, “stripping”)) + steroid.

parole.significato: The process of the successful establishment of a plant or animal species in a habitat that was barren previously or was…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οἴκισις (oíkisis, “colonization”).

parole.significato: The portion of water in a sample of soil that is not available to vegetation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”) + ἄρδω (árdō, “to water, to irrigate”).

parole.significato: A unit of sound produced by insects that can be broken down into multiple physically more basic sound units (syllables).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἤχημα (ḗkhēma, “a sound”), from ἠχέω (ēkhéō, “I make sound, I chirp”) + -μᾰ (-mă, forming nouns form verbal stems). Introduced by Broughton (1976).

parole.significato: Forming compound terms denoting something prickly or, specifically, indicating the sea urchin.
parole.testo: From combining form of Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos, “hedgehog”).

parole.significato: A red blood cell with abnormal appearance characterized by many small, evenly spaced thorny projections.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos, “hedgehog; sea urchin”) + -cyte.

parole.significato: Synonym of sono-.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ, “echo, protracted sound”).

parole.significato: One of a set of eight modes, octoechoi, of music in Byzantine music. It selects the chant style or genre.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἦχοι (êkhoi, “sounds”), plural of ἦχος (êkhos).

parole.significato: The involuntary repetitive echoing of words or phrases spoken by another person; either immediate or delayed.
parole.testo: From echo- + -lalia; echo- ultimately from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ, “reflected sound, echo”), -lalia from λαλιά (laliá, “talk, chat”).

parole.significato: An omission of words needed to fully express the sense of a phrase.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “disappearance, abandoning”). Doublet of eclipse.

parole.significato: A coarse-grained metamorphic rock, a mixture of pyroxene, quartz, and feldspar with inclusions of red garnet.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”), + -ite.

parole.significato: A language variety unique to a household.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + English -lect (“[language] variety”).

parole.significato: Fear of one’s home.
parole.testo: From eco- + -phobia, from Ancient Greek: οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) and φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: interjection; ecphonesis
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκφώνημα (ekphṓnēma, “something called out”), from φωνέω (phōnéō, “produce sound”).

parole.significato: Exclamation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκφώνησις (ekphṓnēsis, “pronunciation, exclamation”).

parole.significato: Serving to dissolve or clear viscous matter or secretions, and so remove obstructions
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκφράσσω (ekphrássō, “to open or unblock”), from φράσσω (phrássō). Compare French ecphractique.

parole.significato: Feeling or characterized by ecstasy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκστατικός (ekstatikós). By surface analysis, ecstasy + -tic.

parole.significato: Synonym of ectasis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκτασία (ektasía), from ἔκτασις (éktasis, “a stretching out”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix), from ἐκτείνω (ekteínō, “to stretch out”) + -σῐς (-sĭs), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

parole.significato: The dilation or distention of a hollow or tubular part of the body, typically due to disease or injury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔκτασις (éktasis).

parole.significato: An exposition or setting out; used by Aristotle in setting forth various proofs, though the nature of the process is di…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκθετικός (ekthetikós).

parole.significato: The dropping out or suppression of a consonant from a word, with or without a vowel.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔκθλιψις (ékthlipsis).

parole.significato: The slender, hollow thread of a nettling cell or cnida.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκθορέω (ekthoréō, “to leap out”), from θρῴσκω (thrōískō, “jump”), + Latin -eum.

parole.significato: Outside.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκτός (ektós, “outside”). Sense 2 ("ghost-related") is a reinterpretation of this prefix in the word ectoplasm (“paranormal substance believed to be involved in the materialization of the dead”), for the etymology of which see there.

parole.significato: A parasite that lives on the surface of a host organism; such as the Demodex mite, which lives in human hair and eyelas…
parole.testo: From ecto- (from Ancient Greek ἐκτός (ektós, “outside”)) + parasite.

parole.significato: A condition of loose eyelids, characterized by the turning outward of the lower eyelid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκτρόπιον (ektrópion).

parole.significato: That tends to prevent the development of something, especially a disease.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔκτρωσις (éktrōsis, “abortion”).

parole.significato: An impression (in wax, clay, &c.) of a seal or medal.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔκτυπος (éktupos, “worked in relief”), from ἐκ- (ek-) + τύπος (túpos).

parole.significato: All known inhabited and civilized areas of the world.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οἰκουμένη (oikouménē, “inhabited world”), from οἰκέω (oikéō, “I inhabit, dwell”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “residence”).

parole.significato: The largest theoretical human settlement, a planetwide conurbation.
parole.testo: From ecumene (“inhabited world”) + -polis (“city”). From use as a common noun of Ecumenopolis, applying the concept to diverse scenarios. Ultimately from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Ground.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔδαφος (édaphos, “ground”).

parole.significato: Relating to soils and the ecosystems within them
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔδαφος (édaphos) + ecological.

parole.significato: of or pertaining to edaphology
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔδαφος (édaphos, “ground”) + -logic.

parole.significato: of or pertaining to edaphology
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔδαφος (édaphos, “ground”) + -logical.

parole.significato: any plant that grows with its roots in the soil and shoots in the air
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔδαφος (édaphos, “ground”) + -phyte. By surface analysis, edapho- + -phyte.

parole.significato: edema
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οἰδήμᾰτος (oidḗmătos, “swelling”), genitive of οἴδημα (oídēma), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “I swell”).

parole.significato: awakening; resurrection
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔγερσῐς (égersĭs).

parole.significato: The belief in ghosts or phantoms; spiritualism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, apparition, phantom, ghost”) + -ism.

parole.significato: An image or representation of an idea; a representation of an ideal form; an apparition of some actual or imaginary ent…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “figure, representation”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “sight”), from εἴδω (eídō, “I see”). Doublet of aidoru, idol, and idolum and related to idea.

parole.significato: A rhetorical technique in which a speech is attributed to a deceased person, a phantom, an image or an idol.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἰδωλοποιία (eidōlopoiía, “formation of images; putting words into the mouth of a dead person”), from εἰδωλοποιός (eidōlopoiós, “producing phantom-like appearances”), from εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “phantom”) + ποιός (poiós, “-like”).

parole.significato: An early motion picture system.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “figure, representation”) + -scope.

parole.significato: Form; essence; type; species.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “species”)

parole.significato: A kind of orrery that combined mechanical movement with a method of back projection.
parole.testo: Neologism based on Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “that which is seen”) + οὐρανός (ouranós, “the firmament”) + -ιον (-ion, parasynthetic compound suffix).

parole.significato: Describing the properties of a class of partial differential equation encountered in descriptions of wave propagation.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “image”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greece, a tax on sea trade at the rate of a twentieth (5%).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἰκοστή (eikostḗ), feminine of εἰκοστός (eikostós, “twentieth”).

parole.significato: A proposal to resolve disputes and reconcile differences in order to advance peace, strengthen or establish unity, or f…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἰρηνικόν (eirēnikón), neuter form of εἰρηνικός (eirēnikós), from εἰρήνη (eirḗnē, “peace”).

parole.significato: An interpretation, especially of Scripture, that reflects the personal ideas or viewpoint of the interpreter; reading s…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εἰς (eis, “into”) and English exegesis. Historically unrelated to the Ancient Greek εἰσήγησις (eisḗgēsis, “proposing, advising”).

parole.significato: A truce around the time of the ancient Olympic Games to protect the hosts, competitors, and spectators.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκεχειρία (ekekheiría, “armistice, truce”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “hold back”) and χείρ (kheír, “hand”), with kh > k by Grassmann's Law.

parole.significato: The scientific study of human settlements, and the planning and design of cities and other communities.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οἰκίστικα (oikístika), from οἰκιστής (oikistḗs, “colonizer”). Coined by Constantinos Apostolou Doxiadis in 1942.

parole.significato: A clear, intense, self-contained argument or verbal description of an object, especially of an artwork.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔκφρασις (ékphrasis, “description”), from ἐκφράζω (ekphrázō, “I describe”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, ex-”) + φράζω (phrázō, “I explain, point out”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to ekphrasis; clear, lucid.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκφραστικός (ekphrastikós).

parole.significato: The supposed periodic destruction of the universe
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐκπύρωσις (ekpúrōsis).

parole.significato: The state of being beside oneself or rapt out of oneself.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis, “displacement, cession, trance”)

parole.significato: A litany in the Byzantine Rite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκτένεια (ekténeia).

parole.significato: A particular steroid glycoside.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil, oil”) + Ancient Greek δένδρον (déndron, “tree”) (similar to glucoside) + -ide.

parole.significato: A variety of nepheline, usually massive and of a greasy lustre and grey to reddish colour.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil, oil”) + -lite.

parole.significato: The more liquid or volatile portion of certain oily substances, such as rose oil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”).

parole.significato: Derived from elaidin (the trans isomer of oleic acid).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “oil”) + -ic.

parole.significato: ricinoleic acid
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”).

parole.significato: A plant organ that secretes oil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek έλαιο (élaio, “oil”) + -phore, from New Latin -phorus, from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”), a derivative of φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”).

parole.significato: A specialized leucoplast responsible for the storage of lipids.
parole.testo: Compound from Ancient Greek: ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”) and πλαστός (plastós, “formed”).

parole.significato: A fleshy structure rich in lipids attached to the seeds of many plant species, usually to attract ants that disperse th…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to, resembling, or characteristic of the red deer, Cervus elaphus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: ethylene
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil, oil”) + -yl. So called by Berzelius from its forming an oil combining with chlorine.

parole.significato: The terminal through which electric current passes between metallic and nonmetallic parts of an electric circuit.
parole.testo: Coined by British scientist Michael Faraday in 1833, first used in his Diary (laboratory notebook) from the Ancient Greek words ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”) (from which the word electricity is derived) and ὁδός (hodós, “way”). By surface analysis, electro- + -ode

parole.significato: An exciting and depolarizing acid solution used in certain cells or batteries.
parole.testo: From electro- + Ancient Greek -ποιός (-poiós, “producing”).

parole.significato: Serving to refute, refutative, especially as part of a systematic interrogation; pertaining to rhetorical elenchus or c…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐλενκτικός (elenktikós, “refutative”).

parole.significato: The commander of a military corps of elephants.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐλεφαντάρχης (elephantárkhēs).

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Elephantine or the Elephantine people.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ἐλεφαντίνη (Elephantínē).

parole.significato: A great desire for or obsession with freedom.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐλευθερία (eleuthería, “freedom”) + -mania.

parole.significato: Fear of freedom.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐλευθερία (eleuthería, “freedom”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: of or pertaining to the Subphylum Eleutherozoa
parole.testo: From eleuthero- + -zoic, from Ancient Greek ἐλεύθερος (eleútheros, “freedom”) + ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an ellipse.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”). By surface analysis, ellipse + -tic.

parole.significato: In a shape of, or reminding of, an ellipse; oval.
parole.testo: From elliptic + -al, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”).

parole.significato: An orthorhombic-pyramidal mineral containing hydrogen, oxygen, silicon, sodium, and zirconium.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐλπίς (elpís, “hope”) + -ite.

parole.significato: A sheath or outer covering, especially around the spinal cord or over the hindwings of certain insects.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔλυτρον (élutron, “sheath”).

parole.significato: Oil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”).

parole.significato: Automatic speech; verbalization that occurs without conscious effort by the individual, such as repetitions and filler…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “something thrown in”) + -lalia.

parole.significato: A blood clot or swelling, particularly one that blocks an artery; an embolus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμβολον (émbolon, “wedge, plug”).

parole.significato: An arcade or porticoed street in Constantinople.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “bolt; portico”).

parole.significato: embolic invagination
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐμβολή (embolḗ, “a putting into”), from ἐμβάλλω (embállō).

parole.significato: The material from which an embryo is formed and nourished, mostly consisting of secretions from the uterine glands.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: The act or process of vomiting.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμεσις (émesis), from ἐμέω (eméō, “vomit”). Compare ἔμετος (émetos, “vomit”, noun). By surface analysis, suffixed with -esis.

parole.significato: Relating to vomit or emesis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐμέω (eméō, “I vomit”).

parole.significato: A tragic dance in Ancient Greek theatre.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐμμέλεια (emméleia).

parole.significato: An herb that stimulates blood flow in the pelvic area and uterus, causing menstruation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμμηνα (émmēna, “menses”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “leading”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of menstruation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμμηνα (émmēna, “menses”) + -o- + -logy.

parole.significato: Embossed, especially of Ancient Greek art.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐμπαιστικός (empaistikós, “embossed”), from ἐμπαίω (empaíō), from παίω (paíō, “strike”).

parole.significato: To dress in a full suit of armour; to panoply.
parole.testo: From em- (prefix meaning ‘on, onto; covered’) + panoply (“complete set of armour”); panoply is derived from Ancient Greek πᾰνοπλῐ́ᾱ (pănoplĭ́ā, “suit of armour”), from πάνοπλος (pánoplos, “in full armour”) (from παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all, every’) + ὅπλον (hóplon, “armour; arms, weapons”)) + -ῐ

parole.significato: A perfumed powder to be sprinkled on the body to mask the odor of sweat.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμπασμα (émpasma, “dusting powder”), ultimately from πάσσω (pássō). Compare catapasm.

parole.significato: Identification with or understanding of the thoughts, feelings, or emotional state of another person.
parole.testo: A twentieth-century borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐμπάθεια (empátheia, literally “passion”) (formed from ἐν (en, “in, at”) + πάθος (páthos, “feeling”)), equivalent to em- + -pathy, coined by Edward Bradford Titchener in 1909 to translate German Einfühlung. The modern word in Greek εμπάθεια (empátheia

parole.significato: Characterized by emphasis; forceful.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐμφατικός (emphatikós, “emphatic”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “I show, present”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “I shine, show”); related to ἔμφασις (émphasis) and English emphasis.

parole.significato: A vesicular tumour.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φλέω (phléō, “overflow”).

parole.significato: A plaster.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron, “daub, salve”).

parole.significato: before, in front
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμπροσθεν (émprosthen). By surface analysis, em- + prostho-.

parole.significato: A condition in which the body is bent sharply forward.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔμπροσθεν (émprosthen) + τόνος (tónos, “tension”). See further at opisthotonos. From emprostho- + tonos.

parole.significato: Hemorrhage from the lungs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔμπτυσις (émptusis).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek mythology, a kind of spectre sent by Hecate to guard roads and devour travellers.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek Ἔμπουσα (Émpousa)

parole.significato: A collection of pus within a naturally existing anatomical cavity (as opposed to an abscess, which occurs in a newly fo…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐμπύημα (empúēma, “gathering, abscess”).

parole.significato: The particular smell and taste arising from products of decomposition of animal or vegetable substances when burnt in s…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐμπύρευμα (empúreuma, “a live coal covered with ashes”). Compare French empyreume. See empyreal.

parole.significato: A general fire; a conflagration.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek in + to burn.

parole.significato: Transformation from one grammatically correct form to another.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐναλλαγή (enallagḗ, “interchange, variation”).

parole.significato: A lesion of the mucous membrane (especially of the mouth)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐνανθέω (enanthéō), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + ἀνθέω (anthéō, “to blossom”).

parole.significato: An eruption on the skin from internal disease, such as scarlet fever or measles.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in, intra”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”), i.e. “efflorescence from within”. Compare enanthem.

parole.significato: Opposite, opposed, opposing.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐναντίος (enantíos, “opposite”), its English equivalent literally being en- + anti-.

parole.significato: The principle in Jungian psychology whereby the superabundance of one force inevitably produces its opposite, as with p…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐναντιοδρομία (enantiodromía, “running in a contrary direction”), from ἐναντίος (enantíos, “opposite”) + δρόμος (drómos, “running”).

parole.significato: A mirror image, a form related to another as an object is to its image in a mirror.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐναντίος (enantíos, “opposite”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”). By surface analysis, enantio- + -morph.

parole.significato: Any of an extinct group of protobirds of the Enantiornithes.
parole.testo: From enanti- + + Ancient Greek ὄρνιθος (órnithos, “bird”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which what is to be understood affirmatively is stated negatively, and vice versa; affirmation by…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐναντίος (enantíos, “contradiction”).

parole.significato: An ulcer in the eye, upon the cornea.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἔγκαυμα (énkauma, “mark caused by burning”). See encaustic.

parole.significato: Prepared by means of heat; burned in.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐγκαυστικός (enkaustikós, “burning in”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the brain.
parole.testo: From en- + cephalo-. From Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “brain”) (within the head), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: The area of central nervous system that includes all higher nervous centers, enclosed within the skull and continuous w…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “within the head”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: The encephalon.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: An ancient Illyrian tribe inhabiting Enchele.

parole.significato: writing

parole.significato: Any variety of slate suitable to be written on.

parole.significato: A saint who was martyred after suffering great torture.

parole.significato: Of or relating to hebephrenia.

parole.significato: Sacred writing.
