parole.significato: Having layers of water that do not intermix.
parole.testo: Scientific neologism (1935), after holomictic. From Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part, portion”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”). By surface analysis, mero- + -mictic.

parole.significato: A sclerite on the side of the thorax of an insect, above the coxae of the mid and hind legs.
parole.testo: Back-formation from epimeron, ultimately from Ancient Greek μῆρος (mêros, “thigh”).

parole.significato: A term used to denote a thing that is a part of something else.
parole.testo: From mero- + -onym, from Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”).

parole.significato: The relationship of being a constituent part or member of something; a system of meronyms.
parole.testo: From mero- + -onymy (from Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”)); compare meronym.

parole.significato: Able to speak.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέροψ (mérops, “endowed with speech”), perhaps from μέρος (méros, “portion”) + ὄψ (óps, “voice”).

parole.significato: the proximal segment of the hind limb; the thigh
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μηρός (mērós, “thigh”).

parole.significato: the plain surface between the channels of a triglyph
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part”).

parole.significato: The thigh.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μηρός (mērós, “thigh”).

parole.significato: rumination syndrome
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μηρυκάζω (mērukázō, “to chew the cud”) + -ism.

parole.significato: mesenteric
parole.testo: From meso- + Ancient Greek ἀραιός (araiós, “narrow, slender, thin, fine”).

parole.significato: Having a cranium with a medium ratio of length to breadth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσατος (mésatos) (superlative degree of μέσος (mésos)) + -cephalic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the midline of the body.
parole.testo: Irregular derivation from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos).

parole.significato: Characterized by an intermediate degree of moisture, in between xeric (dry) and hydric (wet); somewhat moist.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos). Compare with xeric and hydric.

parole.significato: In between the "macro" and "micro" levels of sociological structures.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”).

parole.significato: Middle or centre in location/position.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”). Doublet of mid- and medio-.

parole.significato: The middle layer of the pericarp of a fruit. In many fruits such as drupes and tomatoes, the mesocarp is fleshy
parole.testo: From meso- + -carp (from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit”)).

parole.significato: Part of a lyric or choral ode which occurs between the strophe and antistrophe.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεσῳδός (mesōidós); see meso-, ode.

parole.significato: The repetition of terms within successive sentences
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + δίπλωσις (díplōsis, “a doubling”)

parole.significato: The gelatinous matrix within a sponge, filling the space between the external pinacoderm and the internal choanoderm.
parole.testo: From meso- (“middle”) + Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “wood, timber, matter”) (whence English hyle).

parole.significato: thomsonite
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”).

parole.significato: The study of the mutual interrelationships between organisms and their environment; branch of biology; former term for…
parole.testo: From meso- + -logy; a compound with components derived from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “meso-, middle”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study”). The term arose in various European languages c. 1850, but did not exist in Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The mesial plane dividing the body into similar right and left halves.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσον (méson, “middle”). Doublet of medium.

parole.significato: Any phanerophyte between 8 and 30 metres in height
parole.testo: From meso- (“middle, intermediate”) + phanerophyte, from Ancient Greek φανερός (phanerós, “visible”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: cortex
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + φλόος (phlóos, “bark”).

parole.significato: glabella (the space between the eyebrows and nose)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεσόφρυον (mesóphruon), from μέσος (mésos, “between”) and ὀφρύς (ophrús, “eyebrow”).

parole.significato: The middle one of the three main basal plates in the fins of certain fishes.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek meso- middle + a fin.

parole.significato: Having a medium orbital index, between megaseme and microseme.
parole.testo: From meso- + Ancient Greek σῆμα (sêma, “sign, mark”). Compare French mésosème.

parole.significato: An acrostic that spells out a word or message with its middle letters.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) and στίχος (stíkhos, “line”).

parole.significato: A zeugma where the governing word occurs in the middle of the sentence and governs clauses on either side.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos) + ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “yoke, bond”)

parole.significato: A member of the ancient inhabitants of the region of Apulia in Southern Italy.
parole.testo: From Messapi + -ian, from Ancient Greek Μεσσάπιος (Messápios).

parole.significato: Behind.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μετα- (meta-), from μετά (metá), from Mycenaean Greek 𐀕𐀲 (me-ta), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *meth₂ (“in the middle”).

parole.significato: A change or mutation of disease, symptoms, or treatment.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεταβολή (metabolḗ, “change”); μετά (metá, “beyond”) + βολέω (boléō, “throw”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to metabolism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μεταβολικός (metabolikós), from μεταβολή (metabolḗ, “change”) + -ικός (-ikós), thus by surface analysis, metabola + -ic. Compare metabolism.

parole.significato: To undergo metabolism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετᾰβολή (metăbolḗ, “change, mutation”) + -ize.

parole.significato: The change in shape undergone by euglenids as they move or evolve
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεταβολή (metabolḗ, “change”).

parole.significato: An error in chronological ordering in which a character or an event is placed at too late a time.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after, behind”) + χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Exhibiting or relating to metachrosis.
parole.testo: From meta- + + Ancient Greek χρωτικός (khrōtikós), from χρωσις (khrōsis), from χρώς (khrṓs).

parole.significato: Communication or discussion, especially involving academic analysis, about communication itself.
parole.testo: From meta- + communication; from Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after, beyond; with; adjacent; self”) + Latin commūnicātiō (“imparting, communicating”); from commūnicō (“share, impart, inform”).

parole.significato: Exchange; replacement; substitution; metathesis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετάληψις (metálēpsis). Compare metalepsis.

parole.significato: metal
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek μέτᾰλλον (métăllon).

parole.significato: prostration as an expression of reverence in a church
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετάνοια (metánoia). Doublet of metanoia.

parole.significato: Metanoia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μετανοῆτε (metanoête), subjunctive of μετανοῶ (metanoô, “to repent”), from the Gospel of Luke: : οὐχί, λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀλλ’ ἐὰν μὴ μετανοῆτε, πάντες ὁμοίως ἀπολεῖσθε. oukhí, légō humîn, all’ eàn mḕ metanoête, pántes homoíōs apoleîsthe. I tell you, no! But unless you repent, yo

parole.significato: A fundamental change of mind.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετάνοια (metánoia, “repentance”, literally “afterthought”), a compound of μετά (metá, “after, with”) and νοέω (noéō, “to perceive, to think”).

parole.significato: A literal, word-for-word translation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεταφράζομαι (metaphrázomai, “consider after”). By surface analysis, meta- + phrase.

parole.significato: The part of a long bone that grows during development.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after”) + Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis, “growth”), equivalent to meta- + -physis.

parole.significato: A metasomatic rock.
parole.testo: From meta- + somatic + -ite from metamorphosis and Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós, “bodily”), from σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: A triclinic lemon mineral containing aluminum, hydrogen, oxygen, uranium, and vanadium.
parole.testo: From meta- + vanuralite. Named because it is a dehydrated form of vanuralite; mineralogical naming convention uses Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “above”) for minerals whose only difference is the hydration level.

parole.significato: middle ground
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μεταξύ (metaxú)

parole.significato: The Transfiguration of Christ.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετεμορφώθη (metemorphṓthē), third person singular passive aorist of μεταμορφόω (metamorphóō, “to transform”) (thus meaning "he was transformed").

parole.significato: The suppression of a day in the calendar to prevent the date of the new moon being set a day too late, or the suppressi…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μετέμπτωσις (metémptōsis), from μετεμπίπτω (metempíptō).

parole.significato: A change of body by the soul, reincarnation, metempsychosis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετενσωμᾰ́τωσῐς (metensōmắtōsĭs).

parole.significato: A rapid accumulation of gas in the intestine. It is typically a sign of bowel necrosis from bacterial infection, a life…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετεωρίζω (meteōrízō, “raise up, of wind rising from the stomach, suffer from flatulence”).

parole.significato: The science that deals with the study of the atmosphere and its phenomena, especially with weather and weather forecast…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μετεωρολογία (meteōrología), from μετέωρα (metéōra, “celestial phenomena”), nominalized from the neuter plural of μετέωρος (metéōros, “high in the sky”), + -λογία (-logía, “study of”). By surface analysis, meteor (“atmospheric phenomenon”) + -ology (“study of”).

parole.significato: Divination by interpreting meteorological phenomena such as meteors.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετέωρος (metéōros, “in mid-air”) + -mancy.

parole.significato: An originally Ancient Greek form of theatre in which the audience participates and improvises.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μέθεξις (méthexis)

parole.significato: Methyl.
parole.testo: From methyl + -o-. Ultimately from Ancient Greek μέθυ (méthu, “wine”).

parole.significato: methodical
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós, “going to work by rule, systematic, crafty”).

parole.significato: In an organized manner; proceeding with regard to method; systematic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós, “going to work by rule, systematic, crafty”) + -al.

parole.significato: alcoholism
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέθυ (méthu, “wine”) + -mania.

parole.significato: Practical intelligence; street smarts.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῆτις (mêtis).

parole.significato: An ecclesiastical embassy church within Eastern Orthodox tradition.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετόχιον (metókhion).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, a word or phrase that names an object from a single characteristic of it or of a closely related ob…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετωνυμικός (metōnumikós, “of or like metonymy”), from μετωνυμία (metōnumía, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”). By surface analysis, metonym + -ic.

parole.significato: A craniometric point midway between the frontal eminences.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέτωπον (métōpon, “forehead”) + -ion.

parole.significato: The uterus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μήτρα (mḗtra, “womb”).

parole.significato: A pocket instrument combining a thermometer, level, plummet, and lens.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέτρα (métra), plural of μέτρον (métron, “measure”).

parole.significato: Moderation of the passions.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μετριοπάθεια (metriopátheia, “moderation of passions”).

parole.significato: metre (US: meter), poetic measure
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron). Doublet of meter, metre, and mether.

parole.significato: A device, containing an inverted pendulum, used to mark time by means of regular ticks at adjustable intervals; an elec…
parole.testo: Coined in English from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure”) + νόμος (nómos, “regulation, law”).

parole.significato: A sulfide of silver and antimony.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek meyon, "smaller", and argyros, "silver", as its silver content is lower than most silver sulfides.

parole.significato: A noxious atmosphere or emanation once thought to originate from swamps and waste, and to cause disease.
parole.testo: First attested in 1665. From Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “stain; pollution”).

parole.significato: A supporter of the theory of miasmatism.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “miasma”) + -ist.

parole.significato: Very small in scale or scope.
parole.testo: From micro-, typically as shortened forms for modern words formed with the prefix, ultimately from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”).

parole.significato: Very small.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μῑκρο- (mīkro-), from μῑκρός (mīkrós, “small”). By surface analysis, micr- + -o-.

parole.significato: A microbe.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: Any relatively small, generally aquatic, oligochaete, a member of a sometimes used size-based division of the class Oli…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + δρῖλος (drîlos, “worm”).

parole.significato: Formed of small stones.
parole.testo: From micro- + -lith + -ic or microlith + -ic, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”).

parole.significato: The study of trivialities and minutiae, or focusing on the small details rather than the whole picture.
parole.testo: Sense 1 is borrowed directly from Ancient Greek μικρολογία (mikrología, “pettiness, stinginess, triviality”), with the suffix reinterpreted as -logy. Sense 2 is micro- + -logy, effectively the same etymological components.

parole.significato: The condition in which a limb is abnormally shortened.
parole.testo: From micro- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Synonym of breve.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μικρόν (mikrón), neuter of μικρός (mikrós, “small”).

parole.significato: a very small pachycephalosaurid, ornithischian dinosaur of the genus Micropachycephalosaurus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + παχύς (pakhús, “thick”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard, reptile”).

parole.significato: Any phanerophyte between 2 and 8 metres in height
parole.testo: From micro- (“small”) + phanerophyte, from Ancient Greek φανερός (phanerós, “visible”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: A disorder in which objects appear much smaller than normal, most often the result of a neurological dysfunction.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μικροψία (mikropsía), from μικρός (mikrós, “little, small”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”).

parole.significato: Having the orbital index relatively narrow, therefore having eye sockets far away.
parole.testo: From micro- + Ancient Greek σῆμα (sêma, “sign, mark”). Compare French microsème.

parole.significato: Any of a group of mammals characteristically of small size, including various rodents (used in the 19th century by Jame…
parole.testo: From micro- + Ancient Greek σθένος (sthénos, “might, strength”).

parole.significato: mixed
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῑκτός (mīktós, “mixed”), from μῑ́γνῡμῐ (mī́gnūmĭ, “to mix”).

parole.significato: Someone who lacks experience or courage.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek γαλακτοπότης (galaktopótēs, “a milk drinker”), a derogatory term which the Greeks used in reference to the barbarians.

parole.significato: A unit of mimetic information.
parole.testo: Anglicized as if from a noun derived from Ancient Greek μῑμέομαι (mīméomai) with the deverbal suffix -μα (-ma), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitation, copy”). By surface analysis, mime + -eme.

parole.significato: The representation of aspects of the real world, especially human actions, in literature and art.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῑ́μησις (mī́mēsis), from μιμεῖσθαι (mimeîsthai, “to imitate”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “a mime”). By surface analysis, mime + -esis.

parole.significato: mimicry
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μίμησις (mímēsis, “imitation”) + -ism. Compare Greek μιμητισμός (mimitismós).

parole.significato: An arsenate mineral which forms in lead deposits, usually by the oxidation of galena and arsenopyrite.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek Μιμητής (Mimētḗs), "imitator", from its similarity to pyromorphite.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the civilization that developed in Crete from the neolithic period to the Bronze Age (about 3000-1050…
parole.testo: Sir Arthur Evans, not knowing the Minoan term for “Minoan” at the time, coined this name in the early 20th century, from Ancient Greek Μίνως (Mínōs), the mythical king of Crete. The actual name is probably reflected in Egyptian kftjw (perhaps reconstructible as *Káftayu) and Biblical Hebrew כַּפְתּו

parole.significato: Of a geologic epoch within the Neogene period from about 23 to 5.3 million years ago; marked by the drift of continents…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μείων (meíōn, “less”) + καινός (kainós, “new”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1831 for Charles Lyell, who introduced it in 1833 in his book Principles of Geology. By surface analysis, meio- + -cene.

parole.significato: A free-living motile form of a trematode, covered with cilia, which settles in a mollusc intermediate host to become a…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μειράκιον (meirákion) + -idium.

parole.significato: One who has a negative view of the entire human race.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man; human”); compare miser.

parole.significato: A negative view or hatred of the human race.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μισανθρωπία (misanthrōpía), from μισάνθρωπος (misánthrōpos), from μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”) + ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”). The word is analysable as miso- + -anthropy.

parole.significato: hatred; dislike; aversion
parole.testo: Combining form of Ancient Greek μῑσέω (mīséō, “to hate”), from μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”).

parole.significato: Disliking smoking and tobacco smoke.
parole.testo: From miso- + capno- (stem of Ancient Greek καπνός (kapnós, “smoke”)) + -ic.

parole.significato: One who hates tobacco smoke.
parole.testo: From miso- + capno- (stem of Ancient Greek καπνός (kapnós, “smoke”)) + ist.

parole.significato: One who hates laughter.
parole.testo: From miso- + Ancient Greek γελαστής (gelastḗs, “laughter”).

parole.significato: Synonym of misogynist.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μισογύνης (misogúnēs).

parole.significato: One who professes misogyny; a hater of women.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῑσογύνης (mīsogúnēs), from μῑσέω (mīséō, “I hate”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”), equivalent to misogyny + -ist.

parole.significato: Hatred of, contempt for, or prejudice against women.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μισογυνία (misogunía) and μισογύνης (misogúnēs, “woman hater”), from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”). By surface analysis, miso- + -gyny.

parole.significato: Hatred or fear of reasoning or argument.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μισολογία (misología), from μισόλογος (misólogos), from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) + λόγος (lógos, “account, reason”).

parole.significato: A person with hate or contempt for beards.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μισοπώγων (misopṓgōn, “somebody who hates beards”), which is incidentally the title of a book by Emperor Julian, from μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”) + πώγων (pṓgōn, “beard”).

parole.significato: One who hates wisdom or knowledge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μῑσόσοφος (mīsósophos, literally “hater of wisdom”).

parole.significato: Hatred of God or gods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μισόθεος (misótheos, “hating the gods”), from μίσος (mísos, “hatred”) + θεός (theós, “god”). The Greek compound is found in Aeschylus (Agamemnon 1090; compare dystheism). The English word appears as a nonce-coinage, used by T. De Quincey in 1846. Attested as worthy of rev

parole.significato: The premature death of a vulnerable human due to a failure to provide appropriate help in the context of social injusti…
parole.testo: A neologism coined by Brazilian bioethicists, from mis- (“badly, wrongly”) + -thanasia (as in euthanasia, dysthanasia), from Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”).

parole.significato: Synonym of mithridate.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Μιθριδατικόν (Mithridatikón, “Mithridatic (thing)”), from Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs) + -ικός (-ikós), the Greek form of the name of Mithridates VI of Pontus. Doublet of mithridate, mithridatium, and mithridatum.

parole.significato: Thread.
parole.testo: # From Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread of the warp”). # From mitosis.

parole.significato: The induction of cellular mitosis.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + -genesis

parole.significato: The denser part of the protoplasm of a cell.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “a thread”) + -ωμα (-ōma). According to the OED, the functional origin of -ome.

parole.significato: A dactylic hexameter with short penultimate syllable.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μείουρος (meíouros), from μείων (meíōn, “curtailed, lesser”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: reproduction by the fusion of gametes
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μίξις (míxis, “mingling”).

parole.significato: Designating the Mixolydian mode, the highest of the ancient Greek modes, and now having final G and D dominant.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μιξο-Λυδιος (mixo-Ludios, “half-Lydian”), from μιξο- (mixo-) (from base of μιγνυναι (mignunai, “to mix”)) + Λυδιος (Ludios, “Lydia (an ancient country in Asia Minor)”); named in reference to Lydian (another Greek mode).

parole.significato: memory
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μνήμη (mnḗmē, “memory”).

parole.significato: The study of techniques for remembering anything more easily.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μνημονικά (mnēmoniká, “mnemonics”), plural of μνημονικόν (mnēmonikón, “mnemonics”), neuter of μνημονικός (mnēmonikós, “mnemonic”); see mnemonic.

parole.significato: A Daco-Thracian tribe who inhabited present-day Serbia and Bulgaria, part of the then Roman province of Moesia.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek Μοισοί (Moisoí)

parole.significato: Writer's cramp.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόγις (mógis, “with toil and pain”) + -graphia.

parole.significato: Difficulty in speaking, triggered by the effort of singing or speaking loudly.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόγις (mógis, “with toil and pain”) + -phonia.

parole.significato: The three Fates, personifications of destiny.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μοῖρα (moîra).

parole.significato: A soulmate or life partner, especially one who exerts a calming influence.
parole.testo: Coined by American author and webcomic artist Andrew Hussie in his multimedia fiction work Homestuck. Reportedly constructed from the Ancient Greek μοῖρᾰ (moîră, “lot, destiny”). Presented with the coordinate term moirallegience, which seems to be a blend of moira + allegience, with the -ail suffix

parole.significato: A sacrifice that is partially burned to ashes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μοῖρα (moîra, “part”) + καυστός (kaustós, “burnt”).

parole.significato: A professional mourner.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μοῖρα (moîra, “fate”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration”).

parole.significato: divination by interpreting shapes formed when molten metal, typically lead or tin, is dropped into water.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”) and the suffix -mancy. Probably after Greek μολυβδομαντεία (molyvdomanteía) or French molybdomancie.

parole.significato: A hexagonal-trapezohedral mineral containing hydrogen, lead, magnesium, oxygen, and silicon.
parole.testo: For its composition, Ancient Greek μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”) and crystal habit φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”), + -ite. Note that the prefix molybdo- + here does NOT denote molybdenum; the element is named after the same Greek root.

parole.significato: A morbid fear of dirt, germs or contamination.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek molysma, filth, infection, + phobos, fear.

parole.significato: A persistent critic
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Μῶμος (Mômos, “the god of satire, mockery, censure, writers, poets”) + -ist.

parole.significato: The persistent sense that one is out of place or otherwise does not belong.
parole.testo: Coined by American author and neologist John Koenig, creator of The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, from Ancient Greek μοναχός (monakhós, “single, solitary”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view, sight”).

parole.significato: of, relating to, or being a monad
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μοναδικός (monadikós, “single”), from μονάς (monás, “a unit”); see monad. By surface analysis, monad + -ic.

parole.significato: The lower, dense stratum of a meromictic lake (one with permanently stratified layers) that does not mix with the water…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνιμος (mónimos, “stable, permanent”) + -limnion (from Ancient Greek λῐ́μνη (lĭ́mnē, “lake”) + -ion), first appearing in the writings of British ecologist George Evelyn Hutchinson (1903–1991).

parole.significato: An isometric-hexoctahedral mineral containing antimony, calcium, lead, and oxygen.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνιμος (mónimos, “stable, permanent”) + -lite because it is a mineral that resists chemical decomposition.

parole.significato: union of the quadrate and squamosal, not permitting movement
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνιμος (mónimos, “fixed in place”) + -styly, from Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”).

parole.significato: one, single, only
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μονο- (mono-), combining form of μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”).

parole.significato: Having a single head.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μονοκέφαλος (monoképhalos). By surface analysis, mono- + -cephalous.

parole.significato: The quality of having only one independent channel for conveying color information in the eye, i.e. total color blindne…
parole.testo: mono- + Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).

parole.significato: Having only one color, represented by differing hues and tints. For example shades in a black and white television.
parole.testo: From mono- + chromatic, mono- from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”), chromatic from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).

parole.significato: A black and white image, especially such a photograph.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μονόχρωμος (monókhrōmos), from μόνος (mónos, “one”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”); mono- + -chrome.

parole.significato: A condition in which the pulse curve or sphygmogram shows only a single crest, the dicrotic elevation entirely disappea…
parole.testo: From mono- + Ancient Greek κρότος (krótos, “a rattling, beating”) + -ism.

parole.significato: One of the Monodelphia.
parole.testo: From mono- + Ancient Greek δελφύς (delphús, “womb, uterus”).

parole.significato: The situation where an ant colony is established at a single nest site.
parole.testo: From mono- + Ancient Greek δόμος (dómos, “house”) + -y.

parole.significato: Having both the male and female reproductive organs in the same individual, either in different flowers or in the same…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, solitary”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house, dwelling-place”), equivalent to mono- + -oecious.

parole.significato: A person with an extensive knowledge of a single subject or field, but little knowledge of others.
parole.testo: From mono- (“one, single”) + Ancient Greek μάθη (máthē, “learning”), from μανθάνω (manthánō, “to learn”). Compare polymath.

parole.significato: Having layers of water that intermix only once per year.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, single”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”). By surface analysis, mono- + -mictic.

parole.significato: Having one and the same nature or essence, especially with regard to the persons of the Trinity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μονοούσιος (monooúsios, “of one substance”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”) + οὐσία (ousía, “being, substance, essence”) + -ian.

parole.significato: A vowel (in the sense of a sound rather than a letter of the alphabet) that has the same sound throughout its pronuncia…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μονόφθογγος (monóphthongos), from μόνος (mónos, “single”) + φθόγγος (phthóngos, “sound”).

parole.significato: Having only one set of teeth.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μονοφυής (monophuḗs, “single”) (μόνος (mónos, “alone”) + φύω (phúō, “produce”)) + ὀδόντος (odóntos) (genitive of ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”)).

parole.significato: That has one form, or that retains its primary form.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?]

parole.significato: A market situation in which there is only one buyer for a product.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, solitary; singular, unique”) + ὀψωνέω (opsōnéō, “to buy fish or victuals in general”) + -y, modelled after monopoly. ὀψωνέω is from ὄψον (ópson, “delicacies”) + ὠνέομαι (ōnéomai, “to buy, purchase”). The English word was coined by British classics scholar Ber

parole.significato: A poem having only one line.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, single”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “line”). See stich.

parole.significato: A harmony of the four Gospels.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos) (though the meaning of Modern Greek μονός (monós) fits slightly better) + τεσσάρων (tessárōn, “out of four”). Attested in Latin since 1552.

parole.significato: Whose spikelets are all similar.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos) and θᾰ́λᾰμος (thắlămos).

parole.significato: Bearing fruit only once; monocarpic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos) + τόκος (tókos).

parole.significato: Of or using the Greek system of diacritics which discards the breathings and employs a single accent to indicate stress…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos, “monotone”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), equivalent to monotone + -ic.

parole.significato: An ancient Spartan military unit of about a sixth of the Spartan army, typically composed of hoplites.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μόρᾱ (mórā).

parole.significato: A bugbear or invented monster.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Μορμώ (Mormṓ, “a hideous she-monster, a bugbear”).

parole.significato: A stupid person; an idiot; a fool.
parole.testo: Coined by American psychologist Henry H. Goddard in 1910, from Ancient Greek μωρόν (mōrón), the neuter form of μωρός (mōrós, “foolish, dull”).

parole.significato: idiocy; fatuity; stupidity
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μώρωσις (mṓrōsis, “mental slowness, dementia”). Compare moron.

parole.significato: A greenish-blue variety of apatite.
parole.testo: Related to Ancient Greek word for a sort of pipe clay.

parole.significato: A recurrent distinctive sound or sequence of sounds representing an indivisible morphological form; especially as repre…
parole.testo: Back-formation from morpheme, from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). Compare German Morph, from Morphem. Attested since the 1940s.

parole.significato: shape, form, or morphology.
parole.testo: Representing combining form of Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form”).

parole.significato: Connected with, or becoming an integral part of, a living unit or of the morphological framework.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μόρφωσις (mórphōsis, “shaping”).

parole.significato: Synonym of efficient cause
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek κινῆσαν αἴτιον (kinêsan aítion, literally “moving cause”).

parole.significato: The 12th letter of the Modern Greek alphabet.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῦ (mû), derived from Phoenician 𐤌𐤌 (mm /⁠mem⁠/, “water”). Doublet of mem.

parole.significato: An imaging technique that makes use of muons.
parole.testo: From mu (“shortening of muon or mu-meson”) + -o- + -graphy. Alternatively, a blend of muon + radiography. Ultimately from Ancient Greek μῦ (mû, “Greek letter”) + γράφω (gráphō, “sketch”).

parole.significato: Synonym of chrism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μῠ́ρον (mŭ́ron).

parole.significato: Relating to muscle
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse, mussel, muscle”)

parole.significato: Abnormal weakness of the muscles; but especially myasthenia gravis.
parole.testo: From my- (“relating to muscle”) + asthenia (“weakness”), from Ancient Greek ἀσθένεια (asthéneia, “weakness”). By surface analysis, my- (“muscle”) + a- (“not”) + sthen- (“strength”) + -ia (“disease”).

parole.significato: fungus
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs, “mushroom, fungus, mushroom-shaped objects”).

parole.significato: Poisoning caused by mushrooms.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs) + -ism.

parole.significato: A complex nitrogenous acid of the alloxan group, obtained as a honey-yellow powder and forming gelatinous solutions.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?]

parole.significato: A subtle or scornful jibe.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυκτηρισμός (muktērismós), from μυκτηρίζω (muktērízō, “I sneer”), from μυκτήρ (muktḗr, “nostril”).

parole.significato: A ptomaine obtained from putrid flesh and herring brines.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυδαλέος (mudaléos, “mouldy”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A poisonous amido acid, C₆H₁₃NO₂, originally obtained from decaying horseflesh and similar in action to curare.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυδάω (mudáō, “be wet”) + toxin.

parole.significato: The teledu.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυδάω (mudáō, “be clammy or damp”).

parole.significato: A white, fatty material, composed of lipids and lipoproteins, that surrounds the axons of nerves.
parole.testo: From myelo- + -in. From Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”).

parole.significato: Inflammation of the spinal cord or of bone marrow.
parole.testo: From myelo- + -itis. From Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”) + -ῖτις (-îtis, “fire”).

parole.significato: Bone marrow.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”).

parole.significato: The central canal of the spinal cord.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek marrow + hollow.

parole.significato: The spinal cord.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”).

parole.significato: The infestation of a living vertebrate by maggots.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυῖα (muîa, “fly”) + -iasis.

parole.significato: Any of the extinct genus †Mylodon of giant ground sloths of Patagonia.
parole.testo: From the genus name, from Ancient Greek μύλη (múlē, “mill”) + translingual -odon.

parole.significato: Any rock that has undergone modifications due to dynamic recrystallization following plastic flow; a schist created by…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυλών (mulṓn, “mill”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Muscle.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse; muscle”).

parole.significato: Divination by interpreting rats or mice. Their cries were believed to indicate the presence of evil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse”); myo- + -mancy.

parole.significato: myoneme
parole.testo: From myo- + the root of Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to show”) (for unclear reasons).

parole.significato: A disorder of the vision where distant objects appear blurred because the eye focuses their images in front of the reti…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μυωπία (muōpía, “shortsightedness”), from μύω (múō, “to shut, close”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: The appearance of muscae volitantes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυῖα (muîa, “fly”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “sight”). Although myopia is superficially very similar in both the English and original Greek forms, the first parts of the two compounds aren't related.

parole.significato: Any of a large family of motor proteins found in eukaryotic tissues, allowing mobility in muscles.
parole.testo: From myo- (“relating to muscle”), and Ancient Greek μυός (muós), genitive of μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + -in.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the muscles.
parole.testo: Irregular formation from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) (genitive μυός (muós)) + -itis.

parole.significato: A ruler or commander over 10,000 people, particularly
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυριάρχης (muriárkhēs) in Herodotus or μυρίαρχος (muríarkhos) in Xenophon, from μυρίος (muríos, “myriad, ten thousand”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs) or -αρχος (-arkhos, “-arch: ruler, commander”), calque of Old Persian *baivarapatiš. As a Mongolian commander, Calque of Mongolian tümen-ü noy

parole.significato: A picture made up of several smaller pictures, drawn upon separate cards so that they can be combined in many different…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυρίος (muríos, “countless, endless, infinite”) + Ancient Greek ὅραμα (hórama, “sight”). By surface analysis, myri- + -orama.

parole.significato: Any holothurian of the family Myriotrochidae
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυρίος (muríos) + Ancient Greek τροχός (trokhós) + -id.

parole.significato: ant
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μύρμηκος (múrmēkos, “ant’s”), genitive of μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”). Doublet of the obsolete term mire.

parole.significato: The study of ants.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek myrmeco- (“ant”) + -logy (“study (of)”).

parole.significato: chrism; myrrh
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μῠ́ρον (mŭ́ron).

parole.significato: fragrant, perfumed
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek μύρον (múron, “unguent, perfume”), + -ic.

parole.significato: dirt, filth
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μύσος (músos, “uncleanness”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the upper lip, or moustache.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μύσταξ (mústax, “moustache”), whence also moustache.

parole.significato: Of or relating to mystagogy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Ancient Greek μυσταγωγικός (mustagōgikós), corresponding to mystagogue + -ic.

parole.significato: Doctrine and knowledge pertaining to secrets and mystery
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “mystery”) + -sophy (“knowledge or wisdom”).

parole.significato: A speech disorder manifesting as an abnormal repetition of the sound /m/ or replacement of consonants with m-like sound…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυτακισμός (mutakismós, “fondness of the letter mu”). By surface analysis from mu (Greek letter representing /m/) + -tacism.

parole.significato: A traditional story which embodies a belief regarding some fact or phenomenon of experience, and in which often the for…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”). Attested in English since 1830. Doublet of mythos.

parole.significato: myth
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos).

parole.significato: A basic core element, motif or theme of a myth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell mythical tales”), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “myth-teller”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “mythical narrative”) + -λόγος (-lógos). The -em could be interpreted as an analogue of -eme.

parole.significato: the subject of a myth; the material covered in a given myth.
parole.testo: From mytho- +Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma).

parole.significato: Creation of any myth.
parole.testo: From mytho- + -poeia, dated 1846 CE, based on Ancient Greek μυθοποιία (muthopoiía, “myth-making”).

parole.significato: Giving rise to myths; pertaining to the creation of myth.
parole.testo: From Hellenistic Ancient Greek μυθοποιία (muthopoiía, “mythopoeia”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A mythmaker.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μυθοποίησις (muthopoíēsis, “mythmaking”), from Ancient Greek μυθοποιώ (muthopoiṓ, “to mythmake”).

parole.significato: Creation of myth.
parole.testo: Attested since 1882; mytho- + Latin poesis, based after Ancient Greek μυθοποίησις (muthopoíēsis).

parole.significato: mucus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μῠ́ξᾰ (mŭ́xă, “mucus”). By surface analysis, myx- + -o-.

parole.significato: A rhizopod or moneran.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “mucus, slime”) + -pod.

parole.significato: Any of a group of RNA viruses of the Orthomyxoviridae and Paramyxoviridae families.
parole.testo: From myxo- + virus, from Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “mucus”), because they react with mucin (mucoprotein) on the surface of red blood cells.

parole.significato: Any member of the family Myzopodidae of bats; Madagascar sucker-footed bat.
parole.testo: From the family name, from Ancient Greek μυζάω (muzáō, “suck”) + πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: A member of an ancient Christian Gnostic sect who claimed to have been taught their doctrines by Mariamne, a disciple o…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek, possibly from Hebrew נָחָשׁ (“snake”).

parole.significato: A small male filament in certain green algae.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos, “dwarf”) + ἀνδρός (andrós, “male”) + -ium.

parole.significato: An extreme form of micromelia.
parole.testo: From nano- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Any phanerophyte between about 10 and 80 inches in height
parole.testo: From nano- (“tiny”) + phanerophyte, from Ancient Greek φανερός (phanerós, “visible”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: The study of ecclesiastical or sacred buildings.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ναός (naós, “temple”) + -logy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to stupor, sleep, or a state of unconsciousness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “I put to sleep”); in terms relating to drugs, it is a back-formation from narcotics, which ultimately derives from the same source.

parole.significato: Unconsciousness caused by a drug, anaesthetic or other chemical substance.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νάρκωσις (nárkōsis). By surface analysis, narco- + -osis.

parole.significato: A western vestibule leading to the nave in some Christian churches.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νάρθηξ (nárthēx, “giant fennel; casket”), a Pre-Greek word, as suggested by the suffix. See also νάρδος (nárdos, “nard”).

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring a ship's heeling or inclination at sea.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ναῦς (naûs, “ship”) + ῥοπή (rhopḗ, “weight”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The supposed ability to detect incoming ships, before they come into visual range, by studying certain atmospheric effe…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ναῦς (naûs, “ship”) + -scopy.

parole.significato: Shaped like the hull of a ship.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós) + -iform.

parole.significato: The contemplation of one's navel as an aid to meditation.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek ὀμφαλοσκοπία (omphaloskopía). By surface analysis, navel + gazing.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Nazareth or its people.
parole.testo: In the sense "person from Nazareth", from Ancient Greek Ναζαρηνός (Nazarēnós, “of Nazareth”), an ethnonym of Ναζαρέθ (Nazaréth). In the sense "a member of a certain sect", from Ancient Greek Ναζωραῖος (Nazōraîos), which may or may not be related. For a list of theories as to the further etymology of

parole.significato: Relating to youth or the early stages.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεανικός (neanikós), from νεᾱνῐ́ᾱς (neānĭ́ās, “young person”) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: Clouded with indistinct colour markings.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?]

parole.significato: Death or dead tissue.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεκρός (nekrós, “dead body”), from the Proto-Indo-European suffixed full-grade *nekro- of *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”); see also Middle Welsh angheu (“death”), Breton ankou, Old Irish éc, Latin noxius (“harmful”), nocēo (“to hurt, harm”), nex (“murder, violent death”) (as opposed t

parole.significato: A kind of foul-smelling feldspar.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: The name of a person who has died.
parole.testo: From necro- + -onym; from Ancient Greek νεκρός (nekrós, “death”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: An animal that eats dead and decaying flesh.
parole.testo: Composed by necro- + -phage, from Ancient Greek νεκροφάγος (nekrophágos), from νεκρός (nekrós, “cadaver”) and φάγος (phágos, “one who eats”).

parole.significato: A pathological attraction to dead bodies.
parole.testo: From necro- (Ancient Greek νεκρός (nekrós, “corpse, dead”)) + -philia (Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “affection”)), after German Nekrophilie (in Krafft-Ebing 1887).

parole.significato: The localized death of cells or tissues through injury, disease, or the interruption of blood supply.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis), equivalent to necro- + -osis.

parole.significato: swimming, nektonic
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νηκτός (nēktós, “swimming”). Compare nekton.

parole.significato: A limb adapted for swimming in certain molluscs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νηκτός (nēktós, “swimming”) + -pod. By surface analysis, necto- + -pod.

parole.significato: Any member of the Neleidae, the descendants of Neleus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νηλεῖδαι (nēleîdai).

parole.significato: A variety of brucite, occurring in slender fibers which are elastic and easily separated, having a color of white with…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῆμα (nêma, “thread”) + -lite.

parole.significato: Characteristic of, pertaining to, or possessing a filiform structure.
parole.testo: Representing νημᾰτ- (nēmăt-), the stem of the Ancient Greek νῆμᾰ (nêmă, “thread”). Compare -nema.

parole.significato: A kind of fructification on certain red algae, consisting of an external mass of filaments that separate into tetraspor…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῆμα (nêma, “thread”) (compare nemato-) + θήκη (thḗkē, “sheath”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Whose molecules align in loose parallel lines.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νήματος (nḗmatos), genitive of νῆμα (nêma, “thread”).

parole.significato: An enemy, especially an archenemy.
parole.testo: From the Greek goddess of retribution Nemesis (Ancient Greek Νέμεσις (Némesis)).

parole.significato: We have won (the cry of Pheidippides after reaching Athens from Marathon).
parole.testo: Transliteration of Ancient Greek νενικήκαμεν (nenikḗkamen, “we are victorious”).

parole.significato: A helot who was freed from the Spartan army after serving as a hoplite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νεοδαμώδεις (neodamṓdeis).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the New World, or Western Hemisphere.
parole.testo: From neo- + Ancient Greek γαῖα (gaîa, “earth”) + -an.

parole.significato: Of a geologic period within the Cenozoic era, comprising the Miocene, Pliocene, Pleistocene and Holocene epochs from ab…
parole.testo: From neo- + -gene. From Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”) + γενεά (geneá, “generation”). Compare Ancient Greek νεογενής (neogenḗs).

parole.significato: The guardian of a temple in Ancient Greece
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νεώκορος (neṓkoros).

parole.significato: One who coins a new word or new words.
parole.testo: Back-formation from neologism, equivalent to Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”) + -ist. Compare French néologiste.

parole.significato: The rearing of offspring by animals
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol Ne) with an atomic number of 10. The second of the noble gases, it is a colourless, odorle…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νέον (néon), neuter of νέος (néos, “new”), from earlier *νέϝος (*néwos), from Proto-Hellenic *newos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. By surface analysis, neo- + -on (suffix used in all noble gases).

parole.significato: A word or phrase which has recently been coined; a new word or phrase, a neologism.
parole.testo: Formed irregularly from the Ancient Greek νέον (néon) (neon: neuter singular form of νέος (néos), neos, “new”) + the English -ism; compare the closely related neo- and neon, as well as the earlier synonym neologism.

parole.significato: The salivary secretion various swift species use to make their nests.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: The study of young birds.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: An innovation or novelty
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεότερος (neóteros) + -ism.

parole.significato: A neologist (someone who introduces new words)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεότερος (neóteros, “newer”) + -ist.

parole.significato: To neologize, to coin as a new word.
parole.testo: Since the 1870s; from Ancient Greek νεωτερίζω (neōterízō, “to (forcibly) innovate; to revolutionize”) (from νεώτερος (neṓteros, “newer”)). By surface analysis, neoteric + -ize.

parole.significato: The practice of abstaining completely from the drinking of alcohol; teetotalism
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νηφάλιος (nēphálios, “sober”), from νήφω (nḗphō, “to be sober”).

parole.significato: One who practises nephalism; a teetotaller
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νηφάλιος (nēphálios, “sober”), from νήφω (nḗphō, “to be sober”).

parole.significato: Producing clouds of smoke.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”) + -genous. Coined by Oliver Wendell Holmes in 1862.

parole.significato: A feldspathoid mineral of silica-poor igneous, plutonic and volcanic rocks. Chemically, nepheline is a plagioclase feld…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”), because crystals become cloudy when exposed to acid, + -ine.

parole.significato: Synonym of nepheline.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”) + -ite.

parole.significato: The act of seeking and finding shapes in clouds.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Νεφελοκοκκυγία (Nephelokokkugía). The word comes from the play The Birds by the Greek playwright Aristophanes.

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring various aspects of the suspended particles in a fluid; especially in a colloid.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The measurement of the concentration of a solution, suspension or dispersion based upon its light-scattering properties.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”) + -metry.

parole.significato: An instrument for demonstrating cloud formation by compression of moist air.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”) + -scope.

parole.significato: cloud
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νέφος (néphos, “cloud”).

parole.significato: Relating to or connected with a kidney.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the kidneys.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφρός (nephrós).

parole.significato: The basic structural and functional unit of the kidney, which filters the blood in order to regulate chemical concentra…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”) + -on.

parole.significato: A genetic disorder of the kidneys which affects children.
parole.testo: From nephron + -o- + phthisis (“progressive wasting disease”), from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis, “wasting away, perishing, decay”).

parole.significato: A kidney-like organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”).

parole.significato: immature
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νήπιος (nḗpios, “infant”) -n- + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of infantophilia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νήπιος (nḗpios, “infant”) and φιλία (philía, “(fraternal) love”).

parole.significato: Wakefulness and watchfulness; a state of sobriety following a period of catharsis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νῆψις (nêpsis)

parole.significato: A period of 600 years.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῆρος (nêros), from Akkadian 𒐞 (nēr).

parole.significato: insular; of islands
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νησιώτης (nēsiṓtēs, “islander”).

parole.significato: Relating to Nesogaea—Polynesia or Oceania, New Zealand excepted, with regard to the distribution of its animals.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νήσος (nḗsos, “island”) + γαῖα (gaîa, “the Earth”) + -an.

parole.significato: Synonym of orthosilicate.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῆσος (nêsos, “island”) + silicate.

parole.significato: Medical treatment by reducing food intake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νῆστις (nêstis, “fasting”) + therapy.

parole.significato: A wise old man, especially one who serves as a counselor or adviser.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Νέστωρ (Néstōr), possibly from νέομαι (néomai, “to return safely”), νόστος (nóstos, “homecoming”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the nerves, neurons or the nervous system.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “a sinew, nerve”) + -al.

parole.significato: Relating to the nerves, nervous tissue, or the nervous system.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νευρο- (neuro-), combining form of νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”). By surface analysis, neur- + -o-.

parole.significato: An aversion to or fear of neurology or the nervous system, especially among medical students or professionals intimidat…
parole.testo: Combination of neuro- + -phobia, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve, sinew”) and Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A fibrous network of nervous tissue that forms the gray matter of the brain
parole.testo: Probably an abbreviation of obsolete neuropilema, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”) + πίλημα (pílēma, “felt”); or neuro- + Ancient Greek πῖλος (pîlos, “hair”).

parole.significato: neuropil
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”) + πίλημα (pílēma, “felt”).

parole.significato: Strong reaction or overreaction of a nerve to a stimulus.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron) + Ancient Greek σθένος (sthénos). By surface analysis, neuro- (“nerve”) + sthen- (“strength”) + -ia (“disease”).

parole.significato: Affected with a neurosis.
parole.testo: Formed of neuro- (“of nerves or the nervous system”) + -otic (“having abnormal condition”). The initial element, in turn, is from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”). Attested from the 17th century. Compare French névrotique.

parole.significato: A line segment of prescribed length, fitted between two given curves, part of a line that passes through a given point.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νεῦσις (neûsis, “inclination, tendency”), from νεύω (neúō).

parole.significato: A woman of great pulchritude.
parole.testo: An attributive use of Ancient Greek Νέαιρα (Néaira, “Neæra”), a nymph of Greek mythology.

parole.significato: To be kept hidden, in the manner of the Pharisee Nicodemus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Νῑκόδημος (Nīkódēmos), from νῑ́κη (nī́kē, “victory”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”).

parole.significato: An athletic shoe or other piece of athletic gear produced or licensed by athletic brand Nike.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Νίκη (Níkē), from νίκη (níkē, “victory”).

parole.significato: A crying woman; a woman who is bereaved or inconsolable.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Νιόβη (Nióbē).

parole.significato: A triclinic brown mineral containing fluorine, hydrogen, iron, manganese, niobium, oxygen, potassium, silicon, sodium,…
parole.testo: For its composition of niobium, and Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”) for its foliated crystal habit, + -ite.

parole.significato: The ecclesiastical ceremony of washing the feet; maundy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νιπτήρ (niptḗr, “basin”).

parole.significato: nitrate, nitrogen
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron). See niter.

parole.significato: The perceived as perceived
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόημα (nóēma, “concept”, “idea”, “perception”, “thought”).

parole.significato: A timing instrument, used to measure the duration of various cognitive tasks.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόημα (nóēma, “the understanding”) + tacho- + -graph.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the understanding.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νοηματικός (noēmatikós, “rational, of or related to thought”). See noetic.

parole.significato: Cognition, the functioning of intellect.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νόησις (nóēsis, “concept”, “idea”, “intelligence”, “understanding”), from νοεῖν (noeîn, “to intend”, “to perceive”, “to see”, “to understand”) (from νοῦς (noûs, “mind”, “thought”), from νόος (nóos)) + -σις (-sis), suffix forming nouns of action.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the mind or intellect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νοητικός (noētikós), ultimately from νοέω (noéō, “I see, understand”).

parole.significato: law, legislation
parole.testo: Representing νομ- (nom-), the stem of the Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “law”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to nomads.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νομαδικός (nomadikós), equivalent to nomad (“a member of a society or class of herdsmen”) + -ic (forming adjectives).

parole.significato: The governor of an ancient Egyptian nome.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νομάρχης (nomárkhēs), νόμαρχος (nómarkhos), corresponding to nome + -arch.

parole.significato: A type of musical composition in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos), from νέμω (némō, “to divide”). Differs from Etymology 1 in the position of Ancient Greek accent, though from the same root. Doublet of nomos and namus.

parole.significato: Customary; ordinary; applied to the usual spelling of a language, in distinction from strictly phonetic methods.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νομικός (nomikós, “relating to laws”), from νόμος (nómos, “law, custom”).

parole.significato: The following of religious laws or commandments as the chief aspect of religiousness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “law”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Money or currency (modern).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma), from νομίζω (nomízō, “to use customarily”) + -μα (-ma, “nominal suffix”), from νόμος (nómos, “custom”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix), from νέμω (némō, “to distribute”) + -ος (-os). Related to French numismatique, Latin numismat- + -ique, varia

parole.significato: law
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos).

parole.significato: Having a separate and simple tendon to flex the first toe, or hallux.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “division, distribution”) + πέλμα (pélma, “sole of the foot”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A magistrate, in ancient Greece, who was the custodian of the texts of the law.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νομοφύλαξ (nomophúlax, “nomophylax”), from νόμος (nómos, “law”) + φύλαξ (phúlax, “guard”).

parole.significato: The body of law, especially that governing human behaviour.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos). Doublet of nome and namus.

parole.significato: A territorial division of ancient Egypt; a nome.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “district”), from νέμω (némō, “to divide”). Doublet of nome.

parole.significato: A lawgiver; a legislator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νομοθέτης (nomothétēs, “law-giver”).

parole.significato: Relating to the underlying laws of a subject.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νομοθετικός (nomothetikós).

parole.significato: system defining laws or rules
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νομοθετικός (nomothetikós).

parole.significato: Rule by intellect; a government which weds power with intelligence.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόος (nóos, “mind”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: The systematic study and organization of everything dealing with knowing and knowledge.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόος (nóos, “mind”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy”), equivalent to noos + -logy.

parole.significato: Any substance purported to increase or enhance cognitive abilities.
parole.testo: Coined by Romanian psychologist and chemist Corneliu E. Giurgea in 1972, derived from the Ancient Greek words νόος (nóos, “mind”) and τροπέω (tropéō, “to turn”). By surface analysis, noo(s) + -tropic, literally “mind changing”.

parole.significato: disease
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νοσο- (noso-, “disease”), combining form of νόσος (nósos, “disease”).

parole.significato: An abnormal fear of hospitals.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: The ability of a person to recognize his or her own medical disorder.
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) and γνῶσις (gnôsis, “knowledge”).

parole.significato: Producing disease.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) + ποιητικός (poiētikós, “producing”).

parole.significato: an overwhelming desire to return to familiar surroundings, or to one's home
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “a return home”) + -mania.

parole.significato: A fear of, or aversion to, returning to one's home.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “a return home”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: A homecoming, as after a long journey.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos).

parole.significato: A bone formed of fused vertebrae behind the shoulder of many species of birds and pterosaurs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῶτον (nôton, “back”).

parole.significato: Used to form names of taxonomic ranks of hybrids
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νόθος (nóthos, “crossbred”).

parole.significato: Relating to a nothogenus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νόθος (nóthos, “bastard”) + generic.

parole.significato: Any of various sharks of the obsolete family Notidanidae, at present corresponding to the Hexanchidae.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: south, southern
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νότος (nótos) "south".

parole.significato: back
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νῶτον (nôton) "back (part of body)".

parole.significato: A triangular opening at the back edge of a brachiopod's brachial valve through which the pedicle may partially protrude.
parole.testo: From noto-, from Ancient Greek νῶτον (nôton) + θῠ́ρᾱ (thŭ́rā) + -ium.

parole.significato: Any of several extinct, hoofed, herbivorous mammals of the order †Notoungulata, from Cenozoic South America.
parole.testo: From Notoungulata (order name), from Ancient Greek νότος (nótos, “south”) + Ungulata.

parole.significato: The back; the dorsal side of the thorax in insects or nudibranches.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῶτον (nôton).

parole.significato: The mind or intellect, faculty for rationality or reason using the necessary common sense or awareness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νοῦς (noûs) or νόος (nóos, “mind”).

parole.significato: Being or relating to a form of Evangelical Protestant pastoral counseling based upon the Bible and focused on Christ.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νουθετέω (nouthetéō, “to admonish”).

parole.significato: The letter of the Greek alphabet Ν (N) and ν (n).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νῦ (nû), name for the letter of the Greek alphabet Ν (N) and ν (n).

parole.significato: A period of one day and one night, a date: in the West, a period of 24 consecutive hours.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νυχθήμερον (nukhthḗmeron), noun use of the neuter singular form of νυχθήμερος (nukhthḗmeros, “lasting a day and night”), from νύξ (núx, “night”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

parole.significato: Night or darkness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νύκτ- (núkt-), stem of νύξ (núx, “night”).

parole.significato: The inability to see clearly in dim light; night blindness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νυκταλωπία (nuktalōpía), from νύξ (núx, “night”), ἀλαός (alaós, “blind”), and ὄψ (óps, “eye”).

parole.significato: Night.
parole.testo: From Latinized form of Ancient Greek νυκτι- (nukti-), from νύξ (núx, “night”).

parole.significato: Turning or bending at night into different positions.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νύχτατροπικός (núkhtatropikós, literally “night-turning”).

parole.significato: nympha, nymphae (labia minora).
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young woman, adolescent girl”).

parole.significato: A person in a state of nympholepsy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νυμφόληπτος (numphólēptos, “caught by nymphs, frenzied”), from νύμφη (númphē) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “I take”).

parole.significato: Any of various colonial marine hydroids of the genus Obelia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀβελία (obelía, “a round cake”).

parole.significato: A craniometric point on the sagittal suture between the parietal foramina near the lambdoid suture.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀβελός (obelós) + -ion.

parole.significato: To mark (a written or printed passage) with an obelus; to judge as spurious or doubtful.
parole.testo: From Hellenic Ancient Greek ὀβελίζειν (obelízein), from ὀβελός (obelós, “obelus”).

parole.significato: Synonym of obolus: a silver coin of Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós, literally “spit”). Doublet of obole and pul.

parole.significato: A manipulator of a mob who holds sway by use of inflammatory rhetoric, casting opprobrium, and by appeal to the lowest…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀχλαγωγός (okhlagōgós), from ὄχλος (ókhlos, “mob”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “leading, guiding”).

parole.significato: Crowd-poisoning; a disease occasioned or aggravated by overcrowding, especially due to lack of ventilation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὄχλος (ókhlos, “multitude, crowd”) + -esis.

parole.significato: Crowd, mob.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄχλος (ókhlos, “crowd”).

parole.significato: A person with a phobia, or fear, of mob-like crowds, as opposed to simply open spaces like agoraphobia or large crowds…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὄχλος (ókhlos, “crowd”) + -phobist.

parole.significato: A personality type characterised by avoidance of dangerous of unfamiliar situations, and the reliance on other people f…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀκνέω (oknéō, “to shrink from, fear, hesitate”) + -o- + -phile with the final "e" dropped. Coined by Hungarian psychoanalyst Michael Balint in 1955.

parole.significato: Eight.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀκτα- (okta-, “eight”); compare ὀκτώ (oktṓ).

parole.significato: A musical instrument with eight strings.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: A four-dimensional object analogous to a cube, constructed out of eight cubes.
parole.testo: From octa- (“eight”) + -choron (“room”), from Ancient Greek ὀκτά- (oktá-, “eight”) and χῶρος (khôros, “room”).

parole.significato: Synonym of octennium: An 8-year period, particularly (historical) in Greek calendrical and astronomical calculations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀκταετηρίς (oktaetērís, “8-year [period]”).

parole.significato: a polyhedron with eight faces; the regular octahedron has regular triangles as faces and is one of the Platonic solids.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀκτάεδρον (oktáedron). By surface analysis, octa- + -hedron.

parole.significato: A variant of octo-, used for multiplication with a second numerical prefix: octakishexahedron
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀκτάκις (oktákis, “eight times”).

parole.significato: A metre or verse of eight feet.
parole.testo: From octa- + -pody, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) and πούς, ποδός (poús, podós, “foot”).

parole.significato: A poem or strophe of eight verses or lines.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀκτάστιχος (oktástikhos). By surface analysis, octa- + stich.

parole.significato: Any of the Octodontidae, a family of rodents including the common degu (Octodon degus) and 12 other South American spec…
parole.testo: From Octodon + -id < Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + ὀδών (odṓn, “tooth”), according to the wear pattern of the teeth of these rodents, which resembles a figure 8.

parole.significato: A member of the crab family Ocypodidae.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: An ancient Greek or Roman building used for performances of music and poetry.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ᾠδεῖον (ōideîon), from ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).

parole.significato: A volatile liquid, said to have an unpleasant garlicky odour, obtained by boiling sulfur with linseed oil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀδμή (odmḗ, “stench”) + -yl.

parole.significato: Relating to roads.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road, path, way”).

parole.significato: The study of roads or paths.
parole.testo: Coined by John Brinckerhof Jackson, from Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road, path, way”) + -logy.

parole.significato: tooth
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”).

parole.significato: The generation, or mode of development, of the teeth.
parole.testo: From odonto- (root of Ancient Greek ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”) + root of Ancient Greek γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born”). Compare French odontogénie.

parole.significato: Resembling a tooth, especially in shape
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ὀδών (odṓn, “tooth”) + -oid

parole.significato: An identifying name given to a street; a street name.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”), equivalent to odo- + -onym. Compare French odonyme and Italian odonimo.

parole.significato: Synonym of od (“a hypothetical force or natural power, now proved not to exist, which was supposed by Carl Reichenbach…
parole.testo: From od + Ancient Greek ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood; material, matter, substance”).

parole.significato: Synonym of algometer.

parole.significato: A type of metamorphic rock formed from clay-rich sediments called pelites.

parole.significato: Leaf, leaves.
parole.testo: Combining form of Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greece, the showering of a victorious athlete or bridal couple with leaves or flower petals.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φυλλοβολία (phullobolía), from φύλλον (phúllon) and βάλλω (bállō).

parole.significato: tribes, races or phyla

parole.significato: A tubercle, tumor, or abscess on any external part of the body.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φῦμα (phûma).

parole.significato: One should attend to one's own flaws or defects before presuming to advise others about theirs.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek ἰατρέ, θεράπευσον σεαυτόν (iatré, therápeuson seautón) and Latin medice, cūrā tē ipsum, from Luke 4:23.

parole.significato: physical; pertaining to physics
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek; see physical.

parole.significato: nature
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φῠ́σῐς (phŭ́sĭs, “nature”).

parole.significato: The study of physiognomy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμονικός (phusiognōmonikós, “physiognomic”).

parole.significato: A natural philosophy concerning natural history and relationships.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek physio- (“nature”) + philosophy.

parole.significato: Knowledge or wisdom concerning nature.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek physio- (“nature”) + -sophy (“knowledge, wisdom”).

parole.significato: Nature, as contrasted with law or custom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis).

parole.significato: A mainly Scandinavian medical specialty that deals with musculoskeletal physiology and diseases.
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis, “nature”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: A combining form meaning “bladder,” used in the formation of compound words.

parole.significato: A fish whose swim bladder is not open to its esophagus. .

parole.significato: A form of microsome present in the cytoplasm of some algae
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φυσοειδής (phusoeidḗs, “like a bladder”), from φῦσα (phûsa). By surface analysis, physo- + -ode.

parole.significato: An enlargement of the abdomen in certain insects, especially in termite queens.
parole.testo: From physo- + Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “belly”) + -y.

parole.significato: Any siphonophore of the suborder Physonectae
parole.testo: From the taxon name, from physo- + Ancient Greek νηκτός (nēktós, “swimming”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or derived from plants.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek φῠτόν (phŭtón, “plant”).

parole.significato: nature printing
parole.testo: From phyto- + Ancient Greek γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”) + -y.

parole.significato: The study of methods for uniquely recognizing or predicting physiological processes in plants based upon one or more in…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek (phyto) "plant" + (metron) "measure".

parole.significato: One of the parts which by their repetition make up a flowering plant, each being a single joint of a stem with its leaf…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φυτόν (phutón, “plant”).

parole.significato: Plankton, especially those small in size, that obtain energy by photosynthesis.
parole.testo: From phyto- + plankton. From Ancient Greek φυτόν (phutón, “plant”) + πλαγκτόν (planktón), neuter of πλαγκτός (planktós, “wandering”). However, they are no longer classified as plants, so the terminology is showing a historical meaning.

parole.significato: A small, water-filled cavity in a tree or any similar environment such as the axil of a bromeliad
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φυτόν (phutón, “plant”) + τέλμα (télma, “pond”).

parole.significato: A variety of high-magnesium olivine basalt.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”) + -ite.

parole.significato: bitter
parole.testo: Ancient Greek πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”).

parole.significato: A fibrous variety of serpentine, possibly antigorite.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”) + -lite: compare French picrolithe.

parole.significato: A colourless viscous substance having a bittersweet taste, formerly supposed to be the essential principle of bile, but…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?], meaning "bitter honey".

parole.significato: A triclinic-pinacoidal mineral containing arsenic, calcium, hydrogen, magnesium, and oxygen.
parole.testo: For its composition: from Ancient Greek πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”) in allusion to its magnesium content and φάρμακον (phármakon, “drug, medicine, poison”) for its arsenic content, with the mineral suffix from λίθος (líthos, “stone”). It is similar but not closely related to pharmacolite.

parole.significato: The Muses.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Πιερίδες (Pierídes).

parole.significato: Forms terms related to piezoelectricity or other effects of mechanical stress or pressure.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πῐέζω (pĭézō, “to squeeze”).

parole.significato: A regmaglypt.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πιέζειν (piézein, “to press, squeeze”), and γλυπτόν (gluptón, “a carving, sculpture”).

parole.significato: A cap of cells covering the growing extremity of a root; a rootcap.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πῖλος (pîlos, “cap”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”).

parole.significato: The free-swimming larva of certain proboscis worms, somewhat resembling a deerstalker hat. It has no resemblance to its…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πῑλίδιον (pīlídion, “little cap”), diminutive of πῖλος (pîlos), probably influenced by other formations in -idium, like miracidium, planidium, and coracidium.

parole.significato: A hexagonal mineral containing hydrogen, nickel, oxygen, and silicon.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πιμελή (pimelḗ, “fat”) for being a mineral with a greasy appearance, + -ite.

parole.significato: The outermost layer of cells (pinacocytes) in the phylum Porifera (sponges), equivalent to the epidermis, and character…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet, dish, plank”) + -derm.

parole.significato: The face of a crystal parallel to two of the axes.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek πινάκιον (pinákion, “slab, tablet”) + -oid.

parole.significato: any tetra-substituted derivative of ethylene glycol, of general formula R₂C(OH)-C(OH)R₂, especially the simplest exampl…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet”) + -ol. Actualized from pinacone.

parole.significato: Synonym of pinacol.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet”) ̺+ -one. So called because it unites with water to form tablet-shaped crystals.

parole.significato: A chitin plate on the skin of a caterpillar.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax) + Latin -ulum.

parole.significato: A monoclinic-prismatic black mineral containing boron, magnesium, manganese, and oxygen.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πινάκιον (pinákion, “tablet”) and λίθος (líthos, “stone”) because of the thin, tabular appearance of the crystals.

parole.significato: An ancient pinax or tablet.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πινάκιον (pinákion).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or similar to pirates.
parole.testo: From Latin pīrāticus + -al, from Ancient Greek πειρᾱτικός (peirātikós); equivalent to pirate + -ical.

parole.significato: The fear of trusting people or one's partner in a romantic relationship.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίστις (pístis, “trust”) + anthro- + -phobia.

parole.significato: The science or study of faith.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίστις (pístis, “faith”) + -ology.

parole.significato: ape.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίθηκος (píthēkos, “ape, monkey”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the anthropoid apes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πῐθηκοειδής (pĭthēkoeidḗs, “ape-like”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of apes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίθηκος (píthēkos, “ape”) + -ology.

parole.significato: A form of hysteria that can be cured by persuasive suggestion.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πείθω (peíthō) + -ism; coined by Joseph Babinski.

parole.significato: A large ceramic jar used by certain ancient civilizations that bordered the Mediterranean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πίθος (píthos).

parole.significato: A dark blue dyestuff obtained from wood-tar oil, the first to be commercially produced.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek pitch + beautiful: compare French pittacale.

parole.significato: The abnormal and irrational fear of stickers, sticky labels and (sometimes, also) adhesive materials such as glue.
