Field gives the word's formation as Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion, “*sticker”) + -o- + -phobia (used to form nouns meaning the fear of a specific thing), as a neoclassical compound. In reality, this Ancient Greek word does not mean sticker, but Lati

parole.significato: Having the form of, or resembling, bran.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πίτυρον (píturon, “bran”) + -oid.

parole.significato: Provided with or relating to a flat plate or plates.
parole.testo: From (combining form of) Ancient Greek πλάξ (pláx, “plate, tablet”).

parole.significato: Platelike; having irregular, platelike, bony scales, often bearing spines; pertaining to the placoid fish
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλάξ (pláx, stem plak-) + -oid.

parole.significato: A little plate or plaque.
parole.testo: From Latinized form of Ancient Greek πλάκα (pláka, “plate”), from πλάξ (pláx), + -ula.

parole.significato: Having an oblique spiral arrangement of planes, as in levorotatory and dextrorotatory crystals.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios, “oblique”). Also, plagio- + -hedral.

parole.significato: Any trematode of the order Plagiorchiida
parole.testo: From Plagiorchi(s) + -id, from Ancient Greek πλάγῐος (plágĭos, “sideways, slanted”) + Ancient Greek ὄρχῐς (órkhĭs, “testicle”).

parole.significato: A flatbread, of Ancient Greek origin, thought to be a precursor of pizza.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πλακοῦς (plakoûs).

parole.significato: A person who collects dolls.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλαγγών (plangṓn, “(wax) doll”) + -ologist.

parole.significato: The first-instar larva of any species of parasitoidal insect in which the life cycle is an example of hypermetamorphosi…
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”) + -idium.

parole.significato: Related to plankton.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλαγκτόν (planktón, “drifting”), neuter nominative of πλαγκτός (planktós), from πλάζομαι (plázomai, “to wander, drift”), mediopassive of πλάζω (plázō, “to cause to wander, drive astray”). By surface analysis, plankt- + -o-.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to (blood) plasma.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “anything formed or molded”) (genitive πλάσματος (plásmatos)) + -ic.

parole.significato: A microscopic channel traversing the cell walls of plant cells and some algal cells, enabling transport and communicati…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”) + δέσμα (désma).

parole.significato: Fragmentation or division of the cytoplasm without nuclear division.
parole.testo: From plasm + -o- + schisis, from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something molded”).

parole.significato: A set of proteins...

parole.significato: An overly broad or full style of pronunciation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλατειασμός (plateiasmós, “flat, broad pronunciation, describing the Dorians”), from πλατεῖα (plateîa), πλατύς (platús, “flat, broad”).

parole.significato: One of a pair of a paired organ.

parole.significato: flat; especially, relatively flat but wide

parole.significato: Shortness of breath that occurs when the patient is upright, that is, sufficient breathing only when lying flat.

parole.significato: The tissue (prosenchyma or pseudoparenchyma) of a fungus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλεκτός (plektós, “plaited, wicker”, from πλέκω (plékō)) + -enchyma.

parole.significato: the study of complexity and its underlying simplicity
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλεκτός (plektós, “braided”) + -ics, but invented by Murray Gell-Mann.

parole.significato: A loop of helices (especially of nucleic acid) twisted together such that they cannot be separated without breaking them
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλεκτός (plektós, “twisted”) + Ancient Greek νῆμα (nêma, “thread”).

parole.significato: A device for measuring the force of a blow or stroke.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πληγή (plēgḗ, “stroke = blow”) + -o- + -meter.

parole.significato: The influence of a single gene on multiple phenotypic traits; pleiotropism.
parole.testo: Coined by German zoologist Ludwig Plate in 1910, from Ancient Greek πλείων (pleíōn) + -tropy; by surface analysis, pleio- + -tropy.

parole.significato: Of a geologic epoch within the Quaternary period from about 2,588,000 to 11,700 years ago (earlier definition 1.7 milli…

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek pottery vessel with a high foot supporting a wide bowl.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek πλημοχόη (plēmokhóē)

parole.significato: supernumerary; many; more.
parole.testo: From the Ancient Greek πλείων (pleíōn), πλέων (pléōn), πλεῖον (pleîon, “more”).

parole.significato: A black variety of spinel.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?] abundant, rich; compare French pléonaste.

parole.significato: Greedy; covetous.

parole.significato: Excessive or insatiable greed, avarice, covetousness, the desire to have more, a greedy desire for certain goods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πλεονεξία (pleonexía, “greediness”).

parole.significato: honey-pot ant
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλήρης (plḗrēs, “full”) + ergate.

parole.significato: A nebula powered by the pulsar wind of a pulsar.
parole.testo: Coined by Weiler & Panagia (1978), from Ancient Greek πλήρης (plḗrēs, “full”).

parole.significato: Close, near.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλησίον (plēsíon, “near”).

parole.significato: Almost, but not quite, synchronous.
parole.testo: From plesio- + chrono- + -ous from Ancient Greek πλησίον (plēsíon, “near”) + χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

parole.significato: Any of the Plethodontidae, a family of lungless salamanders.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Plethodontidae (family name), from Plethodon (genus name), from Ancient Greek πλῆθος (plêthos, “great number”) + ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”).

parole.significato: A former Greek unit of length equal to 100 Greek feet (podes).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλέθρον (pléthron).

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring changes in volume within an organ or whole body (usually via fluctuations in the amount of…

parole.significato: Any instrument designed to measure small changes in volume, usually via the displacement of water
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πληθυσμός (plēthusmós, “increase”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Capable of being withdrawn by a backward movement of the parts from which it protrudes so that it becomes engulfed.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλευρά (pleurá, “a rib, a side of something”) + Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, stopper”).

parole.significato: A lateral sclerite of a thoracic segment of an arthropod between the tergum and the sternum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πλευρόν (pleurón, “rib, side”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to pleurothetism.

parole.significato: A pattern of orientation among most bivalves whereby they come to rest on their left or right sides.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, pleuro- + -thet(ic) + -ism. (Second element from Ancient Greek τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”).)

parole.significato: Sideways, to the side.

parole.significato: A rare neurological disorder characterized by dystonia and abnormal and sustained involuntary muscle contraction.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλευρόθεν (pleuróthen, “sidewards”) (from πλευρᾱ́ (pleurā́) + -θεν (-then)) + τόνος (tónos, “tension”). By surface analysis, pleurotho- + tonus. See further at opisthotonos.

parole.significato: The organisms that live floating at the surface of water.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλεῦσις (pleûsis, “sailing”), from πλέω (pléō) + -on. The -t- is on analogy with the coordinate terms.

parole.significato: Something used to absorb the energy generated by the strike from a percussion hammer, during medical percussion. Usuall…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλῆξις (plêxis, “stroke, percussion”) + -meter.

parole.significato: A hammer (or other instrument) used to test a person's reflexes.
parole.testo: From Hellenistic Ancient Greek πλῆξις (plêxis, “stroke”) + -or, after flexor etc.

parole.significato: A form of clay that is rich in iron and poor in humus
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Of a geologic epoch within the Neogene period from about 5.3 to 1.7 million years ago; marked by the appearance of huma…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλείων (pleíōn, “more”) + καινός (kainós, “new”). Coined by English philosopher and historian of science William Whewell in 1831 for Charles Lyell, who introduced it in 1833 in his book Principles of Geology. By surface analysis, pleio- + -cene.

parole.significato: Any extinct flightless seabird in the family Plotopteridae.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek πλωτός (plōtós) + -pter + -id.

parole.significato: wealth or money
parole.testo: From combining form of Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth, riches”).

parole.significato: Government by the wealthy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλουτοκρατία (ploutokratía, “rule of the wealthy”), from πλουτοκρατέω (ploutokratéō, “I rule through wealth”), from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth”) + κρατέω (kratéō, “I rule”) (from κράτος (krátos, “power”, “might”)).

parole.significato: Someone who rules by virtue of his or her wealth.
parole.testo: From pluto- + -crat, after plutocracy, from Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth, riches”) + κράτος (krátos, “power, might”).

parole.significato: The science that deals with wealth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth”) + -logy. Coined in the 1870s as a book title, Plutology, where the term was capitalised

parole.significato: Synonym of Plutonian (“of or relating to Pluto, the Greek and Roman god of the underworld; demonic, infernal”).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “Pluto, Greek and Roman god of the underworld”) (from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “riches, wealth”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to fly; to flow; to run”)) + -ων (-ōn)) + -ic (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). The English word is co

parole.significato: A form of exercise that involves the rapid stretching and contracting of muscles to develop muscular power.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλείων (pleíōn, “more”) + -metric (“measure”). Additional details are available in Wikipedia at plyometrics § Etymology.

parole.significato: A neume.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “I blow, breathe”). Doublet of neume.

parole.significato: Relating to air.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma).

parole.significato: A group of cells with spiral secondary wall thickenings, present in a velamen; acts as an airway for gas exchange for r…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma) (breath) and ὁδός (hodós) (pathway)

parole.significato: The study of spiritual beings and phenomena, especially the interactions between humans and God.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “breath”) + -logy.

parole.significato: the alteration of rocks and minerals by gases or magmatic fluid within volcanos etc
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “vapor”) + λύειν (lúein, “to set free”). By surface analysis, pneumato- + -lysis.

parole.significato: Relating to the lungs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”).

parole.significato: Relating to air.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “air”).

parole.significato: Inflammation of the lungs caused by viruses, bacteria or other infectious microorganisms.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía, “lung disease”), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: Any binary compound of a pnictogen
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνίγειν (pnígein, “to choke, to stifle”) (a property of nitrogen), from Pre-Greek, + -ide. By surface analysis, pnicto- + -ide.

parole.significato: Any element from group 15 of the periodic table, which includes nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony and bismuth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πνικτός (pniktós) + -gen. The first element derives from Ancient Greek πνίγω (pnígō, “to choke, to stifle”) (a property of nitrogen), which is ultimately Pre-Greek. By surface analysis, pnicto- + -gen.

parole.significato: Gout in the big toe.

parole.significato: Pain in the foot.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποδαλγία (podalgía). By surface analysis, pod- + -algia.

parole.significato: A limb of a crustacean when ambulatory.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”) + -ite (“bodypart”).

parole.significato: Relating to a foot or a footlike part.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πούς (poús).

parole.significato: A pedicel rising from the base of a flower with the ovary at the top.
parole.testo: From podo- (“foot”) + Ancient Greek γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”) + -ium (“structure”).

parole.significato: The eyestalk of a crustacean.
parole.testo: From podo-; Ancient Greek ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmós, “eye”); -ite.

parole.significato: Each of a pair of ski-shaped canoe-like floats attached to the feet, used for walking on water.
parole.testo: From podo- + Ancient Greek σκάφη (skáphē, “light boat”).

parole.significato: The funiculus (stalk of a seed or ovule).
parole.testo: From podo- + Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed”). Compare French podosperme.

parole.significato: Mottled with various colours; variegated; spotted.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποικίλος (poikílos, “many-coloured, variegated”) + -ite or -lite.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a poem, or to poetry; poetical.
parole.testo: From an uncommon Ancient Greek ποιηματικός (poiēmatikós); a more common Greek word was ποιητικός (poiētikós).

parole.significato: A bearded dragon, any lizard of the genus Pogona, native to Australia.
parole.testo: From the genus name, from Ancient Greek πώγων (pṓgōn, “beard”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a beard.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πώγων (pṓgōn, “beard”) + -ic.

parole.significato: The furthest-forward part of the chin.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πωγώνιον (pōgṓnion, diminutive of πώγων), with parallel meaning in Greek πιγούνι (pigoúni, “chin”). By surface analysis, pogono- + -ion.

parole.significato: beard
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πώγων (pṓgōn).

parole.significato: An act or process of creation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make”). Doublet of poesy.

parole.significato: creative, formative
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós). Doublet of poetic.

parole.significato: Describing the texture of an igneous rock that has small crystals of one mineral scattered among larger crystals of ano…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ποικίλος (poikílos, “scattered”)

parole.significato: Variable, subject to change.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποικίλος (poikílos, “spotted, embroidered”).

parole.significato: pastoral theology
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποιμενικός (poimenikós), from ποιμήν (poimḗn, “shepherd”).

parole.significato: A specific type of metafiction in which the story is about the process of creation (sometimes the creation of the story…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ποιούμενον (poioúmenon), "product".

parole.significato: War, battle, fight.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόλεμος (pólemos, “war, battle, fight”).

parole.significato: To attack in speech or in writing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολεμίζω (polemízō).

parole.significato: The study of human conflict and war.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόλεμος (pólemos, “war; battle”) + -logy (suffix indicating the study of a particular subject). The word is cognate with French polémologie. By surface analysis, polemo- + -log + -y.

parole.significato: The wobble of a spinning body.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πόλοδος (pólodos), meaning "path of the pole", from πόλος (pólos, “pole, axis”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way, road”).

parole.significato: manganese dioxide, occurring in hard tetragonal crystals
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?] to become grey.

parole.significato: The intentional destruction of a nation.
parole.testo: Coined based on Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis, “city; state”) and the suffix -cide.

parole.significato: An outpatient clinic, especially of a hospital.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis, “city”) + English clinic.

parole.significato: A Greek city-state.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis, “fortified town; city state”). Doublet of Puri and puri

parole.significato: A ruler or magistrate, especially one within a politocracy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολῑτᾰ́ρχης (polītắrkhēs).

parole.significato: citizenship
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “city, state, system of government”). Doublet of police and policy.

parole.significato: A person driven by political motives.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek πολιτικὸν ζῷον (politikòn zōîon), originally a concept taken from Aristotle at various places (History of Animals, Politics), though later as character type – possibly inherited in political families – introduced into everyday politics without philosophical background.

parole.significato: One who does not try for honors at university, but is content to take a degree merely; a passman.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολλοί (polloí, “the many, the masses”), as in hoi polloi.

parole.significato: One who takes an ordinary university degree, without honours.
parole.testo: Blend of poll (“ordinary university degree”) + man. First part from Ancient Greek πολλοί (polloí, “the many, the masses”). Second part from Middle English man, from Old English mann m (“human being, person, man”).

parole.significato: A variety of petalite always found with castor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Πολυδεύκης (Poludeúkēs), from Greek mythology; also see etymology at castor (“a mineral”).

parole.significato: The chewing of food long enough to reduce it to the consistency of porridge.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόλτος (póltos, “porridge”) and the suffix -φαγία (-phagía), combining form of φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”). See also suffix -phagy.

parole.significato: many
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús (“much, many”). Unrelated to -poly.

parole.significato: A polyhedron.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολῠ- (polŭ-) and ᾰ̓́κρον (ắkron).

parole.significato: Having stamens combined in more than two groups.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek ἀδελφός (adelphós) + -ous. By surface analysis, poly- + adelphous.

parole.significato: A mass grave or communal tomb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολυάνδριον (poluándrion).

parole.significato: A tomb
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυάνδριον (poluándrion).

parole.significato: Of a termite or ant colony, spread over multiple mounds or nests.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek καλιά (kaliá, “hut, wooden dwelling”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of many annelid worms, of the class Polychaeta, such as the lugworm; they have a segmented body with pairs of brist…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + χαίτη (khaítē, “chaeta”), equivalent to poly- + chaeta.

parole.significato: A four-dimensional polytope.
parole.testo: From poly- + -choron, from Ancient Greek πολῠ́ς (polŭ́s, “many”) and χῶρον (khôron, “room; space”).

parole.significato: A medicine that serves for many uses, or that cures many diseases.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύχρηστος (polúkhrēstos, “multipurpose, highly useful”), from πολύς (polús) + χρηστός (khrēstós, “useful”).

parole.significato: Having many branches
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek κλάδος (kládos, “shoot, branch”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to polycrotism; manifesting polycrotism
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “multiple, many”) + κρότος (krótos, “knocking, rattling”), modeled on dicrotic.

parole.significato: Polydactylous.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυδάκτυλος (poludáktulos), equivalent to poly- + -dactyl.

parole.significato: A congenital condition in which a person or animal has more than the usual number of digits (fingers or toes) on at lea…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυδάκτυλος (poludáktulos) + -y, from πολυ- (polu-, “many”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “digits”), equivalent to poly- + dactyly or polydactyl + -y.^((Etymology 3))

parole.significato: The situation where an ant colony is established across multiple nest sites.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek δόμος (dómos, “house”) + -y.

parole.significato: Passing through several distinct larval forms; having several distinct kinds of young.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “form”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A plane figure bounded by edges that are all straight lines.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”), equivalent to poly- + -gon.

parole.significato: The state or practice of a man having more than one wife at a time; plurality of wives; marriage between one man and mu…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύ (polú, “many”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman, wife”). By surface analysis, poly- + -gyny.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an insect (especially a bee) which collects pollen from the flowers of a variety of unrelated plants.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “a lot of, much”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús (“many, much”), from the root *pleh₁- (“to fill”)) + λέγειν (légein), from λέγω (légō, “to arrange, choose, gather; to count, reckon”) (from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather”)) + -ic.

parole.significato: The fact or condition of having more than two mammae or nipples.
parole.testo: From poly- + -mastia (corresponding to Ancient Greek μαστός (mastós, “breast”)).

parole.significato: A person with extraordinarily broad and comprehensive knowledge.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολυμαθής (polumathḗs, “having learnt much”), first attested in 1624. From πολύς (polús, “much”) (for more, see poly-) + μανθάνω (manthánō, “to learn”). Compare opsimath, philomath, polyhistor, polymathic, polymathist, and polymathy.

parole.significato: The knowledge of many arts and sciences; variety of learning.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek πολυμαθής (polumathḗs, “having learnt much”). By surface analysis, polymath + -y (“having the quality of”). See polymath for details.

parole.significato: A congenital defect characterized by extra limbs
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”) + -ia.

parole.significato: A long or larger molecule consisting of a chain or network of many repeating units, formed by chemically bonding togeth…
parole.testo: From poly- + -mer, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + μέρος (méros, “part”). Coined by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1833, though his definition was quite different from the modern one.

parole.significato: Describing a bird that has a syrinx with multiple distinct muscles
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυ- (polu-, “many, much”) + μυώδης (muṓdēs, “muscular”) + -ian.

parole.significato: Having many eyes or eye-like organs.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek ὄμμα (ómma, “eye”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The use of many names for the same thing or person.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many, much”) and ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: A glass through which objects appear multiplied, but diminished in size.
parole.testo: From poly- + -optrum (compare Ancient Greek εἴσ-οπτρον (eís-optron), ἔσ-οπτρον (és-optron, “mirror”)).

parole.significato: Belief in multiple impersonal nontranscendent deities embodied by natural phenomena.
parole.testo: Immediately from poly- + pantheism. Ultimately from poly- + pan- + Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god, divine”) + -ism.

parole.significato: An excessive appetite for food
parole.testo: From poly- + -phagia, from Ancient Greek πολῠ́ς (polŭ́s, “many”) and ἔφᾰγον (éphăgon, “eat”).

parole.significato: The use of multiple drugs to treat multiple concurrent disorders in the same (now especially elderly) patient, chiefly…
parole.testo: From poly- + pharmacy, after Ancient Greek πολυφάρμακος (poluphármakos).

parole.significato: Of the sea, noisy, roaring, thundering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολύφλοισβος (polúphloisbos, “loud‐roaring”).

parole.significato: Synonym of polyphonic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύφωνος (polúphōnos) + -al.

parole.significato: A kind of mouth organ or harmonica.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυφωνίᾱ (poluphōníā, “variety of tones”).

parole.significato: Musical texture consisting of several independent melodic voices, as opposed to music with just one voice (monophony) o…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολυφωνία (poluphōnía); equivalent to poly- + -phony.

parole.significato: Any animal whose teeth are continuously replaced.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many, much”) + φύω (phúō, “produce”) + ὀδόντος (odóntos) (genitive of ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”)).

parole.significato: A busybody or troublemaker or someone who looks only to their own concerns.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυπράγμων (poluprágmōn).

parole.significato: Meddlesomeness, officiousness.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολυπραγμοσύνη (polupragmosúnē, “meddlesomeness”), from πολυπράγμων (poluprágmōn, “meddlesome”) (from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “act”)) + -σύνη (-súnē, “-ness”). See poly-, pragmatic.

parole.significato: The belief that a person may have multiple souls; the theory that one's mind can contain multiple psychic elements.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A work consisting of multiple painted or carved panels joined together, often with hinges.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύπτυχος (polúptukhos, “with many folds”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “a fold”).

parole.significato: polythelia (the condition of having more than two nipples)
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: Giving birth to multiple offspring at the same time; multiparous.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύς (polús) + τόκος (tókos).

parole.significato: Someone who visits many places.
parole.testo: From poly- + Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”) + -ian, apparently influenced by utopian.

parole.significato: Able to take various courses of action; resourceful, versatile, adaptable.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολύτροπος (polútropos) (used in Homer to describe Odysseus) + -ic. In later senses after German polytrop, polytropisch.

parole.significato: having several different taxa of the next lower rank, especially having several subspecies
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πολῠ- (polŭ-) + τῠπῐκός (tŭpĭkós). By surface analysis, poly- + type + -ic.

parole.significato: Having the nostril covered with a scale.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: The study of evil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πονηρός (ponērós, “grievous, knavish”) + -ology; compare Ancient Greek πονηρολογίᾱ (ponērologíā, “bad reasoning”).

parole.significato: A fear of overwork.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόνος (pónos, “fatigue”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: A plant that grows best in grass-covered meadows.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πόα (póa, “grass”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant”). By surface analysis, poa + -phyte.

parole.significato: The point on the human skull located at the upper margin of each ear canal, and underlying the tragus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “opening”) + -ion.

parole.significato: A proposition affirming the possibility of finding such conditions as will render a certain determinate problem indeter…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόρισμα (pórisma, “a deduction from a previous demonstration”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a porism; of the nature of a porism.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ποριστικός (poristikós, “able to supply or procure”).

parole.significato: Lascivious; licentious.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόρνη (pórnē, “prostitute”) + ἐραστής (erastḗs, “lover”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Relating to prostitutes or prostitution.
parole.testo: From πορν- (porn-), the stem of the Ancient Greek πόρνη (pórnē, “prostitute”). Sense 2 from porno(graphy) and porno(grapher), both ultimately also from πόρνη (pórnē, “prostitute”).

parole.significato: Born into the purple (royalty or the ruling class)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple, purple dye”) + -gene.

parole.significato: The study of the dosages of drugs, especially the determination of appropriate dosages.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόσος (pósos, “how much?”) + -ology (suffix indicating a branch of learning).

parole.significato: Of the foreskin.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πόσθη (pósthē).

parole.significato: A softshell turtle (family Trionychidae)
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ποτᾰ́μιος (potắmios, “of or from a river”), from ποτᾰμός (potămós, “river”).

parole.significato: river
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποταμός (potamós).

parole.significato: An account or description of a river, or rivers.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποταμός (potamós, “river”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: A device used for measuring the rate of water uptake of a leafy shoot due to photosynthesis and transpiration.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποτό (potó, “drunken”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Relating to potometry.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποτό (potó, “drunken”) + -metric.

parole.significato: Measurement of the rate of water uptake of a leafy shoot due to photosynthesis and transpiration.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ποτό (potó, “drunken”) + -metry.

parole.significato: A place to stand upon; a locus standi; a foundation or basis for operations.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek, literally "where I may stand", in reference to the reputed saying of Archimedes: "Give me where I may stand and I will move the whole world with my steelyard."

parole.significato: The Greek foot, a unit of length based on the shod foot, generally equal to 16 fingers (δάκτυλοι) or ¹⁄₆₀₀ stade (στάδι…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of foot, pes, and pie (“Spanish unit of length”).

parole.significato: The holders of power or the authorities in a given situation, especially if seen as being faceless or unreasonably bure…
parole.testo: After Romans 13:1 in the Tyndale Bible and the King James Version. The phrase is a translation of the Ancient Greek αἱ οὖσαι ἐξουσίαι (hai oûsai exousíai, “the existing authorities”). The verb be is the archaic third-person plural present indicative form, equivalent to the modern are, and not a subj

parole.significato: The theory concerning the hierarchic structure of mind and how it relates to processes in the brain
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”) and ποίησις (poíēsis, “making”).

parole.significato: A compiler directive; data embedded in source code by programmers to indicate some intention to a compiler.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “a thing done, a fact”). In the technical senses perhaps a back-formation from pragmatic or a clipping of pragmat used earlier in ALGOL.

parole.significato: The pursuit of practicality over aesthetic qualities; a concentration on facts rather than emotions or ideals.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek stem of πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “act”) + -ism.

parole.significato: One who acts in a practical or straightforward manner; one who is pragmatic; one who values practicality or pragmatism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “thing”).

parole.significato: The description of an action.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πρᾱγμᾰτογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (prāgmătogrăphĭ́ā), from πρᾱ́γμᾰτα (prā́gmăta) + -ο- (-o-) + -γρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (-grăphĭ́ā).

parole.significato: green
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “leek-green, green”), from Ancient Greek πράσον (práson, “leek”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Pr) with an atomic number of 59, a soft, silvery, malleable and ductile rare earth metal, va…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “leek-green”) + didymium.

parole.significato: Any of various flagellate, unicellular green algae of the class Prasinophyceae
parole.testo: Ancient Greek πρᾰ́σῐνος (prắsĭnos, “leak-green, light green”) + -phyte (“plant”)

parole.significato: The study of human action or conduct.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis) + -logy.

parole.significato: Any of various predatory, cannibalistic insects of the order Mantodea that have a prayer-like stance.
parole.testo: Mantis from Ancient Greek μάντις (mántis). Named "praying mantis" for their stance, with the forelegs held together in a way that resembles a person praying. Similar designations exist in many European as well as non-European languages. Compare for example French mante religieuse (literally “religio

parole.significato: A word that has more recognition than a protologism but less recognition than a neologism.
parole.testo: From pre- + Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word”) + -ism, by analogy with protologism and neologism.

parole.significato: One who has presbyopia: a farsighted person
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old”) and ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”).

parole.significato: Inability of the proprioceptive system to accurately interpret actual limb position or movement due to physiological ag…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old”) and Latin proprius (“own”).

parole.significato: An image of the god Priapus, often used as a scarecrow in ancient gardens.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek Πρίαπος (Príapos).

parole.significato: A petrel of the genera Pachyptila and Halobaena.
parole.testo: From Prion (former genus name), from Ancient Greek πρίων (príōn, “saw”).

parole.significato: Relating to sawfishes of the family Pristidae.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρίστις (prístis, “saw, sawfish”).

parole.significato: earlier; prior
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”).

parole.significato: A problem set forth in the Ancient Greek scholarly tradition.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma). Doublet of problem.

parole.significato: A bony projection, especially the occipital protuberance of the skull.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek προβολή (probolḗ).

parole.significato: The kindling of a disease into action; the procatarctic cause.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek προκαταρκτικός (prokatarktikós, “first beginning”), from προκατάρχω (prokatárkhō).

parole.significato: An ancient Greek jug, with or without a handle, for water or wine.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρόχοος (prókhoos).

parole.significato: A clitic that joins with the following word phonetically, graphically, or both.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek προκλίνω (proklínō, “to lean forward”). By surface analysis, from pro- + clitic.

parole.significato: Dealing with the rectum and anus; anorectal; sometimes also the distal colon.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek πρωκτός (prōktós, “anus”).

parole.significato: Government or management by “arseholes” (i.e., inconsiderate, obnoxious, or otherwise highly objectionable people).
parole.testo: First attested in March 2002; formed as procto- (“anus”) + -cracy (“rule”); equivalent to a hypothetical Ancient Greek etymon of the form *πρωκτοκρατία (prōktokratía), from πρωκτός (prōktós, “anus”) + κράτος (krátos, “dominion”, “power”).

parole.significato: The back ectodermal part of an alimentary canal.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρωκτός (prōktós, “rectum”) + a latinized and nominalized form of Ancient Greek ὁδαῖος (hodaîos, “on the way”). Compare stomodeum, urodeum, coprodeum, and phallodeum.

parole.significato: Of certain Turbellaria: having the digestive canal furnished with an anal aperture.
parole.testo: From procto- + Ancient Greek -οῦχος (-oûkhos, “having”), from ἔχω (ékhō).

parole.significato: A statement intended to prepare one’s audience for something shocking or offensive; an extreme form of protherapeia.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek προδιόρθωσις (prodiórthōsis, “previous correction”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + διόρθωσις (diórthōsis, “correction, making straight”).

parole.significato: A precursor or harbinger; also a warning event.
parole.testo: Probably by analogy with syndrome (pro- + -drome), but consistent with Ancient Greek προδρομή (prodromḗ, “running forward, sally, skirmish”).

parole.significato: a skirmisher cavalry unit used in an Ancient Greek army for scouting ahead of the main force
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρόδρομος (pródromos, “forerunner”).

parole.significato: A figure of reasoning in which, at the conclusion of an argument, a justifying reason is provided.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek [Term?]. Coined from προέκθεσις (proékthesis), from πρό (pró, “before, forth”) + ἔκθεσις (ékthesis, “a putting out, exposition”).

parole.significato: The grassy area that separated the orchestra from the audience; or the front rows of the audience.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek προεδρία (proedría).

parole.significato: A figure in which the speaker blames or reproaches oneself beforehand in order to secure the attention or favor of the…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek προεπίπληξις (proepíplēxis, “blaming beforehand”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἐπίπληξις (epíplēxis, “blame, reproof”).

parole.significato: Having the two flexor tendons of the toes entirely separate, and the flexor hallicus going to the first toe only.

parole.significato: A Byzantine unit equal to 20,000 Greek feet or 33⅓ stades.

parole.significato: The head of a school of philosophy in Ancient Greece

parole.significato: Forms words related to shade.

parole.significato: A vertical section of a building; a sciagraphy.

parole.significato: The art of representing shadows as realistically as possible.

parole.significato: Dispelling shadows.

parole.significato: Belonging or relating to a sundial.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an optical arrangement for forming images in a darkened room.

parole.significato: False or pretended knowledge of science or natural phenomena.

parole.significato: severe discipline

parole.significato: induration of the tissues

parole.significato: The abnormal hardening of body tissues, such as an artery; the appearance of hardenings, indurations, lesions, nodules.

parole.significato: That part of the skeleton which is developed in tendons, ligaments, and aponeuroses.

parole.significato: A monoclinic-domatic mineral containing aluminum, calcium, hydrogen, oxygen, and silicon.

parole.significato: Crooked, bent, or winding; relating to scoliosis or other lateral deviations.

parole.significato: Of or relating to scoliography, the description, measurement, or representation of scoliosis.

parole.significato: Any of a genre of songs sung in turn by symposiasts to the accompaniment of a lyre.

parole.significato: A fossil worm or its trace.

parole.significato: A tubular structure found in sedimentary rocks, such as sandstone, believed to be the fossil burrow of a marine worm.

parole.significato: Pertaining to mackerel.

parole.significato: Of or relating to scopophobia.

parole.significato: Jeering; jesting; jokey.

parole.significato: An orthorhombic-dipyramidal mineral containing arsenic, hydrogen, iron, and oxygen.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or appearing like a scorpion.

parole.significato: After dusk.

parole.significato: darkness
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σκότος (skótos, “darkness”). By surface analysis, scot- + -o-.

parole.significato: A form of vertigo involving sudden dizziness, headache, and blurred vision
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek σκοτοδινία (skotodinía), from σκότος (skótos, “darkness”) + δίνη (dínē, “whirling”). Equivalent to scoto- + dino- + -ia.

parole.significato: dizziness with dimness of sight
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σκοτωμία (skotōmía, “dizziness”). By surface analysis, scot- + -omy.

parole.significato: a hardened mass of feces

parole.significato: Relating to tanning; applied to tannin and gallic acid.

parole.significato: A person who carried images and symbols in processions of the imperial cult of Ancient Rome.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Secotiaceae, now subsumed into Agaricaceae.

parole.significato: One of several spores arranged in a chain, as in certain algae.

parole.significato: A shaking of the Earth's surface; an earthquake or tremor.

parole.significato: Related to, or caused by an earthquake or other vibration of the Earth.
parole.testo: Based on Ancient Greek σεισμός (seismós, “shaking, earthquake”) + -ic, equivalent to seismo- + -ic.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an earthquake.

parole.significato: A sacred enclosure, sanctuary or cella in an ancient Greek temple.

parole.significato: Unreasonable fear or dislike of sharks.

parole.significato: A soft, glassy form of gypsum (chemical formula CaSO₄·2H₂O).

parole.significato: Relating to the Moon

parole.significato: Able to provide for oneself independently of others; not needing external support.

parole.significato: Communicating meaning.

parole.significato: Of or relating to semantics or the meanings of words.

parole.significato: The use of symbols to communicate information, such as with musical or mathematical notation, road signs, or emojis.

parole.significato: Semantics; a discipline within linguistics concerned with the meaning of a word independent of its phonetic expression.

parole.significato: Acting as a sign of danger.

parole.significato: A unit of time, a division of a foot; a mora.

parole.significato: semiotics

parole.significato: Of or relating to semiotics or to semantics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek σημειωτικός (sēmeiōtikós, “observant of signs”), ultimately derived from σῆμα (sêma, “mark, sign”). Compare semiotics.

parole.significato: The study of signs and symbols, especially as means of language or communication.
parole.testo: Coined by John Locke from Ancient Greek σημειωτικός (sēmeiōtikós, “fitted for marking, portending”), from σημειόω (sēmeióō, “to mark, interpret as a portend”), from σημεῖον (sēmeîon, “a mark, sign, token”), from σῆμα (sêma, “mark, sign”).

parole.significato: A unit of semiology or semantics.
parole.testo: From sem- as in semantic and semiotics, from Ancient Greek σημεῖον (sēmeîon, “sign”), + -on. By surface analysis, seme + -on.

parole.significato: Having long oral processes.

parole.significato: A serious medical condition in which the whole body is inflamed, causing injury to its own tissues and organs as a resp…

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sepsis.

parole.significato: One of six parts.

parole.significato: A tumor or swelling of a salivary gland.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to saliva.

parole.significato: A silver coin of Achaemenid Persia worth one twentieth of a daric and weighing about 5.6 grams.

parole.significato: The eighteenth letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets (Σ, σ), the twentieth letter of Old and Ancient.

parole.significato: Having the consonant s added to the root in order to form a tense or case stem.

parole.significato: Any of the Sigmodontinae subfamily of rodents, including New World rats and mice.

parole.significato: To employ signcryption

parole.significato: A dance performed in Ancient Greek satyr plays.

parole.significato: A satirist.

parole.significato: food, especially grain

parole.significato: food, especially grain

parole.significato: An official in charge of a granary in Ancient Greece.

parole.significato: The larva of a bee.

parole.significato: An element of ancient Greek theater: the structure at the back of the stage.

parole.significato: A design feature copied from a similar feature in another object, even when not functionally necessary.

parole.significato: The incorporation of obsolete or skeuomorphic elements into a design, for familiarity or out of tradition, even though…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σκεῦος (skeûos, “implement”) + -morphism, or skeuomorph + -ism.

parole.significato: A picture or image created from shadows, especially with X-rays.

parole.significato: Synonym of skeuomorph.

parole.significato: A retinoscope.

parole.significato: A kind of cathode ray tube that replaces the conventional light-emitting phosphor layer on the face of the tube screen…

parole.significato: Romantically attracted to non-cisgender people.

parole.significato: Sexually attracted to non-cisgender people.

parole.significato: The function of a written or spoken text, especially in the context of translating and interpreting.

parole.significato: A chamber pot.

parole.significato: A soft-sided brimless cap of various shapes, worn by clergy or monastics.

parole.significato: A deep two-handled wine cup of Ancient Greece.

parole.significato: Any of many clay phyllosilicate minerals that have a relatively open structure.

parole.significato: A city or place full of sin and vice.

parole.significato: To commit a solecism.

parole.significato: A cradle, as for a broken limb.

parole.significato: Having a tube, a duct or a pipe

parole.significato: A wise legislator or lawgiver.

parole.significato: Part of, or relating to the body of an organism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós, “bodily”), σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: body
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”). Compare soma.

parole.significato: A somite.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”) + τομή (tomḗ, “cut, incision”).

parole.significato: One of the seven men that served in high-ranking military positions during the times of Alexander the Great
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σωματοφύλαξ (sōmatophúlax, “bodyguard”).

parole.significato: A fold of tissue, in the embryo of a vertebrate, from which the walls of the body and the amnion develop.

parole.significato: A congenital fissure of the body wall or trunk.

parole.significato: The directional movement of an organism in response to a stimulus.

parole.significato: Relating to technology.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τετράκις (tetrákis, “four times”).

parole.significato: A word occurring only four times in a given corpus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τετράκις λεγόμενον (tetrákis legómenon, “(something) said only four times”), from τετράκις (tetrákis, “four times”) and λεγόμενον (legómenon), passive participle of λέγω (légō).

parole.significato: Synonym of tetra- used for multiplication with a second numerical prefix.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τετράκις (tetrákis, “four times”).

parole.significato: A symbolic arrangement of four differing elements, or the combination of four disparate elements in one unit.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τετράμορφος (tetrámorphos). By surface analysis, tetra- + -morph.

parole.significato: A text presented in four parallel versions, especially (historical) the version of the Bible presented in such a fashio…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τετραπλᾶ (tetraplâ), neuter plural of τετραπλοῦς (tetraploûs, “fourfold”), from τετρα- (tetra-, “tetra-: four”) + -πλόος (-plóos, “-fold”).

parole.significato: A quadriplegic.
parole.testo: From tetra- and -plegic, from Ancient Greek πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike”); probably patterned after paraplegic from the Ancient Greek παραπληγή (paraplēgḗ, “the paralysis of half of the body”).

parole.significato: Having four sets of chromosomes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τετραπλός (tetraplós) + Ancient Greek είδος (eídos), equivalent to tetra- + -ploid.

parole.significato: A set of four metrical feet.
parole.testo: From tetra- + -pody, from Ancient Greek τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) and πούς, ποδός (poús, podós, “foot”).

parole.significato: A Roman-style cubic structure with a gate on each of its four sides.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τετράπυλον (tetrápulon, literally “four gates”). By surface analysis, tetra- + pylon.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a tetrarch or tetrarchy.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: Equivalent to four short syllables, consisting of four moras as a dactyl, anapest, or spondee.
parole.testo: From tetra- + Ancient Greek σημεῖον (sēmeîon, “sign”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A figure consisting of four limbs, radiating from the center; especially a fylfot or swastika.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τετρασκέλιον (tetraskélion, “four-legged”).

parole.significato: A four-sided colonnade, typically enclosing a courtyard
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τετράστῳον (tetrástōion), from neuter of τετράστῳος (tetrástōios, “having four porticoes”) from Ancient Greek τετράς (tetrás, “four”) + στοά (stoá, “portico, colonnade”).

parole.significato: A word comprising four syllables.
parole.testo: Formed from tetra- (“four”) + syllable; compare Ancient Greek τετρασύλλαβος (tetrasúllabos, “of four syllables”).

parole.significato: A cicada, especially in Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τέττιξ (téttix), or perhaps a modern Greek descendant thereof.

parole.significato: A small squid.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τευθίς (teuthís).

parole.significato: Feeding on cephalopods.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τευθίς (teuthís, “squid”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: The branch of malacology dealing with cephalopods.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τευθίς (teuthís, “squid”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy”).

parole.significato: A state barge fitted with cabins, on the Nile
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θᾰλᾰμηγός (thălămēgós).

parole.significato: Any of a group of inherited disorders in which the amount of hemoglobin in the blood is reduced.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θάλασσα (thálassa, “sea”) (see also thalass-) and -emia (“blood”) (from αἷμα (haîma)). The etymology is suggestive of the epidemiology of the disorder, which is more common in people of Mediterranean descent. First attested in 1932.

parole.significato: Any sea tortoise.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek the sea.

parole.significato: sea
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θάλασσα (thálassa, “sea”).

parole.significato: A state whose power derives from its naval or commercial supremacy on the seas.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαλασσοκρατία (thalassokratía, “empire of the sea”), from θάλασσα (thálassa, “sea”) + -κρατία (-kratía, “government, rule”). By surface analysis, thalasso- + -cracy.

parole.significato: A metallic chemical element (symbol Tl) with atomic number 81: a gray post-transition metal that discolors when exposed…
parole.testo: Coined based on Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “green branch”) (after the color of the radiation spectra), + -ium.

parole.significato: An undifferentiated plant body, such as in algae.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “young shoot, twig”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelh₁- (“to bloom”).

parole.significato: A grasshopper that lives in trees (as opposed to underbrush).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek, meaning "bush-loving"; see θάμνος (thámnos, “bush”) and -phile.

parole.significato: Death.
parole.testo: Combining form of Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”).

parole.significato: Foreshadowing death.
parole.testo: From thanato- + Ancient Greek γνώμη (gnṓmē, “sign, mark”) + -ic.

parole.significato: The scientific study of death and the practices associated with it, including the study of the needs of the terminally…
parole.testo: From thanato- + -logy, from Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”).

parole.significato: Prone to thanatopsis; morbid.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”) + τοπικός (topikós, “Pertaining to a place or topic”).

parole.significato: Contemplation of death.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “seeing”), via the poem "Thanatopsis" by William Cullen Bryant. Although a surface analysis of thanato- + -opsis readily suggests itself and might invite a semantic expectation of deathliness, Bryant's sense of the word corresponds to "th

parole.significato: The death drive in Freudian psychoanalysis.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Θάνατος (Thánatos).

parole.significato: A hexagonal-dipyramidal mineral containing calcium, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, silicon, and sulfur.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαυμάζω (thaumázō, “to wonder”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Miracle; wonder; marvel.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαυματ- (thaumat-), combining form of θαῦμα (thaûma, “a miracle”).

parole.significato: An optical toy made of a card with an image on each side; when twirled, the images appear to combine.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαῦμα (thaûma, “miracle”) + τρόπος (trópos, “a turn”), thauma + -trope.

parole.significato: The working of miracles, wonderworking; magic, witchcraft, wizardry.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαυματουργία (thaumatourgía), from θαῦμα (thaûma, “miracle, wonder”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.parola: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must
parole.significato: The weak cannot resist the decisions of the strong; power, not morality, decides the outcome of any dispute.
parole.termine_origine: δυνατὰ δὲ οἱ προύχοντες πράσσουσι καὶ οἱ ἀσθενεῖς ξυγχωροῦσιν

parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek δυνατὰ δὲ οἱ προύχοντες πράσσουσι καὶ οἱ ἀσθενεῖς ξυγχωροῦσιν (dunatà dè hoi proúkhontes prássousi kaì hoi astheneîs xunkhōroûsin) in Thucydides’s History of the Peloponnesian War 5.89 (the Melian dialogue). Thucydides presents the sentence as part of an ultimatum from Athens

parole.significato: The study of or reflection upon the or a goddess, or the feminine divine, e.g. from a feminist viewpoint.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεά (theá, “goddess”) + -logy.

parole.significato: Partaking of, or combining, both divinity and humanity.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θεός (theós) + Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos) + -ic

parole.significato: A state of being God and man.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θεός (theós) + Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos) + -ism

parole.significato: Christ regarded as having both a divine and human nature.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεάνθρωπος (theánthrōpos) Equivalent to the- + -anthrope.

parole.significato: Beliefs of or pertaining to theanthropism.
parole.testo: From theanthropos, from Ancient Greek θεάνθρωπος (theánthrōpos), from θεός (theós, “god”) + ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”) + -sophy, from Ancient Greek σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”).

parole.significato: The ruler of a thearchy, a monarch of gods
parole.testo: Related to thearchy, from Ancient Greek θεαρχία (thearkhía), from θεός (theós, “god”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “rule, ruling”). By surface analysis, the- + -arch.

parole.significato: A government ruled by God or a god; a theocracy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεαρχία (thearkhía), from θεός (theós, “god”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “rule, ruling”). By surface analysis, the- + -archy.

parole.significato: Government by an assembly of citizens in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεᾱτρο-κρᾰτίᾱ (theātro-krătíā, literally “theatre rule”) or θεᾱτρο-κορασίᾱ (theātro-korasíā).

parole.significato: A poisonous alkaloid, paramorphine, obtained from opium; not used in medicine.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Θῆβαι (Thêbai, “Thebes”)

parole.significato: Having the teeth enclosed in sockets in the alveoli of the jaws.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “case, chest”) + -odont.

parole.significato: the divine, especially a divine fire
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεῖον.

parole.significato: Belief in the existence of at least one deity.
parole.testo: Coined, theo- + -ism. ultimately from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”). Attested in English from 1678, theist being attested 16 years earlier in 1662. Cognate French théisme, as in Diderot Principes de la philosophie morale (1745), which was probably borrowed from English.

parole.significato: Of or relating to theism.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Nipple.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”).

parole.significato: Inflammation of the nipple or teat.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”) + -itis. By surface analysis, thel- + -itis.

parole.significato: The female genital structure of some shrimp
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θηλυκός (thēlukós, “feminine”).

parole.significato: A form of parthenogenesis in which females are produced from unfertilized eggs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θηλυτοκίᾱ (thēlutokíā), from θῆλυς (thêlus, “female”) + τόκος (tókos, “birth”).

parole.significato: A subject or theme.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θέμᾰ (thémă). Doublet of theme.

parole.significato: Relating to or having a theme (“subject”) or a topic.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεματικός (thematikós), from θέμα (théma, “theme”). Equivalent to theme + -atic.

parole.significato: To convert (a sentence or a part of it) into a theme.
parole.testo: From the stem of Ancient Greek θέμα (théma, “theme”) + -ise.

parole.significato: The palm of the hand or sole of the foot.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θέναρ (thénar).

parole.significato: The palm of the hand or sole of the foot.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θέναρ (thénar).

parole.significato: Government under the control of a state religion.
parole.testo: From theo- + -cracy, originally from Ancient Greek θεοκρατία (theokratía, “rule of (a) God”), a term coined in the 1st century by Josephus (Against Apion 2.17) in reference to the ancient Israelite polity under the Mosaic covenant. Attested in English from the 1620s, first by John Donne in A Sermon

parole.significato: Interaction, admixture, and conflation of divine principles.
parole.testo: From theo- (“god”) + -crasy (“mixing”), from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) and Ancient Greek κρᾶσις (krâsis, “mixing, tempering”).

parole.significato: The origination of gods or a narrative describing the origin of gods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θεογονία (theogonía). By surface analysis, theo- + -gony.

parole.significato: Possession by a deity; divine inspiration.
parole.testo: From theo- + -lepsy, or directly from Ancient Greek θεοληψία (theolēpsía, “divine inspiration; superstition”).

parole.significato: A student of theology.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεόλογος (theólogos, “one who discourses of the gods”). By surface analysis, theo- + -log.

parole.significato: A theological statement which is of individual opinion and not doctrine.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek, θεολογούμενον (theologoúmenon, “that which is said about God”), neuter present passive participle of θεολογέω (theologéō, “to speak about God”).

parole.significato: A fight against the gods, as the mythological battle of the giants against the gods.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεομαχία (theomakhía, “battle of the gods”), from θεός (theós, “god”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle”). Equivalent to theo- + -machy.

parole.significato: A kind of divination drawn from the responses of oracles.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek; theo- + -mancy

parole.significato: The bestowal of divine attributes on humanity.
parole.testo: From theo- + -morphism, from Ancient Greek θεος (theos, “god”) + μορφη (morphē, “shape, form”).

parole.significato: Containing the name of a deity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεόφορος (theóphoros, “bearing a god”) + -ic.

parole.significato: The property of bearing the name of a deity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεόφορος (theóphoros, “bearing a god”) + -y.

parole.significato: Inspired or possessed by a god.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεόπνευστος (theópneustos), from θεός (theós, “god”) + stem of πνεῖν (pneîn, “to breathe, blow”).

parole.significato: The scheme of divine intervention; the art of introducing deities into poetry.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) + τέχνη (tékhnē, “skill”) + -y.

parole.significato: A hymn to Mary, the Theotokos, read or chanted during the Divine Services of the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θεοτοκίον (theotokíon).

parole.significato: Hospitality towards a god who visits as a guest.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θεοξενία (theoxenía), equivalent to theo- + xenia.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the taxonomic subclass Theria.
parole.testo: From translingual Theria + -ian. From Ancient Greek θηρίον (thēríon, “wild beast”).

parole.significato: The science of medicine involving animals such as veterinary medicine or the treatment of animal bites.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θήρ (thḗr, “wild beast”) + ἰατρός (iatrós, “doctor”).

parole.significato: wild animal.
parole.testo: Representing the combining form of Ancient Greek θηρίον (thēríon), diminutive of θήρ (thḗr, “wild beast”).

parole.significato: Having the form of a beast.
parole.testo: From therio- (“beast, wild animal”) + -morphic. Originating from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A unit of heat equal to 100,000 British thermal units, often used in the context of natural gas.
parole.testo: 1920s, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “heat”). See also thermo-, -thermic, etc.

parole.significato: An antidote to heat, especially a rotating fan attached to a window.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θέρμη (thérmē) + antidote.

parole.significato: Of, related to, or associated with heat; thermal.
parole.testo: Mid 19th century, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “heat”) + -ic.

parole.significato: An artificial alkaloid resembling thalline, used as an antipyretic.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?] for "heat" + Latin fugere to flee.

parole.significato: Thermal: of, being, or pertaining to heat or temperature.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “warm, hot”).

parole.significato: Describing various weapons that use atmospheric oxygen to produce a blast wave of a significantly longer duration than…
parole.testo: From thermo- + baric, derived from the Ancient Greek words for “heat” and “pressure”: θερμοβαρικός (thermobarikós), from θερμός (thermós, “hot”) + βάρος (báros, “weight, pressure”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

parole.significato: The property possessed by heat of being composed, like light, of rays of different degrees of refrangibility, which are…
parole.testo: From thermo- + Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”).

parole.significato: A bottle, flask or similar vessel having a vacuum between its inner and outer silvered walls; designed to maintain the…
parole.testo: Genericization of the trademark Thermos, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “warm”). Possibly related to English warm.

parole.significato: A unit of measure whose identification remains very unclear.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θέρμος (thérmos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to heat; produced by heat.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θερμότης (thermótēs, “heat”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Bestial, resembling an animal.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θήρ (thḗr, “beast, fantastic animal”). Compare Theropoda.

parole.significato: The stage where a tomite elongates (swims away) after being released from the cyst.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θήρ (thḗr, “beast, fantastic animal”) + -ont.

parole.significato: Any plant which survives unfavourable seasons in the form of seeds only
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θέρος (théros, “summer”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: The accumulation of a substance in a cell or organ in abnormally large amounts.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θησαύρισμα (thēsaúrisma, “store”) + -osis. First used in the 1930s in thesaurismosis glycogenica, another name for glycogen storage disease.

parole.significato: A lung storage disease thought to be caused by inhalation of hair spray.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse”) + -osis.

parole.significato: A junior archon in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θεσμοθέτης (thesmothétēs).

parole.significato: The eighth letter of the Modern Greek alphabet, ninth in Old Greek: Θ, θ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θῆτα (thêta).

parole.significato: A soul, spirit or being.
parole.testo: c. Mid 20th c., Coined by Scientology founder L. Ron Hubbard, from theta + -n, from Ancient Greek θῆτα (thêta, “theta”), used in Scientology to represent the source of life.

parole.significato: The lowest social class of citizens in ancient Athens.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θῆτες (thêtes), plural of θής (thḗs, “hired laborer”).

parole.significato: Laid down; absolute or positive, like a law or constituting the truth.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θετικός (thetikós), from θέσῐς (thésĭs). See thesis and compare hypothetical.

parole.significato: Something stealthy or that occurs without warning.
parole.testo: A calque from Ancient Greek κλέπτης ἐν νυκτί (kléptēs en nuktí).

parole.significato: In ancient Greece, a woman wearing a peplos with a split up the side, thus revealing the upper leg.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek φαινομηρίδες (phainomērídes).

parole.significato: a pseudomorph of ikaite, found in Quaternary lake basins of Nevada.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θίνα (thína, “dune, shore”) + -lite.

parole.significato: containing sulfur, especially a compound in which oxygen has been replaced by this element
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek θεῖον (theîon, “sulfur”).

parole.significato: lime sulfur.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεῖον (theîon, “sulfur”) ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”).

parole.significato: An artificial red or violet dyestuff consisting of a complex sulfur derivative of certain aromatic diamines.
parole.testo: Of Ancient Greek [Term?] origin. See thio- (“sulfur”).

parole.significato: The doctrine that when the body dies, the intangible soul and/or spirit also goes to sleep or in other words the person…
parole.testo: From ecclesiastical Ancient Greek θνητόψῡχος (thnētópsūkhos), from θνητός (thnētós, “mortal”) and ψῡχή (psūkhḗ, “soul”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A dome, or domed building; a cupola.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θόλος (thólos, “dome”). Doublet of tholus and thole.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an obsolete group of carnivores, including wolves and dogs.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θώς (thṓs, “jackal”) + -oid.

parole.significato: Of the thorax.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θωρακικός (thōrakikós, “suffering in the chest, of the thorax”), from θώραξ (thṓrax, “thorax”).

parole.significato: One of the rowers on the topmost of the three benches in a trireme. They were usually the best rowers.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρανίτης (thranítēs), from θρᾶνος (thrânos, “bench”).

parole.significato: The field of breeding or propagating plants and animals.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρέμμα (thrémma, “nursling”) + -ology.

parole.significato: Relating to a threne
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θρηνητικός (thrēnētikós, “inclined to lament, querulous”). By surface analysis, threne + -etic.

parole.significato: A dirge or funeral song.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρηνῳδία (thrēnōidía). Doublet of threnody, compare similar terms in -ode, like epode.

parole.significato: A song or poem of lamentation or mourning for a dead person; a dirge; an elegy.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρηνῳδία (thrēnōidía, “lamentation”). Compare the New Latin thrēnōdia.

parole.significato: Synonym of threnody.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos).

parole.significato: The study of nutrition.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρέψις (thrépsis, “nourishing”) (from τρέφω (tréphō)) + -logy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to nutrition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρεπτικός (threptikós, “able to feed”), from τρέφω (tréphō, “I nourish”, of food).

parole.significato: Any of the many small insects of the order Thysanoptera, especially those that attack useful plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρίψ (thríps, “wood-worm”).

parole.significato: A protein produced by the liver and kidney, which regulates the production of platelets
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρόμβος (thrómbos, “lump, piece, blood clot, milk curd”) and ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker”) and -in.

parole.significato: The formation of thrombi in the blood vessels of a living organism, causing obstruction of the circulation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θρόμβωσις (thrómbōsis, “curdling, clotting”). By surface analysis, thrombus + -osis.

parole.significato: Frankincense obtained from conifers such as the Norway spruce, or long-leaved pine.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θύος (thúos, “burnt sacrifice”).

parole.significato: a folded membrane within plant chloroplasts from which grana are made, used in photosynthesis
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θύλακος (thúlakos, “sack, bag”) + -oid.

parole.significato: That area of the soul where feelings of pride, indignation, shame etc are located.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek θῡμός (thūmós, “soul, heart”). Doublet of thymus and fume.

parole.significato: One of the lower segments in the hyoid arch, often consolidated with the body of the hyoid bone and forming one of its…
parole.testo: From thyro- + -hyal, from Ancient Greek ὖ (û, “the letter upsilon”).

parole.significato: Having a vertical bony medial septum supporting the nose.

parole.significato: Any fight between two great forces.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Τῑτᾱνομαχίᾱ (Tītānomakhíā), from Τῑτᾱ́ν (Tītā́n, “Titan”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle”) + -ια (-ia).

parole.significato: Synonym of brontotheriid.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Τιτάν (Titán, “Titan”) + translingual -therium.

parole.significato: A segment or section.

parole.significato: Relating to childbirth.

parole.significato: The branch of medicine that deals with childbirth.

parole.significato: Synonym of Tocharian (“any member of the Tochari, a people who inhabited Bactria”)

parole.significato: A morbid fear of childbirth or pregnancy.

parole.significato: sections; cutting

parole.significato: A morbid addiction to performing or undergoing surgery.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”) + -mania.

parole.significato: An ecclesiastical document, usually promulgated by a synod which communicates or announces important information.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, separate”). Doublet of tome.

parole.significato: Of a geologic period within the Neoproterozoic era from about 1000 to 850 million years ago.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “stretch”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to tension, especially of the muscles.

parole.significato: Tonus: muscle tone, or tension in an organ.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “I stretch”).

parole.significato: The prince or ruler of a small district, city, or petty state; a petty "king".

parole.significato: A yellowish form of andradite

parole.significato: The lived physical place, in opposition to the ideal of a utopia.

parole.significato: place, area or region
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”).

parole.significato: underwater topography; bathymetry.

parole.significato: Description of a place.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τοπογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (topogrăphĭ́ā).. Doublet of topography.

parole.significato: A literary theme or motif; a rhetorical convention or formula.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place”). Compare topic.

parole.significato: Relating to toreutics.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τορευτικός (toreutikós, “belonging to work in relief”), from τορεύω (toreúō), from τορός (torós, “piercing”).

parole.significato: The art of making relief or intaglio designs, especially by chasing, carving or embossing in metal
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τορευτικός (toreutikós, “of metal work”), from τορευτός (toreutós, “worked in relief”), from τορέω (toréō, “I work in relief”), from τορευς (toreus, “a boring tool”), from Proto-Indo-European *terə-.

parole.significato: A specialized epidermal cell in insects, associated with the formation of the socket around the base of a bristle.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόρμος (tórmos, “socket”) + -gen.

parole.significato: The captain of a group of archers in ancient Greece, particularly the mercenaries at Athens.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τόξαρχος (tóxarkhos, “captain of the archers”) (see τόξον (tóxon) and -arch).

parole.significato: Synonym of toxarch.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τοξάρχης (toxárkhēs) (see τόξον (tóxon) and -ᾰ́ρχης (-ắrkhēs)).

parole.significato: Pertaining to archery.
parole.testo: From Toxophilus, the title of a 1545 book by Roger Ascham intended to mean ‘lover of the bow’, from Ancient Greek τόξον (tóxon, “bow”) + φίλος (phílos, “love”); equivalent to τόξον (tóxon) + -philite.

parole.significato: Any fish of genus Toxotes, the archerfishes.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τοξότης (toxótēs, “bowman, archer”).

parole.significato: neck or neck-like structure
parole.testo: Representing the Ancient Greek τράχηλος (trákhēlos, “neck”).

parole.significato: A volcanic rock with a composition between trachyte and basalt.

parole.significato: hoarseness of the voice
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τραχύς (trakhús) + -phonia.

parole.significato: Causing great sadness or suffering.

parole.significato: A condition characterized by the smell of goats in the armpits, excessively stinky armpits.
parole.testo: From trag(us) (“goat”) + -o- + maschal- (“armpit”) + -ia, from Ancient Greek τράγος (trágos, “he-goat”) and Ancient Greek μασχάλη (maskhálē, “armpit”).

parole.significato: A banker or money changer in Ancient Greece
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τραπεζῑ́της (trapezī́tēs).

parole.significato: A stammering or stuttering.

parole.significato: Any injury to the body of a living thing.

parole.significato: odometer
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τρέχω (trékhō, “to run”) + -meter.

parole.significato: A diacritic consisting of two dots ( ¨ ) placed over a letter, used among other things to indicate umlaut or diaeresis.

parole.significato: Dyspnea that is sensed while lying on one side but not on the other.

parole.significato: Thirty.

parole.significato: Having thirty sides.

parole.significato: A vessel with thirty rows of oars for rowers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τριακοντήρης (triakontḗrēs). By surface analysis, triacont- (“thirty”) + -er (“thing to which a certain number applies”).

parole.significato: An early distillation apparatus having three "beaks" to collect the distillate.

parole.significato: friction

parole.significato: A figure or object having three arms or branches.

parole.significato: A candlestick with three lights, signifying the Trinity.

parole.significato: Forming words related to hair.

parole.significato: Affected with trichoma (plica).

parole.significato: The quality of having three independent channels for conveying color information in the eye.

parole.significato: Having three digits on a limb.

parole.significato: A word occurring only three times in a given corpus.

parole.significato: thirteen

parole.significato: A figure composed of three interlocked spirals (or three bent human legs), with threefold rotational symmetry.

parole.significato: A machine with three pulleys which act together to raise great weights.

parole.significato: A subdivision of ancient Attica

parole.significato: cave

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring slight earthquake shocks.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to nutrition.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τροφικός (trophikós, “pertaining to food or nourishment”), from τροφή (trophḗ, “food”).

parole.significato: nourish; nourishment.

parole.significato: The placenta.

parole.significato: An irrational or obsessive fear of irregular patterns or clusters of small holes, such as those found in honeycombs.

parole.significato: A gourmet/connoisseur of cheese.

parole.significato: Relating to, or by means of tychoparthenogenesis
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τύχη (túkhē, “chance, luck, accident”) + -o- + parthenogenetic.

parole.significato: Any benthic organism found amongst plankton because of sea currents etc.

parole.significato: A tumor caused by caseation of the lymphatic glands.

parole.significato: The curdling of milk.

parole.significato: Poisoning by cheese or other dairy products

parole.significato: scar-like

parole.significato: Having woolly hair.

parole.significato: to decrypt

parole.significato: A eukaryotic cell with a single flagellum; thought to be the ancestor of all animals and fungi.

parole.significato: For all time, forever.

parole.significato: The twentieth letter of Classical and Modern Greek; the twenty-second letter of Old and Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Celestial cartography; the mapping of celestial bodies.

parole.significato: A fluorescent radioactive mineral, hydrated uranyl sulfate hydroxide.
parole.testo: From uranium + Ancient Greek πῖλος (pîlos, “felt”) + -ite, alluding to its composition and habit (containing uranium) and felt-like appearance.

parole.significato: A congenital fissure or cleft of the palate.
parole.testo: From urano- + schisis, from Ancient Greek οὐρανός (ouranós, “palate”).

parole.significato: Blood poisoning resulting from the retention of waste products usually excreted as urine.

parole.significato: urination.

parole.significato: Either of the two long, narrow ducts that carry urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.

parole.significato: The tube through which urine exits the body and, in male placental mammals, through which semen is ejaculated.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra, “the passage for urine”), from οὐρέω (ouréō, “to make water”). Recorded in English since 1634.

parole.significato: urethra.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra, “the passage for urine”).

parole.significato: One of the segments of the abdomen or postabdomen of arthropods.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) + -ite.

parole.significato: urine; relating to urine and the urinary system.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to one or more median and posterior elements in the hyoid arch of fishes.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the uronic acids or their derivatives.
parole.testo: Extracted from glucuronic, from glucose and Ancient Greek οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: The posterior part of a bird's body from which the tailfeathers grow.
parole.testo: Mediaeval Latin, from Ancient Greek οὐροπύγιον (ouropúgion, “tail feathers”).

parole.significato: A spiritual being, entity, or divine intellect that rules, governs, or gives shape to a specific realm of existence or…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía, “essence, substance”) + ἄρχων (árkhōn, “ruler, leader”).

parole.significato: A star which seems to move in the sky; a planet.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek ἀστὴρ πλανήτης (astḕr planḗtēs) as distinguished from the fixed stars.

parole.significato: A valve with multiple connections that permits bleeding a large line through several subordinate lines.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek κλεψύδρα (klepsúdra, “pipette”, literally “water-thief”), equivalent to water + thief.

parole.significato: Digamma (Ϝ/ϝ).
