parole.significato: Much depends on the beginning of an endeavor.
parole.testo: Traditional, via Ancient Greek; quoted by Aristotle in his Politics.

parole.significato: Possessing very large eyes.
parole.testo: The traditional translation or calque of Ancient Greek Κύκλωψ (Kúklōps), a folk etymology equivalent to wheel + eye, wherein the mythical one-eyed giants, cyclops, had eyes as large as cartwheels.

parole.significato: One who is outwardly attractive, but unclean or vile on the inside; a hypocrite.
parole.testo: An allusion to Matthew 23:27 in the Bible. From Ancient Greek τάφος κεκονιαμένος (táphos kekoniaménos, “plastered tomb, hypocrite”).

parole.significato: Resembling the dark color (or perhaps other properties) of red wine.
parole.testo: The traditional translation/calque of Ancient Greek οἶνοψ (oînops, “with the appearance of wine”), equivalent to wine + dark.

parole.significato: A word or statement which is very apt for an occasion, or memorable.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek ἔπεα πτερόεντα (épea pteróenta), often used by Homer (said to have been born c. 750 B.C.E.), to whom the Iliad and Odyssey are attributed: from ἔπεᾰ (épeă) (plural of ἔπος (épos, “something spoken: song, speech, story”)) + πτερόεντα (pteróenta) (plural of πτερόεις (pteróeis,

parole.significato: Any of several poisonous perennial herbs of the genus Aconitum.

parole.significato: Any crab in the Xanthidae.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A yellowish colouring of pigments in hair, skin, feathers, etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ξανθισμός (xanthismós), by surface analysis, xanth- + -ism.

parole.significato: yellow
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ξᾰνθός (xănthós, “yellow”).

parole.significato: A division of the human population having fair skin and wavy blond hair.
parole.testo: Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley, from Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “fair, yellow, golden, blond”), and either χρώς (khrṓs, “skin”), or ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale”).

parole.significato: A synonym of clintonite. The International Mineralogical Association's Commission on New Minerals, Nomenclature and Cla…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) and φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”), for its color and micaceous appearance, + -ite.

parole.significato: One who guides strangers; a guide or tour guide.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ξεναγωγός (xenagōgós), from ξένος (xénos, “foreigner; guest; stranger”, noun) (possibly ultimately Pre-Greek) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “(adjective) guiding, leading; (noun) escort, guide”) (from ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to bring along, lead”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h

parole.significato: Having unusual joints.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek. See Xenarthra, xen-, and arthro- for more.

parole.significato: Any mammal of the superorder Xenarthra, of the Americas; an anteater, armadillo or sloth.

parole.significato: Synonym of xenelasy (“the practice of expelling foreigners in Doric Crete and Lacedaemonia”).
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek ξενηλᾰσῐ́ᾱ (xenēlăsĭ́ā, “expulsion of foreigners”); see further at xenelasy.

parole.significato: The practice of expelling foreigners in Doric Crete and Lacedaemonia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ξενηλᾰσῐ́ᾱ (xenēlăsĭ́ā, “expulsion of foreigners”) + English -y (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state). Ξενηλᾰσῐ́ᾱ (Xenēlăsĭ́ā) is derived from ξενηλατεῖν (xenēlateîn, “to expel a foreigner”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine

parole.significato: Hospitable, especially to visiting strangers or foreigners.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξενία (xenía, “hospitality; relations of hospitality between states or between a person and a state; the status of an alien, i.e., not a citizen”), equivalent to xenia + -al.

parole.significato: A ritual offering of a meal in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek

parole.significato: Synonym of ronna- (used before an official prefix existed). Symbol: X
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐννέα (ennéa, “nine”), for the ninth order of 10³, and the letter x, as the third term in a series running backwards through the alphabet (after zetta- and yotta-). The final a conforms to the final vowel of the SI series from mega- upwards.

parole.significato: Synonym of ronto- (used before an official prefix existed). Symbol: x
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐννέα (ennéa, “nine”), for the ninth order of 10³; with the letter x added for the third term in a series running backwards through the alphabet (after zepto- and yocto-). The final o conforms to the final vowels of the SI series from micro- downwards.

parole.significato: Having to do with foreigners.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, of a stranger”).

parole.significato: (obsolete) Friendly to strangers.

parole.significato: Reception of strangers; hospitality.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξενοδοχία (xenodokhía), from ξένος (xénos, “alien”) + δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to receive”).

parole.significato: The transfer of pollen from the anthers of one plant to the stigma of another; cross-pollination.

parole.significato: Any organic compound that stimulates the formation of a haustorium.

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol Xe) with an atomic number of 54. It is a colorless, odorless, unreactive noble gas, used n…

parole.significato: One who hates or fears strangers or foreigners.

parole.significato: Exhibiting or characterised by xenophobia, a fear or hatred of strangers, foreigners, or extraterrestial life.
parole.testo: From xeno- + -phobic, from Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, strange”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the language or style of Xenophon.

parole.significato: A yellow-brown mineral, yttrium phosphate (YPO₄)

parole.significato: The univalent radical derived from diphenyl.

parole.significato: Dryness and brittleness of the hair.

parole.significato: dry; arid.

parole.significato: A restrictive diet (of bread and water, for example) as a punishment or religious form of discipline.

parole.significato: A xerograph (copy).

parole.significato: The process of polishing something.

parole.significato: The 14th letter of Classical and Modern Greek. The 15th in Ancient and Old Greek.

parole.significato: Synonym of xiphoid process.

parole.significato: sword; sword-shaped

parole.significato: Shaped like a sword, ensiform.

parole.significato: A wooden statue used as a cult image in Ancient Greece.

parole.significato: wood

parole.significato: A unit of length in Ancient Greece.

parole.significato: That bores or cuts into wood, as with certain insects.

parole.significato: Razor; razorlike.

parole.significato: A surgical instrument used to scrape bones.

parole.significato: A type of long thrusting lance, used in ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ξυστόν (xustón, “spear, javelin”), of unknown origin. Potentially from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰasto- or *ǵʰasdʰo- (“branch ~ spear, sharp spine”) (whence also gad, goad, and yard), but this is likely a substrate word in view of the various irregularities.

parole.significato: A long and open portico within the gymnasium.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξυστός (xustós, “smooth; scraped”), from ξύω (xúō, “scrape”), referring to its polished floor.

parole.significato: Prime matter, consisting of body and soul.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…

parole.significato: Zeal; zealotry.

parole.significato: Relating to Jupiter
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ζηνο- (Zēno-), combining form of Ζεύς (Zeús).

parole.significato: Pertaining to any of various people named Zeno, or to their philosophies.
parole.testo: From Zeno + -ic, with the terminal "n" from Ancient Greek Ζήνων (Zḗnōn).

parole.significato: The philosophy of Zeno of Citium; stoicism.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἑπτᾰ́ (heptắ, “seven”), for the seventh order of 10⁻³. The final o conforms to the finals vowel of the SI series from micro- downwards; the letter z was added, as a start in a series of terms running backwards through the alphabet.

parole.significato: The sixth letter of the modern Greek alphabet (Ζ, ζ) preceded by epsilon (Ε, ε) and followed by eta, (Η, η); or the sev…

parole.significato: Proceeding by inquiry or investigation.

parole.significato: A class of citizens in ancient Athens having property or an estate above a certain value.

parole.significato: A basilosaurus.

parole.significato: The act of using a word, particularly an adjective or verb, to apply to more than one noun when its sense is appropriat…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “yoking; a bond, a band”), from ζεύγνυμι (zeúgnumi, “to yoke; to join”), from ζεῦγος (zeûgos, “a yoke”).

parole.significato: The fear of Zeus.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Ζεύς (Zeús) + -o- + -phobia.

parole.significato: A form of green tourmaline.

parole.significato: The amorphous amylaceous matter contained in the vertebrate and invertebrate foetal tissues.

parole.significato: A pictograph or ideogram that is used as the standard representation of a specific word.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ζῴδιον (zōídion, “little animal”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

parole.significato: One who writes about the description and behavior of animal.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ζῴδιον (zōídion) (diminutive of ζῶον (zôon, “animal”)) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”) + -er.

parole.significato: Bare or universal life.

parole.significato: An optical toy, in which figures made to revolve on the inside of a cylinder, and viewed through slits in its circumfer…

parole.significato: Showing traces of life; containing organic remains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζωϊκός (zōïkós), from ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: nagging or carping criticism
parole.testo: From the works of Zoilus (Ancient Greek: Ζωΐλος (Zōḯlos)), a classical Greek writer who was highly critical of Homer; + -ism.

parole.significato: A critic characterized as bitter, carping, malignant.
parole.testo: From the name of Zoilus, an ancient Greek rhetorician who severely criticized Homer's poems. From Ancient Greek Ζωΐλος (Zōḯlos).

parole.significato: A reverence for animal life or belief in animal powers and influences, as among primitive groups.
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek ζωή (zōḗ, “life”) + -ism.

parole.significato: animal
parole.testo: From (combining form of) Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: The part of biology relating to the animal kingdom, including the structure, embryology, evolution, classification, hab…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + λόγος (lógos, “knowledge”). By surface analysis, zoo- + -logy. Piecewise doublet of biology.

parole.significato: An animal disease, such as rabies or anthrax, that can be transmitted to humans.
parole.testo: From zoo- + (itself from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”)) + Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) (compare also nosology); the surface analysis is almost, although not quite, zoo- + -osis; compare also anthroponosis.

parole.significato: An artificial group comprising various carnivorous and insectivorous animals.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”)

parole.significato: premature burial
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ζωός (zōós, “alive”) and θάπτω (tháptō, “bury”).

parole.significato: A number of coral polyps on a branch of coral.
parole.testo: From (combining form of) Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) and Ancient Greek θωμός (thōmós, “heap”).

parole.significato: relating to animals or obtained from animal substances
parole.testo: From zoo- + -otic. From Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: Any of the yellow pigmentary particles, or minute corpuscles of yellow coloring matter, found in certain radiolarians.
parole.testo: From (deprecated) genus name Zooxanthella, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + -ella.

parole.significato: In ancient Rome, a small living room, as distinguished from a room for sleeping: an alcove.

parole.significato: union
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”)

parole.significato: One of the articular processes of a vertebra, of which there are usually four, two superior and two inferior.

parole.significato: Any of a set of signs used in early musical notation.
parole.testo: From 15th c. Middle English newme, nevme, neme; from Middle French neume, in turn from Medieval Latin neuma or pneuma, either from Ancient Greek νεῦμα (neûma, “sign”), or else a corruption of πνεῦμα (pneûma, “breath”). In the latter case a doublet of pneuma.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a numen (divinity); indicating the presence of a divinity.
parole.testo: From Latin nūmen (“nod of the head; divine sway or will; divinity”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting possession or presence of a quality). parole.significato: eight
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) and Latin octō (“eight”).

parole.testo: From the plural forms Olimpiades, Olympiades, and Olympiadiz of Middle English Olimpias and Olympias (“ancient Olympic Games, 4-year period between these games, intense battle or competition”) from Middle French Olympiade and Old French Olympiade (“ancient Olympic games, 4-year period between these

parole.significato: A yellow-brown, addictive narcotic drug obtained from the dried juice of unripe pods of the opium poppy, Papaver somnif…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin opium and Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion), from ὀπός (opós, “juice of a plant”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷós (“juice, resin”).

parole.significato: A method of representing a language or the sounds of language by written symbols; spelling.

parole.significato: A chant or song, especially a hymn of thanksgiving for deliverance or victory, to Apollo or sometimes another god or go…
parole.testo: From Latin paeān (“a hymn, especially a victory hymn, to Apollo or another god”), from Ancient Greek παιᾱ́ν (paiā́n, “a chant or song, especially a thanksgiving or victory hymn, to Apollo under the name Παιᾱ́ν (Paiā́n)”), from the phrase Ἰὼ Παιᾱ́ν (Iṑ Paiā́n, “O Paean!, Thanks to Paean!”). parole.significato: A paten (a flat type of dish).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian patina, from Latin patina (“dish, pan”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē), either from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread”) or from Pre-Greek. Doublet of paten, patena, patine, and (possibly) pan.

parole.significato: pederasty
parole.testo: Probably either the post-Classical Latin paederastia or its etymon, the Ancient Greek παιδερᾰστίᾱ (paiderăstíā), suffixed with the English -ice (suffix forming abstract nouns). Compare pederasty.

parole.significato: Alternative form of pelta.
parole.testo: A variant of pelta, borrowed from Latin pelta, from Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē, “small crescent-shaped leather shield of Thracian design”); further etymology uncertain, perhaps either from Thracian, or ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover; to wrap; hide; skin; cloth”).

parole.significato: The thorax of a crustacean, between the head (cephalon) and abdomen (pleon).
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek περαιόω (peraióō, “to transport”), so called from the location of the legs on the thorax. Alternatively, from περί (perí, “around”) + ἰέναι (iénai, “to go”).

parole.significato: A disciple of Aristotle.
parole.testo: From Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περίπατος (perípatos, “strolling, covered walk, conversation while walking”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) + πατέω (patéō, “to walk”). parole.significato: To cause (something) to be physically disordered or disturbed; to cause confusion.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English perturben (“to disturb (someone) mentally, disquiet; to cause disorder to (something), confuse; to hinder (something)”), from Old French perturber, and from its etymon Latin perturbāre, the present active infinitive of perturbō (“to confuse; to alarm, disturb, trouble, pertu

parole.significato: A popular 18th- and 19th-century form of theater entertainment whereby ghostly apparitions are formed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French phantasmagorie, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “ghost”) + possibly either ἀγορά (agorá, “assembly, gathering”) + the suffix -ia or ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to speak publicly”).

parole.significato: A wide-mouthed, deep vessel for holding liquids, with a spout or protruding lip and a handle; a water jug or jar with a…
parole.testo: From Middle English picher, from Old French pichier, pechier (“small jug”), bichier (compare modern French pichet), from Late Latin or Medieval Latin pīcārium, alteration of bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, bacar or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Doublet of beaker.

parole.significato: The abdomen of a crustacean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek πλέων (pléōn), present participle of πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”); from the fact that it bears the swimming limbs. Alternatively, perhaps in the sense of being longer or extended.

parole.significato: A person who possesses, or appears to possess, extrasensory abilities such as clairvoyance, precognition and telepathy,…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós, “relative to the soul, spirit, mind”). Earlier referred to as "psychical"; or from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, mind, psyche”). First appeared (as substantive) 1871 and first records 1895.

parole.significato: Of a purple colour.
parole.testo: From Latin purpureus (“purple, violet; brown, reddish; clothed in purple; (figurative) brilliant, shining; beautiful”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). parole.significato: To build up or be arranged in the form of a pyramid.
parole.testo: From French pyramide, from Old French piramide, from Latin pȳramis, pȳramidis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís), possibly from πῡρός (pūrós, “wheat”) + ἀμάω (amáō, “reap”) or from Egyptian pr-m-ws (“height of a pyramid”), from pr (“(one that) comes forth”) + m (“from”) + ws (“height”). parole.significato: Rhyming verse (poetic form).
parole.testo: From Middle English rim, rime, ryme (“identical letters or sounds in words from the vowel in their stressed syllables to their ends; measure, meter, rhythm; song, verse, etc., with rhyming lines”), from Anglo-Norman rime, ryme (“identical letters or sounds in words from the vowel in their stressed s

parole.significato: The probability of a negative outcome to a decision or event.
parole.testo: From earlier risque, from Middle French risque, from Old Italian risco (“risk”) (modern Italian rischio) and rischiare (“to run into danger”). parole.testo: From Old French roffle, rouffle (earlier romfle, ronfle), or from Italian ronfa (“card game similar to whist”); these words are possibly from Old French triomphe (“a triumph, victory”), Italian trionfo (“triumph; trump card”), from Latin triumphus (“hymn to Bacchus; celebration, triumph”), ultimatel

parole.significato: The fear of rubbish or dirt.
parole.testo: Possibly from Ancient Greek ῥύπος (rhúpos, “filth”) + -phobia (See rhypophobia). Alternatively, related to Latin rupes (“cliff, rock”).

parole.significato: A large triangular bone at the base of the spine, located between the two ilia (wings of the pelvis) and formed from ve…
parole.testo: From Latin os sacrum (“holy bone”), a calque of Ancient Greek ἱερὸν ὀστέον (hieròn ostéon). Apparently so called either because the sacrum was the part of the animal offered in sacrifice or because of a putative belief that it is where a person's soul resides. parole.significato: A type of malignant tumor of the bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, blood vessels, or other connective or supportive tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin sarcoma, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + -ωμα (-ōma, “process”) or from Ancient Greek σαρκόω (sarkóō), itself from σάρξ (sárx); by surface analysis, sarc- + -oma.

parole.significato: Scornfully mocking or cynical.
parole.testo: From French sardonique, from Latin sardonius, from Ancient Greek σαρδόνιος (sardónios), alternative form of σαρδάνιος (sardánios, “bitter or scornful laughter”), which is often cited as deriving from the Sardinian plant (Ranunculus sardous or possibly Oenanthe crocata), known as either σαρδάνη (sard

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Sciaenidae, a family of marine fishes.
parole.testo: Latin sciaena (“a kind of sea fish, perhaps a kind of grayling or ombre: Thymallus thymallus”), from Ancient Greek σκίαινα (skíaina, “a sea fish, probably either Sciaena umbra or Umbrina cirrosa”), + -oid.

parole.significato: A widespread brown mineral, FeCO₃, having the structure of calcite.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σιδηρίτης (sidērítēs, “made of iron”), from Ancient Greek σίδηρος (sídēros, “iron”), or from Latin sideritis (“lodestone”), from Ancient Greek σιδηρῖτις (sidērîtis, “loadstone”). By surface analysis, sider- + -ite.

parole.significato: A secluded religious community in Eastern Orthodox Christianity which is a dependency of, and generally less physically…
parole.testo: From ecclesiastical (medieval) Ancient Greek σκήτη (skḗtē), which is either from a place name in Egypt Σκήτις, Coptic Ϣⲓϩⲏⲧ (Šihēt), or via aphesis from ἀσκητής (askētḗs, “ascetic; monk, hermit”).

parole.significato: A medieval East Slavic actor or harlequin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian скоморох (skomorox), from Old East Slavic скоморохъ (skomoroxŭ), of unknown origin. Possibly from Ancient Greek σκώμμαρχος (skṓmmarkhos, “joke leader”) (σκῶμμα (skômma)+ἀρχός (arkhós)) or from Italian scaramuccia.

parole.significato: Of animal behaviour: deterministic, preprogrammed.

parole.significato: A creature with the head of a person and the body of an animal, commonly a lion.
parole.testo: From Sphinx, from Middle English Spynx, from Latin Sphinx, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx), perhaps either from σφίγγω (sphíngō, “to squeeze, to strangle”) (whence also sphincter), of Pre-Greek origin, or from Egyptian Szp:p-A53-anx-n:x (šzp-ꜥnḫ, “divine image”, literally “living image”).

parole.significato: At the same time, at the same frequency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin synchronus, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos, “contemporaneous”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “with, together”) + χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). parole.significato: lustfulness
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τράγος (trágos, “goat”) + -ism. Alternatively, OED indicates an adaptation from Spanish tragalismo, of the same Ancient Greek origin.

parole.significato: Composed of or relating to trochees, feet of one stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable.
parole.testo: Either via the French trochaïque or directly from its etymon, the Latin trochaicus, from the Ancient Greek τροχαικός (trokhaikós), from τροχαῖος (trokhaîos), whence trochee.

parole.significato: An evaporite, consisting of mixture of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, Na₃HCO₃CO₃·2H₂O.
parole.testo: From Swedish trona or from Spanish trona, both derived from Arabic أَطْرُون (ʔaṭrūn), from نَطْرُون (naṭrūn), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron), ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj: R9. Doublet of natron and niter.

parole.significato: A mythical, horselike creature with a horn on its forehead, supposed to be extremely rare and to be drawn to virgins an…
parole.testo: From Middle English unicorne, unikorn, from Anglo-Norman unicorne, Old French unicorne, and their source, Latin ūnicornis, (from ūnus (“one”) + cornū (“horn”)), a calque of Ancient Greek μονόκερως (monókerōs, “having one horn”, (from μόνος (mónos, “one”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”))). parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: Coined with Latin septem (“seven”) and Ancient Greek ἑπτᾰ́ (heptắ, “seven”) in mind, for the seventh order of 10³. The consonants pt are reduced to tt; the initial z was chosen instead of s to avoid confusion with s (“second”, symbol)
